months ago, the notion had to be given up, as it became far too popular to suit exclusive tastes, but the craze died out, and now leading lights in the millinery and dressmaking worlds, have taken it up again. Many brides this winter have selected white or cream cloth for their going away gowns, and these have invari- ably been touched with gold. Princess Alexander of Teck's travelling gown it will be remembered, was of white cloth trimmed with touches of gold braid, softened by means of white lace over white chiffon. Gold embroidery, gold braid,and gold ornaments,appear on muoh or the new spring milinery, but this all needs to be sparingly used, and delicately softened, or the effect is hard and vulgar. Gold and silver tissues promise to play a considerable part in the " Court" schemes again this year, but these again are almost all softened with draperies of chiffon and lace. The Bridal Hat.—At several of the Society weddings that have taken place this year, the bride and her " maids " have, with regard to headgear, changed places. The former has appeared in a hat, tho latter in veils. Whether the bride in a hat has come to stay remains to be seen, but there is no doubt about a hat being much more becoming than the heavy lace veil under which some brides have been crushed and flattened, and gener- ally mtttle unlovely.' But the same charges cannot be raised against the tulle veil, and it is doubtful whether the most delightful picture hat ever created could rival the charms of a simple square' of tulle, skilfully arranged. Long Earrings.—The long earring has apparently come to stay, and the only difference between the pre- sent day and old-world varieties is, that we are dis- pensing with much of the weight our great grand- mothers thought so desirable. Baron de Forest presented his bride with a pair of long priceless pearl specimens, which the baroness continually wears. Lady Leucea Warner is another Society woman who prefers the long earring to the one time favourite solitaire, and Lady Lansdowne is frequently to be seen wearing long ear- rings of delicate filigree goldwork, studded with dia- monds and coloured stones. Undoubtedly the exces- sively sloping shoulder has had much to do with tile revival of the long earring. We seem now to stand in need of the finishing touch these ornaments most cer- tainly afford. RHUBARB AND ORANGE JAM.—Few people seem to know anything about this delicious preserve, which is both inexpensive and easy of manufacture. Take six oranges, remove the skin, white pith, and pips, and slice the pulp into a preservin,, pan. Next add half the peel shredded, Ills. of crushed loaf sugar, and a quart of finely cut rhubarb. Stir all well, and boil one hour, removing the scum as it rises. MADGE.

div.head: CHILDHOOD'S BEST FRIEND.
div.p: CHILDHOOD'S BEST FRIEND.

Mr. George Allen, 83, The Street, Neatishead, Norwich, Norfolk, tells a touching story how his little girl was restored to health after a long period of serious illness: "In the beginning of 1901," says Mr. Allen, "when my little girl was two years old, she was taken ill. The doctors said she was sufferinc, from Inflammation of the Kidneys. She was very ill and complained of pains In her back and loins. cramps in her limbs, sleep broken and fitful, dark circles around her eyes and shortness of breath. Under the doctor's treatment she seemed to get a little better, but the following year she was again taken ill, and this time worse than before." ' "We were greatly disappointed and did not know what to do until we read of some wonderful cures which Dodd's Kidney Pills had done for others. After using one box, our little girl showed wonderful signs of improvement, so we continued the treatment and she improved day by clay until she was cured. Now, I am thankful to say our dear little girl is well, strong and happy, and the picture of good health. I consider Dodd's Kidney Pills saved my child's life.'
SEVENTY-ONE FEWER LIVERPOOL LICENCES.

The Liverpool licensing justices have made a pretty clean swoop of one district. The annual Licensing Sessions concluded on Tuesday, having occupied eight days. At the opening of the sessions there were 1,749 full licences within the city area. Of these 36 were refused renewal,and for eight no application was made, making 44 extinguished and reducing the total to 1,705. Beerhouses numbered 368, of which 18 were refused renewal, and there was no application for three. 01 the off-beer licences one was refused, and there was no application for five, making 27 struck off and reducing the total to 341. The total of all classes of licences extinguished is 71.

FAILURES IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—Ascording to "Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, Feb. 26th, was 197, viz. :—New Bank- ruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 106 ; deeds of arrangement registered, 91. The res- pective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 88 ; deeds of arrangement, 77 total 165; being a net increase in bankruptcies of 54, and a net increase in deeds of arrangement in 1904, to date, of 92.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Courts.—The presentations at Court this season' will include an unusual number of newly married women. Amongst them will be the Duchess of Norfolk, the Duchess of Rosburghe, the Countess of Kerry, Lady Herbert, Lady Helmsley, and many others who might be mentioned. There will also be a full compliment of young Society girLs, who will appear this spring as d6butantses. So many in fact desire invitations, or pre- sentations) that the Lord Chamberlain finds it very diffi- cult to make arrangements for them at the limited number of Courts to be held before and after Easter. There are, however, some special presentations made to her Majesty apart from the King, and this to some extent relieves the pressure th attend the Courts. The Princess's Anxiety----The Princess of Wales has been greatly concerned about the accident to a young cyclist, who was run over by her carriage, in which her Royal Highness and the Countess of Airlie were driv- ing. Both wheels passed right over the youth, but fortunately no bones were broken, and though bruised and shaken, he does not seem likely to suffer any per- manent injury from the mishap. The Princess stopped the carriage at once,whilst the Countess made inquiries about the youth—a working mechanic—and who was taken to the hospital. His bicycle was not only broken, but promptly stolen amidst the confusion, but this probably need not trouble him as, whoever may have been in fault, there is little doubt that he will get a new machine, which he will be able to prize more than the old one. Women's Emancipation—lt has been seriously sug- gested that the women of this country should subscribe in pennies for a statue of the modern ladies' bicycle, as the emblem of woman's emancipation. The cult of the wheel, more than anything else, is responsible for the great change that has taken place in the social 'position of women, and it is urged that this should be recognised by some suitable monument. It was the bicycle that first gave woman her freedom, and that greater vigour of mind and body which has enabled her to enter into all the pleasures and activities of life. There are still some old fashioned people who hold up their hands in horror at many things which women do, but there are not many who would have us go back to the days when girls could hardly go out without attendance, and the graceful art of fainting was considered one of the most necessary feminine accomplishments. There is little doubt that the organization of a woman's memorial to the era of emancipation would bo a success if put forward in any suitable form. Petticoats in the Pulpit.—Like Alexander women are constantly sighing for new worlds to conquer, and the appointment of Miss Putzold as pastor of the Unitarian Free Church, Jueicester, marks a fresh step in opening the pulpit door to them. The Quakers are of all sects the most favorably disposed towards lady ministers, but even they have not yet adopted regularly appointed women pastors, though in America and in Australia "clergy women" are so numerous that they attract no special attention. For a long time the princi- pal Unitarian Church of Melbourne was presided over by a lady minister who drew large congregations as it seems. Miss Putzold is doing at Leicester. In the United States there is scarcely a sect that does not boast its women pastors and no fewer than 1235 were returned as such at the last census. Irrational Still.—The Rational Dress League still drags out a melancholy kind of existence, but at the last gathering, it was forced to admit that the public had been so hostile to its views, that the movarnent was a failure. Even here,under the League's own roof, out of 26 women present, only four had the courage to discard the conventional skirt. But besides long skirts, there is a lengthy list of feminine and fashionable follies against which the League inveighs, such as tight lacing, tight fitting bodices, tight collars, tight garters, high heels;pointed toes,and so on. In spite however of everythins woman remains irrational still, and seems even going back to the old vicious practice o f tight lacing. Opinions differ, as to who make the fashions, and where they come from, but the theatres have a good data to do with them, and on the stage, there is a decided return to the small waist. Japanese Fabrics.—One effect of the war has been to greatly increase the demand for Japanese silk and Japanese crêpe de chine. No doubt some of the rush to secure these delightful fabrics. is 'due to our warm hearted interest in the plucky little islanders, but it must be confessed that the fear of a possible increase in price for all such goods, has something to do with the eagerness shewn to buy up as much Japanese silk and crepe de chine as possible. The latest idea is to subject both these materials to a process of the finest accordion pleating, when the effect is exceedingly beautiful. They are being greatly used for blouses, tea —or to use their new name "resting" gowns, coffee coats, and entire evening toilettes. The circular yoke is still in favour for blouses, and collars are no longer dispensed with. They may be transparent, or semi- transparent, but they must be there. Silk blonde lace looks exceedingly well on the accordian pleated Japanese silk;or crepe de chino blouse, but Irish lace— especially the Limerick variety—runs this very close in our affection. Touches of !Gold. Both dressmakers and milliners are again touching their creations with gold. Some

div.head: Examiner Saturday, March 5 1904.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, March 5 1904.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

The weather so far has not been at all con. ducive to the production of any novelties, and indeed the modes have not shown any signs of immediate development, but it is early yet and we must wait patiently for a week or two Longer. There is, however, nothing to grum- ble at for the fashions this season are par- ticularly charming, albeit that there is a ten- dency to err on the side of over elaboration. Still, the result is generally satisfactory if the cost is somewhat greater than in the days when simplicity reigned supreme. If the ac- tual modes are still to be evolved there are ; some new materials on view which are most g attractive. These are beautifully soft and supple and drape and hang well in graceful folds. The open meshed canvases with here and there a faint pattern interwoven are not essentially different from those with which we became familiar some months ago but are in every way a distinct improvement on their predecessors. These make up charmingly over a silk foundation. Another variety of canvas will be much in vogue when the wea- ther brightens. This is so woven as to look exactly like a coarse point lace and is twine- coloured, and when worn over a glistening thine silk or a gleaming satin looks very

ONABLE BAT. charming. An old evening gown will %Olen cleaned come in usefully as a lining with Kr overdress of this style. The fashionable hat depicted in my first sketch is draped with a lace embroidered veil, with the inevitable curtain at the back. The shape is the new and fashionable elongated toque which is either worn with the brim depressed over the face or tilted backwards. There is a delightful absence of exaggeration in the present day headgear which does credit to the good taste and common sense of the leaders of the modes. The enormous hats which we are all familiar with are now not con- sidered in good taste as they have the effect of increasing the size of the head and making it look out of proportion to the rest of • the body. Every woman is, however, at liberty to wear just the style of headgear which suits her best without contravening the ordinances of fashion. The Marquise hat shows no sign of waning in popularity, and is seen at its best in the early model fine straws and chips trim- med with the most lovely pompadour wreaths of tiny roses and other small flowers, such as daisies and forget-me-nots. The Watteau

AT BLOUSE. hat has arisen from the ashes of the plateau hat and is certainly less trying to the majority of faces with its upturned brim softened by a draped lace veil. Floral toques will shortly be much en evidence as they but wait the first bright day to make their debut. Meantime some very smart cloth toques are worn simply made with perhaps a little bunch of violets nestling in the folds. The neat blouse depicted is of accor dion- pleated silk with the deep-shaped yoke of lace intersected by: narrow bands of silk embroi- dery. The style is a simple one but very smart and up-to-date. A blouse I recently admired was made of soft pleated black crepe de chine, with a deep yoke of sparkling jet softened by chenille, which is a particularly successful combination as the latter trimming does away with the metallic severity of the i jet, which s somewhat apt to be unbecoming unless thus treated. Polished jet and sequins are always dressy looking and show off a good complexion as nothing else does. There is a charming shade of pink which is much used at present for the formation of evening blouses,

div.head: SMART COAT.
div.p: A SMART COAT.

and even whole gowns, which, while it does not suit all complexions by reason of its vividness, is extremely becoming to those who can stand it. Another fashionable colour is a delicate shade of primrose which proves most fascinating when worn by a dark-haired girl. The smart coat depicted is suited to a girl of ten to twelve years of age. It is nrade of smooth-surfaced grey cloth with bands of white cloth stitched round the collar and loose cuffed sleeves. Grey metal buttons fasten the front and a grey felt hat trimmed with white ostrich feathers completes an exceedingly charming spring outfit. White cloth, of course, looks even more dressy, but in our -limate, and especially in or near a town, the smuts and dirt soon take the look of a pale toned material. Nothing is, of course, pret- tier than white for a young girl but at the same time nothing is so objectionable as the toilette worn when same soiled. That is why I recommend grey or even fawn as these colours do not soil so readily and are sufficiently light, looking for wear during the next six months.l There are really no very distinct modes fori children at present except it be that the 1 French frocks with a sash tied low down like a I boy's but in a smart bow at the back are worn' in the house by girls of four and five, while the loose frock which depends from a yoke is ever fashionable and ever becoming to thA juvenile figure when its angles are apt to become un- pleasantly noticeable and require careful con- tealment

div.head: PICAROON.
div.p: THE PICAROON.
By HERBERT RUSSELL,
Author of "True Blue," "Elmira," "The Long- shoreman," "The Mystery of Whitelady Island," "The Burning Sea, &c.

In the year 1843 I was serving as a midshipman on board H.M. schooner, Wave, then in com- mission upon the West Indian station. Half a century has wrought marvels: nowhere greater than in the sea life; but the transformation has been achieved at the expense of effectually driving all the romance out of the deep. • When I roll my mental vision inwards and gaze down the long, shadowy galleries of memory at the dim phantoms which graced the ocean in my youth, my pulse is quickened by those associations of the past, to which the sea-writer of to-day still has to turn for inspiration and for interest. I know that steam is a fine thing, and I know that it is a great con- venience to be borne, with railway precision, to the ends of the earth in a floatipg hotel; but your old shellback is the most conservative creature in the world; and whilst he is quite capable of appre- ciating utility, you may forgive his sigh for the departed glamour of his calling. But if I am going to spin my yarn I must belay kinking the strands of it in this fashion ere I get them into a tangle. The Wave was one of the loveliest and swiftest models that was ever wafted by wide-spread pinions of canvas across the Antillean sea. She had originally been built as a Cuban slaver • was captured in the Middle Passage by a British frigate, which succeeded in winging her just as she was drawing out of range; and being carried to Jamaica, was condemned. At that period the edict commanding slavers captured by our men-of-war to be sawn in halves, was not in force, so the Sabrina, as she was then named, was purchased into the Royal Navy, to aid in the suppression of the traffic in which she had taken so notorious a part. Her ordnance consisted of a long twenty-four pounder, mounted on a traversing carriage forward, and five brass carronades of a side, with an extremely• useful swivel on each quarter. Eighty-seven heartie3 swung their ham- mocks in the 'tween-decks, where the slaves' quarters had formerly been, and found not any too much room in a space that had been intended to contain one thousand crouching, manacled blacks. Our commander, Lieutenant Lavrock, was a typical British Naval officer of fifty years ago; a stumpy, squarely-built, thick-necked man, with a face of the complexion of underdone beef, and about as resolute and intrepid a seaman as ever reverenced the name of Nelson and swore by the honour of his flag. Tom Cringle blew the type well. We had been out from Port Royal about ten days, having sailed with instructions to go down to leeward in quest of a piratical felucca, named the Elmira, _which was known to be playing havoc among the merchantmen, and had, on plenty of occasions, given her heels to a rather heavy corvette which, for mere decency of appearances rather than for the remotest chance she had, gave chase to the nimble ocean thief. . In the 'forties piracy was still very rife in West Indian waters, and the traditions of the Tortugas and the Cuba Main were yet a living reality. The Elmira had last been heard of off Savanah-la-mar, where she boarded a French barque, took everything of value out of her, secured the crew under hatches, and sent her adirft with square yards and half-a-dozen auger holes in her bilge. She was happily fallen in with by the corvette I have before spoken of, and two hours after her imprisoned occupants had been rescued she sank. This little incident was a clue to the calibre of the gentry with whom we had to deal.

_ We got under way in the early morning from an anchorage where we had brought up for the night, and a fine sailing breeze carried us well to leeward ere it died out with the setting of the sun. It fell a sultry, stirless evening, the blue shadow of the high Jamaica land hovering in the violet air leagues away over our starboard quarter, and the ocean stretching in a burnished surface to the hazy horizon, streaked here and there with long, creep- ing swaithes of subtly stealing current. The sun went down to the western sea-line, rayless and magnified to huge proportions, palpitating like a living heart in the smoky mists which his own heat drew. up, and dipped to his resting-place without casting a glimmer of reflective glow on the violet water that brimmed to the lower limb of his crimson circle. Our schooner lay motionless in the midst of the great hush which fell with the dying of the day, her white canvas seeming to quiver in the invisible steam swimming round about her spars, and the shape of her hull mirrored beneath her symmetric bends as faithfully as though she was set in a vast sheet of glass. Saving the dim and distant streak of the coast, nothing broke the continuity of the Bea circle. The sun vanished, and simultaneously our ensign dropped from the peak. Twilight lingers but briefly in these parallels, and very soon the sea had turned of an ebony hue, with a clear heaven of indigo overhead, glimmering with myriads of stars. It was, indeed, a marvellously fine tropical night, but whew, how hot! This calm was not to prove of long duration, however. Before eight bells had chimed out the end of the dog-watch a soft breeze from the north-east was keeping the pallid shapes of the sails silent and swelling, and raising a pleasant fountain-like murmur of passing foam bells. It was just the weather for a slaver, con- structed to hold her own in shy winds; and when I went below to turn-in the Wave was slipping through it at the rate of some seven knots in the hour, with promise of doing better yet in the gradually increasing slope of her hull. I came on deck again at four o'clock in the morning, and found that the breeze had been lying away for an hour previously, and it was nearly a stark calm again. A narrow horn of moon floated iow down upon its back, like a silver gondola, over the port-quarter. When I stepped on to the quarter-deck I found Lieutenant Lavrock there, in conversation with the officer of the watch, and as I came within earshot I heard the latter exclaim:

"It certainly looks like a vessel on fire, sir." Both of them were staring earnestly ahead, and following the direction of their eyes—which I could perceive plainly enough in the sheen coming from the binnacle lamp-1 beheld a glimmering sort of light, dead on end with our jibboom, but whether one mile or ten distant I could not have told, so illusive it was. We were running nearly right before the wind, which, of course, still further diminished the weight of it, and our speed at this time could not have exceeded four knots.

"I think it must be nearer to us than you fancy," I heard the Lieutenant say. "The light has grown a deal brighter within the last ten minutes." Just then a voice from the forecastle came floating along in subdued tones, calling to the lap.rter-deck. "Hallo 1" answered the Commander. "There's somebody hailing us, sir." . "nailing us! Where away? I hear nothing." "1 can't properly tell, your honour, but the sound seems to come right off the water over the bows." _ _ _

"Ha! the plot thickens. A man hailing us I Heard you anything, Mr. Richards?" "Nothing, sir." "Harkee, then, for a moment or two." He had scarcely fallen into a listening posture when I plainly caught the sound of a faint, reedy hullo, coming from Heaven alone knew where off the black Water. The cry had a weird, unearthly effect to my fancy, sounding as it did from out of the mystery of the night. "There, sir!" exclaimed Richards. "I heard it," replied Lieutenant Lavrock. "Fok'sle there Reep a bright look-out, and report if you see anything like a boat. Get a deck-lantern lighted, and hitch it a hank or two up the forestay." This was done, and the large. globular lamp cast a bright glow over the fore-part of the schooner. Several times during the next few minutes was the hail repeated, growing louder and more distinct, which proved we were approaching the spot whence it came. The light ahead also continued to brighten and enlarge. It wavered and flickered, after the manner of flames heavily obscured by smoke, and I made no doubt that it was a burning vessel. Then the mysterious hailing voice fell silent for a long time, and I was beginning to fancy that we should hear no more of it, till on a sudden it sounded again with startling distinctness right under our bows: "Ship ahoy! For Heaven's sake pick me up!" "Pipe away the gig's crew," exclaimed Lieutenant Lavrock, with as much sang froid as though incidents of this nature were the merest common- places of sea routine. The boatswain's whistle chirruped, and with the alacrity of British blue- jackets the boat that hung at davits over the taffrail was manned and waterborne. The schooner's helm was put down, and she came up into the wind, her canvas rippling in ghostly folds. Presently the gig returned, floating shadowily under the counter; oars were tossed, fall-blocks hoOked on, and up she came to the davits agailk•
"Have you got the man ? " inquired Lieutenant Lavrock.

div.head: JAP PHILANTHROPIC.
div.p: THE JAP PHILANTHROPIC.

Seldom has more intense patriotism been exhibited than is being shown by the Japanese in their national crisis, and from the highest to the lowest each is doing his little bit towards the great whole. Indeed, the national enthusiasm is very remarkable, and is a great contrast to the state of lethargy and discontent in Russia. All the various funds are being supported with the utmost gene- rosity, and the first war loan of a hundred mil- lion yen has been subscribed no less than four times over. In addition, very many voluntary contributions of money and treasure are being made to supply the

sinews- of war. It has for cen- turies been a custom in Japan for the great houses to collect jewels and treasures and lay them aside, not so much in view of their own needs or those of their descendants, but n case of, any national necessity or emer- gency of their country. These they are now producing with lavish hands, and it is at present really impossible to estimate the value of these offerings, many of which are almost priceless. This is the great gift of the nobles, the old aristocracy, and they are being well backed up by people. of lesser degree. For instance, Mr. O'Kura, the well- known merchant prince, has made an unique offer. Having no family reserve fund of generations, he proposes to give up the pro- ceeds of his life's hobby. This, for the last thirty years and more, has been the collec- tion of Japanese and Chinese art treasures and objets d'art, until he has now a perfectly unique museum which cannot be priced. All of this he is willing to give up to his country in a splendid spirit of unselfish Patriotism.

div.head: WONDERFUL MUSICIAN.
div.p: A WONDERFUL MUSICIAN.

We live essentially in an era of excellent muficians, all highly trained and thoroughly ca‘pable. but for their own success and recog- nition there are too many of them. In fact, there are hundreds of brilliant young musi- cians who spend many years of their lives and no inconsi- derable amount of money upon training them- selves for thi delightful pro- fession, dream- ing dreams all the while of success and fame. But many are called, and few are chosen. The majority, if they are lucky, appear at one or two concerts of minor account, applauded and comp limented and then dis- appear into ob- livion. They are good without being great, and FRITZ KREISLER the musical world is overstocked. On the other hand, occasionally a musician of extra- ordinary power, possibly a genius, comes along and takes the world by storm. A Patti. a Paderewski, a Kubelik, is found, and music lovers bow down and worship them. But to succeed in this way the musician has to have ability far out of the common. Last week a young violinist made one of these instantaneous successes, and more will be heard of him in the near future, if con- noisseurs are not mistaken. This is Mr. Fritz Kreisler, who comes from Hungary. He played at the Queen's Hall last week, and was recalled time after time with the utmost enthusiasm by a large audience,

div.head: "THE BOAT THAT WON'T COME OUT."
div.p: "THE BOAT THAT WON'T COME OUT."

The Russian gunboat Mandjour, now popularly known as "the boat that won't come out," from the fact that in spite of the entreaties of China, which desires to observe strict neutrality, she will not leave the port of Shanghai, where she has been since the commencement of hostilities has become a non-combatant. Her com- mander, supported by Russian officials at Shanghai, has agreed to her complete dis- armament. She will remain in the harbour at Shanghai until the conclusion of hostilities. The only alternative to this action was immediate capture by the swift Japanese cruiser Akitsushima. All sorts of disconcert- ing rumours have been afloat in connection

div.head: MANDJOUR.
div.p: THE MANDJOUR.

with this incident. At one time it was officially stated that M. de Lessar, Russian Minister at Peking, had threatened Li-en-fang vice-president of Wiwupu, the Chinese Foreign Office, with the driest consequences should , China insist upon /the Mandjour leaving. M. de Lessar maintains that the presenceZof the gunboat is necessary for the protection of the Russian Consulate. The matter then passed out of the control of the Shanghai officials, and was dealt with by M. Uchida, Japanese Minister at Peking, and Prince Ching, .the Chinese Grand Secretary.

div.head: NEW MEMBER FOR SOUTH BIRMINGHAM.
div.p: NEW MEMBER FOR SOUTH BIRMINGHAM.

Though it had been generally believed that the Sonth Birmingham s election would result in the Unionists retaining the seat, the con- test was conducted with much liveliness, and the actual election was accompanied by con- siderable excitement. There was a heavy, continuous fall of snow during the day, which interfered great- ly with the -operations. The figures of the polling were as follows : Mor- peth (U), 5,299; Hollowell (L), 2,223 ; Union- ist majority, 3076. At the last General• Elec- tion, and also at a by - election in 1895, Mr. Powell - Wil- liams was re- turned unop- posed. At the General Elec-
tion of 1895 the

Unionist ma- ority was 3,573. Lord Morpeth, the new member, has been so recently before the electors that it is only necessary now to repeat that he is the eldest son of the Earl of Carlisle, and a grandson of the second Lord Stanley of Alderley. He will attain his thirty-seventh year next month. After education at Rugby and Oxford, he was for some time a University Extension Lecturer, and acted as assistant - secretary during the sittings of the Royal Commission on the Aged Poor. He was a member of the London School Board for between seven and eight years in the Progressive interest, and as such was an advocate of a liberal educa- tion for the poor. J..,;k7d. Mon,- n;6 married

to the' daughter of Colonel Paget W. LIS& trange, and has been much. assisted in his political work by Lady Morpeth. It will be remembered that last month he contested Gateshead as a Tariff Reformer, and pre- viously to that he had been an unsuccessful candidate for' Chester-le-Street in 1895, and Hexham in 1900. His opponent, Mr. J. Hirst Hollowell, who was brought out by the Liberals as the champion of Free Trade and the amendment of the Education Acts, is fifty-three years of age. He was formerly a Congregational minister, but for the last eight years has been secretary of the Nor- thern Counties Education League.

div.head: MAIDSTONE TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE MAIDSTONE TRAGEDY.

The mystery surrounding the muader at Maidstone of Mrs Tootell, the wife of a well- known local surveyor, and her two daughters would have remained such had it not been dispersed by the discovery of the dead body of the husband, who disappeared immeniate- ly after the tragedy. After a seacrh which lasted all day, the corpse was found in the river Medway just below the high level bridge, and about five minutes' walk from Mr. Tootell's house. Another light was thrown on the crime by the following letter in Mr. Tootell's handwriting, and contained in a blood-stained envelope, which he left be- hind him in the house : "My dear sister,—l have made a great mistake. Take care of Rene (this is the name of the surviving daughter, who 's at a Folkestone boarding school) and let Bill (a brother who resides in London) settle matters. My mind is gone.

MR. TOOTELL AHD THE VILLA WHERE THE TRAGEDY WAS ENACTED. I don't know what will happen.—Charles. As to the motive of the murder nothing has transpired to suggest any other conclusion than that the husband was seized with a sudden fit of madness. The previous night he was happy with his family, there was nothing, strange in his demeanour,, and he appeared to be enjoying the singing which took place in the drawing-room. The scene in the bedrooms the following morning indicated that he had killed his victims with great deliberation. , A separate razor was used on each victim and every one of them was. broken. His wife, to whom he was much attached, was slain in her sleep. So was one of the •daughters, but the other seems to have made a desperate struggle, for her hands were seriously cut. It is thought that after the murder Mr. Tootell returned to his wife's bedroom, and placed his blood- stained dressing-gown on the bed, wiped his hands on the towel, dressed himself, drank some gin, and, arming himself with a re• volver, went out of the house.

div.head: COMMAND IN SOUTH AFRICA,
div.p: THE COMMAND IN SOUTH AFRICA,

The new Army Board and the changes in our military system necessitate no incon- siderable alterations in the existing state of things, and an important reshuffling of ap- pointments in the Army. Of these not the least is the alteration of the supreme com- mand in South Africa, due to the appoint- ment of General Neville Lyttle-
ton to the Army Board, which left vacant what is at the mement
probably the most important
-post ili the whole Army. To
succeed him the
King has been pleased to ap- point that well- tried and popu- lar officer, Gen. Sir Henry Hild- yard, the Direc-
ior of Military Education. This

selection has given unfeigned GENERAL S. iYARD. pleasure throughout the whole service, and it is generally felt that no better man could have been chosen for this arduous post. In standing Sir Henry Hildyard is quite a senior, having entered the Army as far back as 1867 after a short time in the Navy, like so many other great soldiers, and it is close upon twenty years since 'he commanded his regiment. In the recent war he first c---n- -manded the 2nd Brigade in Natal uncle- Sir Redvers Buller, and was then promoted to the sth Division upon the recall of Sir Charles Warren after Spion Kop, and throughout the whole campaign he served with great dis- tinction. Previously General Hildyard had won himself great distinction on active ser- vice in the Egyptian Campaign of the early eighties, and he had, also, seen a good deal af service at headquarters and had been com- mandant at the Staff College. Thus he was chosen to apply the lessons of the South African War to our system of military education at the close of the campaign. Now he vacates this important office for the supreme command, on .the late battle ground, and he will take out with him many good wishes from Aldershot and headquarters.
IR H. HILD

div.head: NEW ZEALAND'S NEW GOVERNOR.
div.p: NEW ZEALAND'S NEW GOVERNOR.

The appointment of a new Colonial Governor is always a subject of considerable interest in these imperialistic days, and none of our Colonies is more popular with the general public than New Zealand. Some Little while back the Earl of Ranfurly's term of office expired, and there haa been a good deal of speculation as to his succes- sor. This point was settled in the last Gazette by the appoint- ment of Lord Plunket,x..n.v.o• to the post. The new Governor must not be con fused with the more widely known Irish- man of the same name, the Right Hon. Horace Plunkett, who spells his name with two " t's "

and belongs to the Dunsany family. Lord Plunket (with one "t ") is the fifth Baron Plunket and succeeded his father, the late Archbishop of Dublin. Primate of Ireland, in 1897. The title originated with the famous Lord High Chancellor of Ireland of the thirties. The present peer was born in December, 1864, and was, educated at Harrow and Trinity College, Dublin. Entering the diplomatic service, Lord Plunket was an attache •at Rome, but in 1900 was appointed private secretary to Lord Cadogan, who was the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland, and then later to the Earl of Dudley, whom he has served up to the present in the same capacity. He is very popular kit the vce-regal household and will be greatly missed upon his departure for New Zealand.
RD PLUNKET

div.head: NORTHERN 1113 it
div.p: THE NORTHERN 1113 it
FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON v. HO'LL KINGSTON ROVERS.

At Warrington, before 6,000 spectators. Davies took the place of Dickenson at centre.Davies started, and ex- changes between Illadley and Isherwood went in favour of the Rovers. The Warrington backs passed well, and Fish essayed to round Phipps, but he was stopped by Sinclair. The Hull forwards, ably led by Starks and Kemp, rushed the game to the opposite end. Hallam drove the visitors back, and grand defensive work by Sinclair frustrated efforts by Bate and Fish. Fish had a shot at gool, which failed, and then the Warrington goal was subjected to a hot fusilade, and West failed when he had the line at his mercy. Half-time arrived with no score.

Turning round Warrington had the better of the open- ing exchanges, and after Harris had been checked at the corner Madley aad Read drove the locals back to half- way. The last-named was hurt, and took no further part in the game. Isherwood got possession from a kick by Fish and passing to Harris, the latter got in at the corner. Hard luck was next experi- enced by the visitors, for Reed raced clean through the Warrington backs, but lost possession a yard from the line. Retaliating, the Warrintonians excelled in some passing, and Thomas scored. In the last minute Isher- wood scored, and Fish landed the goal. Result :—War- rington, 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points) ; Hull Kingston Rovers, nil. Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood, Davies and Harris, three-quarter backs; Bate and Hockenhall, half backs; Boardman, Cook, Jolley, Naylor, Elmand- son, Fairhurst, Harmer, and Thomas forwards. Hull gingstoa Rovers—Sinclair, back; West, Madley. S. Read, and Phipps, three-quarter backs; Reid and Guy, half backs; Fletcher, Starks, Kemp, D. Reed, Wiltshire, Whitcombe, Ellis, and 'Pickering, forwards. _ . .
, . Referee, Mr. F. Clegg, Mrinningham. Touch judge; Messrs. J. Priestley, Salford, and F. Little, St. Helens.
KEIGHLEY v. WIDNES.

At Keighley. The home side first had a look in, but Widnes showed plunk, and beautiful, dodgy passing let Ike Taylor over. No goal resulted. On resuming Keighley invaded, and A. Pearsoa egsayed a drop, but failed. The game grew very keen, and blows were ex- changed. Widnes won by a try (3 points) to nil.

div.head: BATLEY V. S-WINTON.
div.p: BATLEY V. S-WINTON.

At Batley. The home side started, and at once took up a position in the Swinton half. Auty had a good chance, but passed wildly, and half-time arrived with no score. On the restart Oakland got over for Batley: Davies failed at goal. The latter player droppsd a goal. Wallwork scored after a clever run for Swinton, but the goal kick failed. Remit—Batley, 5 points; Swinton, 3 points.

div.head: LEIGH V. OLDHAM.
div.p: LEIGH V. OLDHAM.

At Leigh, before 5,0 n spectators in fins weather. Play was very even in ths first half, but Lsigh ought to have scored from a mull by Civil under the goal. Thomas tried a drop at goal, but missed. Play was evenly con- tested in the second half, first Leigh and then Oldham being dangerous, but the defence was impregnable. Result—A pointless draw.

div.head: RUNCORN v. HUDDE,RSFIELD.
div.p: RUNCORN v. HUDDE,RSFIELD.

At Runcorn, on wretched ground. RuncotT were short of Richs,rdson and Houghton, but pressed strongly, and eventually Walker scored a try, Price misslng the goal. On restarting Price kicked a penalty goal and Jones added a second try after fine wtssing. Resalt—Runcorn 1 goal 2 tries; Huddersfield, nil. HULL v. WIGAN.

At Hull, before 7,009 speatators. Hull had the wind with than, and Thompson dropped a goal, whilst Jack- son scored an unconverted try. Half-time :—Hull, 5 points; Wigan, nil. Hull lost Ritson in the second half, but, although weakened, they played wall, and Jackson scored again, Harrison placing. Leytham scored, and Mason placed the goal. The game ruled fast and exciting. Rasalt :—Hall, I goals 2 tries (10 points) ; Wigan, 1 goal 1 try (5 points).

div.head: BROUGFITON RANGERS v. HUNSLET.
div.p: BROUGFITON RANGERS v. HUNSLET.

This important match took place at Broughton, before 8,000 spectators. The home side had the best of matters throughout, and in the first half Hogg and Widcleson scored unimprovd tries and Oram placed a goal. In the second half bannslet were demoralised, though Albert Goldtgorpe placed a goal, and the Rangers won easily. Result :—Broughton ft' angers,l goal 6 tries (20 points) ; Hunslet, 1 goal (2 points).
SALFORD v. HALIFAX.

Played on the ground of the former, in threatening weather, before 6,000 people. In the first half Lomas kicked a penalty goal for Salford, this being the only score. On resuming, Halifax attacked, but failed to gibt through. J. Williams, from a pass by Lomas, dashed over for Salford, the place kick failing. Result—Salford, 1 goal 1 try (5 points); Halifax, nil.

div.head: LEEDS v. BRADFORD.
div.p: LEEDS v. BRADFORD.

At Headingley, on snow-covered ground, before 10,093 persons. The opening half was very evenly contested, and there were many exciting incidents. However, nothing tangible was scored. Afterwards one of the Bradford forwards and Eagers' scored, the latter's being a fine effort. Immediately afterwards Dunbavin went over from a pass by Marsden. Mosby landed a goal from Eagers' try. Result-3radford, 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points) ; Leeds, nil.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
A RUNCORN DESERTER.

Willian Wood, a native of Runcorn, and lately em- ployed on the Shropshire Union Railway, was charged !before the Chester Castle magistrates on Saturday,with being adeserter from the Chesqire Regiment.—Super- -1 itbtendent Hicks stated that in the " Police Gazette" 1 of the 10th February, 1903, prisoner was described as being an absentee from his regiment. He was appre- hended at Ellesmere Port that morning at 12.30 by • Sergeant Ball.—Prisoner was handed ..,ver to an escort. The sum of 103. was granted to the officer for his vigilance. ED*CA.TIONAL INQUIRY AT RUNCORN. I On Tuesday at Runcorn, Mr. H. J. Simmonds, on ' behalf of the Board of Education, held an inquiry with reference to the objections to the final order for the appointment of foundation managers of the National School, Church-street. The County Council objected to the appointment of the principal officiating minister. They said that the manager should be elected by annual meeting of subscribers, and no religious qualification should be made for serving in the office of manager.— Mr. W. Handley objected to sectarianism.—Can.on Wood, vicar of Runcorn, said for the last ninety years the school had belonged to the Church. as was shown by a complete set of rules and regulations drawn up in 1817.—The inquiry was closed.

div.head: ST. HELENS. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS. HELENS.

RAILWAY HORSE Box INCIDENT. Judge Shand was occupied for several hours on Wednesday, at St. Helens County Court, hearing a case in which the Corporation of St. Helens sued the Wrex- ham, Mold, and Connah's Quay Railway Company for ! 31 damage, ecc., to a hoxse. Mr. Rigby Swift, for the ! Corporation said that on December 29, Councillors ; Green, Dixon, and Hatton, with Mr. W. H. S. Day, veterinary, bought two horses at Lloyd's sale at Wrex- ham. One of the horses was injured during the journey ;to St. Helens, and had been so depreciated by the in- juries that it could note used in the surveyor's hansom but went out at nights with the street sweeper. Ir. was . bought for 78 guineas. Mr. Fenna, of the London and North-Western rt taw ty defog lei. The wittossas said 1 that between Wrexham and Hope Junction the horse I got down on its haunches with one foreleg in the manger, and it groaned and appeared almost strangled by the ropes, &c. The case was not concluded, and was ; adjourned to the next court.

SIR ROBERT HART AND THE BIBLE SOCIETY The following letter has been received by the Bible Society from Peking, from Sir Robert Hart, G.C.M.G., Inspector general of customs and of posts in Chin% "Enclosed please find cheque for 100 guineas which it gives me much pleasure to be able to send as a subscrip- tion to your centenary fund. It is an honour and a. privilege to have even the smallest share in your magni- flcent work, and I wish your appcal the fullest success. ; Sincerely yours, Robert Hart."

div.head: BETTER THAN MONEY IN THE SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: BETTER THAN MONEY IN THE SAVINGS BANK.

The working man to-day gives more attention to the food he has to eat than his forefathers gave, as he realises that his health--the bank—depends very largely upon the properties of what he eats and drinks. It follows, then, that the popular article of food is that which is easy to digest; but more popular still are prepartions which are found to aid and strengthen the digestive organs, and also to act as an energiser for the whole system. Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa is such a food. -

It plft,C-Ws-a. means in 'the hands of everyone to build up and maintain a sound constitution, which enables its possessor to travel life's journey without the aches and pains which are in many cases preventable. Thus we ome round again to sound common sense based on perie n ce.

Aldn•min BsggFar moved the usual resolution as to the confirmation of those minutes of the Education Committee which required the confirmation of the Town Council. It had, he said, been suggested that, as the Mayor would have to leave early owing to the declara- tion of the poll in the election of auditor, it would be as wall to withdraw that portion of the minutes relating to the estimates to the next meeting,a3 they might lead to considerable discussion. They could at the next meeting discuss the estimates of both bodies. It seemed a pity to waste two nights on what were practically parts of the same question. The MAYOR thought it would be better to give one night entirely to the estimates. The Council approved. Alderman Bzgsnur then alluded!to the decision of the E lac ttion Committee to increase the salary of the Director of Education (Mr. J. Moore Murray) £59 a year instead of ,E' 25 until the maximum had been reached. Alderman Bennett thought- that any member of the Council who had thought the matter over care- fully, would be of opinion that the recommendation deserved, atany rate, the strong support of the Conacil, if not their unaiiimeus support. There wa a great deal to be said in favour of the increase. Whaa Mi.. Murray ca me to Warrington, considerable opposition was made to the proposal to increase his salary. To some extent he sympathized with the oopositioa as Mr. Murray was an untried man, and it 8831101 to many me nbars of the Council premature to increase the salary. However, finally, a compromise was arrived at, but since that time they had had opportunities of judging of the manner in which he had discharged his duties. The work could not be done with greater thoroughness or success. • They had in Mr. Murray an admirable official who well deserved the proposed increase. (Hear, hear.) Alderman PrEaromr seconde I. —Councillor LORD asked whether, seeing that the Council had already passed a resolution fixing the Director's salary for the next few years, the Town Council ware in o:der in disc tsiing and passing anther resolution bearing up la and altering the terms of the previous resolution passed by th 3 Council without first_ rescinding the former resolution? The MAYOR: The Town Clerk says it is quite in order.

Councillor Loan said that from a question he asked the Chairman of the E ideation Committee at the meet- inc., a week ago, he gathered the information that Mr. Murray hal not made application Vol. an increase of salary. They had it from Ar.Jolley, that the desire of the committee was to pay a market value for the posi- tion of Director of Education in Warrington. Watt that was he did not klow, but he was certain of one thing, and that was that there were hundreds of highly qualified men who would he glad to accent a position similar to that held by Nit.. 7qurray at £359 a year.with anannual increase of £23 per annun to a maximum of £5OO. It seemed that the Education Committee scarcely knew how to deal with the ratepayers' money. It was provinm itself a most extravagant body and it- was this duty of that Council to take care that it did not abuse its powers. It was their dqty as a town council, directly responsible to the ratepayers, to see to it that those who had not to face the electorate did not place upen their shoulders as grave responsibility by their mad rush to mike War- rington the pioneer in education. It was not 13 months since Ar. Murray commenced his duties, and his salarys had already been increased, and the annual increment- fixed. He had nothing to say against Mr. Murray perm serially, but in considering the salaries of Corpora,tio o-ncials they ought to remember that the ratepayers were compelled to pay, whereas the officials were at liberty to choose whether or not they accepted the salary offered. HP moved as an amendment "That resolution 8109 in the minutes of the Education Com- mittee be rejected." Councillor PENI3IRTON seconded, and observed that the matter WAS well thrashed oat eight or nine months ago. and the salary was fixed for s'afile years. It was now too early to brinzth matec for,va-d again. It was shown that the number of applicants even at a salary of £3OO was considerable and there was a good supply of candidates. The rates were going up to an enormous extent, and where they would end one did not know.

Councillor JAMES EVA.NS said no one disputed Mr. Murray's abilities or qualifications, but no argument had been advanced either in the Education Committee or in the Council to show that Mr. Marray's work had increased in such a way as to warrant the proposed increase, or that he had asked for an increase. If the Council were anxious about increasing salaries because officials were doing something more than they bargained for in undertaking the work, that was another matter, but he saw no reason why he should vote for this increase.

001170i11Or ASFICR.9I/T pointed out that th 3 Education Committee consisted of 21 members, but only eight were present at the meeting in question. Where were the other 13? Seven had voted for this increase and one against it? Councillor A. PE A.c'DOK Slid 113 supported the amend- ment.

Alderman PIERPOINT said a gaod deal had been made of the fact that Mr. Murray had not applied for the increase. He failed to see th.at the argument applied, since a fel, weeks ago Mr. Lengdin's salary was increased by £lOO, and Mr. Longdin prided himself upon the fact that he had never upon any occasion asked for an increase. He would also say unhesitatingly that Mr. M ray'n work had increased and to an axtent that more than warranted the increase of £25.

Councillor DODDS said he was the only member on the Finance Committee of the Education authority who had voted against the increase, and he would have to be consistent that evening, although no one had a higher opinion of Mr. Murray's capabilities than he had. He was a first class man, and he (the speaker) would like to see him get to the maximum salary. He had, however, only been with them 15 months, and at the end of the current year he would have received £675 from the Corporation, which was an increase of £75 over what he engaged to come for in two years, and that rate of increase was, he thought, good enough for any man. He thought that Mr. Murray should be content to do as others would under the circumstances, namely. serve an apprenticeship to the position. When he himself came to Warrington he had done so. At the end of the year they might take up the question of increasing the salary by annual increments of £5O until the maximum of £5OO had been reached.

Councillor P. PEACOCK said he felt he was only doing his duty in protesting against this increase to a gentle- man who had only been with them 15 months. Councillor WILKINSON said be lookod upon the matter from the point of view that they had got a very good servant. At the present rate of increase it would take Mr. Murray eight years to reach the maximum, and during that time education would have made rapid strides. He thought that surely Mr. Murray would be worth £509 in five years. Councillor A. PEACOCK: What about a possible change of Government.? (Laughter.) Councillor WILKINSON pointed out that the incre- ments were not so alarming when it was considered theta larze portion of the cost of education was paid by grants. Alderman BENNETr replied, and said he felt strongly that the increase should be given. He was a little sur- prised to hear Councillor Dodds make the admission that he thought Mr. Murray was worth more than he was receiving, and there was somo inconsistency in his action.

Councillor DODDS: No, no. I said many a good man is worth more than he is getting and would be ' willing to wait a time before he got it. A.ld,wman BENNETT Said he considered the fact that Mr. Murray had not made an application was a failing of a virtuous order, and many had not the modesty that was characteristic of Mr. Murray. In conclusion he quoted figures of what was given in other towns in support of his contention that the increase should be made. The voting was as follows : For Councillor Lord's amendment :—Councillors Davies, Ashcroft, James Evans, Barton, Dodds Peter Peacock, Arthur Peacock, Lord, Pemberton; Stott, and Thornton (11). Against: Alderman Fairclough, Sutton, Hutchinson, Bennett, Pierpoint, Councillors Tinnion, John Evans, Wilkinson, John Roberts, Brough, Maginn and Rogers (12). The amendment was, therefore, lost by one vote, and the minutes were adopted. SANITARY WORKS

A STAN-ERIS-WAGES QUESTION. The Sanitary Works Committee met on February 3rd. when it was resolved that suitable rooms at the disused lodge be converted into a drawing office at a cost of £25. It was resolved that the tender of Messrs. John Melbourne, Limited, for the supply of a cast-iron tank, at £ll9 17s. 4d., be accepted; that the tender of Mr. H. iirclough, for the construction of a reservoir at

Councillor WILKINSON pointed out that Councillor James Evans would be a valuable member of the Com- mittee and the Stables Sub-Committee owing to his knowledge of horses and provender. Ceuncillor Saaerr suggested that the matter be re- ferred back, to'give Councillor James Evans an oppor- tunity of resigning some of his committees. The Ma.vort : He gives you his word. On the voting it was found that the number both for and against the amendment was 11. The Mayor gave his casting vote in favour of passing the minutes, which were eons equently adopted. THE PRICE OF GAS.-3LOT morEa CHARGES. At a meeting of the Gas Cernmittee held on the sth February, an application for the supply of gas to Burton- wood was considered, and it Was agreed to lay the mains on a guarantee of an amount su iieieat to cover the committee against loss. ' It was decided to make no reduction in the price of gas supplied through slot meters. The DEPUTY AA.YOR moved the adoption of the minutes.—rjouncillor JOFIN ROBERTS seconded. Councillor SteTr remarked that those who were of opinion that the price of gas to slot meter users was too high would keep on with their agitation. The minutes were then approved. TRAMWAY DEVELOPMENTS. THE MARKET GATE OF THE FUTURE. At a meetine of the Electricity and Trameiys Com- mittee it was resolved that Mr. John Worrell, of New Brighton, be appointed tramways manager, at a salary of .£1.20 per annum, rising by annual inerements of £lO to a maximum of £150; that the salary of Mr. F. V. L. Mathias, as electrical engineer and engineer of the tram- ways department be £250 per annum. At a meeting on February 3rd a letter, dated 29th January, 1904, from Mr. John Worrell. was read stating that circumstances had arisen since he appeared before the com- mittee which rendered it impossible for him to accept the appointment of tramways manager. It was resolved that Mr. J. Telfer, of Rotherham, be appointed tramways manager, at a salary of £129 per annum, rising by annual increments of £lO to a maxi- mum of £159. The Town Clerk submitted a plan of the proposed tram lines at Market Gate, prepared by Messrs. Preece and Cardew. together with the following letter: Dear Sir,—Referring to yours of the Bth and 15th December, we return herewith the large scale ordnance map, and also send you tracing to the same scale, which can be superposed, and showing the tramway lines as suggested by us. We also send you a drawing of the same lines to a larger scale. The arrangement provides forcers arriving by any of the four roads, being diverted down any of the other roads, or returning along the real by which they came. The drawing shows circus having a diameter of 160 ft. at the building line with pavements 12ft. Gin, wide all round. The roads approaching to the circus are 601 t. wide at the building line with 10ft. footpaths on each side, leaving a 40ft. roadway. This allows of the tracks being widened out so that the centre poles could be used for carrying the trolley wires. For supporting the trolley wires in the circus we have suggested the use of four bracket poles fixed on small islands, this leaves the centre of the circus open, and we think the islands would be found convenient as refuges when crossing the circus. If pre- ferred these four poles might possibly be dispensed with, and a larger pole erected in the centre with span wires running out in four directions. We think you will probably desire to keep the centre open with a view biter on of some memorial possibly being erected. Yours truly, PREECE & CARDBW. It was resolved, that the plan and suggestions of Messrs. Preece and Cardew be approved and adopted. Messrs. Preece and Cardew wrote with reference to the Corporation Light Railway to Stockton Heath. stating that they had received the previsional approval by the Board of Trade of the arrangements propoced for secur- ing safety at the Swing Bridge. It was decided that tenders be obtained for the permanent way and over- head equipment of Light Railway No. 1. Seven tenders for the supply of slack were opened and considered and it was resolved that three truck load of slack be ordered for the purpose of testing from the following firms, at prices named: Messrs. Thrutchley and Co., ss. 10d. per ton ; Messrs. W. and J. Richardson 6s. 6d. per ten; Messrs. The Warrington Slate Co. Ltd., 6s. 2d. per tea ; Messrs. Pendlebury and Co., 6s. sd. per ton. It was resolved, that the wages of Mr. James Newton, clerk in the electricity department, be in- creased to 255. per week. That being the last meeting which Mr. Grintsdale would attend before leaving War- rington, the committee desired to express their appre- ciation of his services as electrical engineer and tram- ways manager, and to wish him success in the position be was about to assume. A letter from Mr. Councillor Wilson respecting the issue of id. tickets for school children was referred to the manager to report thereon. Councillor WrrxresoN said he was very glad to see the prices had been inserted in the list of tenders, and he hoped that in future other committees would do the. same.
Councillor BA.RTOV splka in supplrt of Councillor Wilson's request for Id. tram tickets for school children.

Alderman BENNETT said he hopsd the effect of the report on the development of the tramways through Market Gate would be to urge the Property Purchasing Committee to proceed with the widening. It would be of the greatest possible advantage to the town and would tend to secure additional value from the tram- ways. Thealderman paid a tribute to the services of Mr. Grimadale who, he said, had performed his duties with the greatest ability and success. The minutes were approved. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
IMARCH 6, 1904

T h e Government THE NAVY AND have contrived that AB,MY ESTIMATES. fur once in a way the Army and Navy Estimates shall not show a uniform increase. The Navy Estimates have grown, but the taxpayer has the comfort of knowing that there will be a reduc- tion of military expenditure. That comfort may not last long. It is very far frotn certain that the redaction applies to the normal outlay, and is not chiefly concerned with the diminishing burdens of the South African war. Upon the Navy the coun- try expects, and is willing, to spend heavily, always provided it gAs value for its money. A suggestion is thrown out from time to time—it was advocated on Monday evening by a Welsh Liberal "ALE—that some effort should be made to persuade our maritime rivals to reduce their naval armaments. Whether such a proposal will ever be listened to we need not predict ; but it is quite certain that in the present state of international politics it would have no chance. A gret.-it war is raging in the Far East, and several neutral. Powers are anxiously wondering whether they will be able to keep out of it. This is scarcely a propitious moment for suggesting a common agreement to put a stop to naval shipbuilding.

But while it is admitted that:our naval strength must be fully maintained, not as a menace to any Power, but as a national insurance, it is evident that the country is staggering under the accumu- lated cost of the two services. They have grown enormously in recent years. The charge against this Government is not that they have sought to keep up the fighting capacity of England, but that they have employed the most wasteful means. It is now confessed, without any pretence or dis- guise, that Mr. BRODRICK'S Army Corps scheme is absurd and impracticable. The Esher Committee have dismissed it with contempt, and it is evident that their recommendations will be adopted by the Government, or by any succeeding Govern- ment. Whether the reforms now initiated will prove to be final, or whether the new system wil be very less costly than the old, are questions which it would be rash to answer off-hand.

We pride ourselves on being a practical and , rather hard-headed people, but whatever we may say of the leaders of the great spending depart- ments in the publid service—they cannot be des- cribed as hard-headed. It is to men not directly connected with the routine of administration that we owe a scheme of reform quite startling in its thoroughness. They have found the root of the mischief at the War Office in Mne word immortal- isel by the genius of DICKENS "Barnacles.' The TITE BARNACLE family have sapped all vitality in the organisation of the Army, and so they had to be cut out of the system by a process which cannot bo called painless. Henceforward no military official will no allowed to vegetate in Pall Mall until he impersonates the good old crusted formula that all change is had. At the end of four years he will ho replaced by a fresh mind. This drastic proposal is so entirely opposed to tradition that it encounters fierce opposition. We are already told that it will involve the removal of an official just when he has acquired tho necessary experience, and the appointment of somebody who has to learn the business afresh. This might be plausible if we could forget the uses to which the Brnacles have put their boasted experience. The system tiley represent has been found absolutely fatal to ideas. Whether they ever learned anything is doubtful, but it is certain that their knowledge, whatever it was, became utterly useless for practical purposes. It may be hoped that we are now about to sea a method of training which Rill raise the average of intelligence in the whole Army. By insisting upon high qualifications at the top, we shall diffuse through the organism a sense of responsibility not hitherto conspicuous. The Army Council and the general staff must be distinguished by what the Esher Committee call " picked brains." There must be an end of the deference to sleepy seniority. Society must be made to understand that the Army is not kept up for the benefit of high-bred simpletons. This will be the most difficult task of all.

We would remind our readers—though it is probably unnecessary—that an efidctive Lib3ral reply will be given in Parr Hall on Wednesday evening to the Tory-Protectionist oratory of last week. The two principal speakers will be Sir J. T. Brunner and Mr. Joseph Howes, both of whom can be relied upon to show the specious fallacies of the Chamberlain policy in their true light. What Sir John I3runner does not know about commerce, both home and foreign, is hardly worth knowing, and his views on the fiscal question are particularly sound. Mr. Howes has quite recently been addressing meetings • in the town, anu during his brief campaign in the corners of the constitu— ency he added greatly to his reputation as a plat- form speaker. Few men can discuss the political situation with such shrewdness, force, and humour, and we doubt not that Mr. Howes himself will be a great attraction. We would just add a word of congratulation to the Liberal party in having secured the services of Mr. Wm. Long, J.P., on the side of Free Trade. In his capacity as chair- man on Wednesday evening he will be cordially welcomed.

The Liberals of Stockton Heath have of late shown considerable activity, and are certainly making headway in this undoubtedly Conservative stronghold, while the influence of the Tory party is on the wane. This is not at all surprising when its performances do not correspond with its vol- uminous promises. The action, too, of those in charge of the Church Room in refusing the use of it for public meetings of the Liberal party is a "narrow policy and is doing the Conservatives a lot of harm in the district. It is pretty well known in the village that this Church Room was chiefly financed, by a Liberal gentleman—no less than the late Mr. John

Crosfield —who was exceedingly wroth when he learnt that it had been refused several time for public purposes and stated that if he had k.nown that this would happen not one penny of his would have been given towards the erection of the room. He had been under the impression that the room was for the use of the whole of the inhabitants of Stockton Heath irrespective of creed, sect, or patty—and so it should De. We fail to see what right—beyond that of might— the Churchmen and the Tories of the village nave to reserve it for their own selfish end. However, tactics such as these have a way of recoiling, and the trend of opinion in the district is unmistakably, in the direction of Liberal and Free Trade princi- ples. Monday evening's debate resulted in more than one convert to the disciples of Cobden and Bright.

While we are on the topic of local politics we should like to allude to the rapid progress of the Grand Liberal Bazaar scheme. Parr Hall has been engaged for the first week in October,during which momentous period it is anticipated that all bazaar records in the town will be relegated a long way in the background. On Wednesday the bazaar workers at the invitation of Mr. A. H. Crosfield and Miss Crosfield, spent a very pleasant social evening at t. he Liberal Club—a building, unfortunately, but ill adapted for such functions. Someday, perhaps, Liberalism in Warrington will rise to the heights Of a new club—but this by the way. The baziar Project requires plenty of workers, and we hope the re-union of Wednesday will be the means of bringing recruits to the ranks.

The Town Council made a desperate effort on Tuesday to get through the business on the agenda, but again failure was the result. There Was no postponement on this occasion; instead Members just sidled out one by one when they had had enongh of the debate, and at 9 o'clock the discovery was made that there was no quorum. This broueit the proceedings to an abrupt conclusion in the middle of one of Councillor Pemberton's Speeches. We are not sure that this was really Unfortunate, for the speaker's resolution amounted to very little more than "that the standing orders of the Council be observed." Councillor Peinher- ton's object was to make a protest in regard to the way fuel is purchased, and as he has made similar protests over and over again both in Coun- cil and committee, the impatience of his hearers Was excusable. Seeing that his motion was never Voted "'upon, we are mildly interested in noting Whether Councillor Pemberton will place it on the agenda for the third time.

This is a funny Corporation of ours. It raises the salaries of officials without even being asked. Only a month ago £lOO per annum was dumped down upon our Borough Surveyor, but though he made no request so we are told, he has not yet asked for protection against this sort of thing. On Tuesday, the Director of Education was burdened With an extra £25 per year without having applied for it, and bye and bye we expect the Corporation will be distributing those bonuses to ratepayers that Alderman Bennett once spoke about. Some misguided people appear to think t. hat the Corporation should wait till it's asked for increases, but this would never do. No, it is far better to heap gold upon our deserving officials until in their embarrasment they cry "enough, enough 1" But, speaking seriously, We believe Mr. J. Moore Murray to fully merit the increase in his annual increment granted on Tuesday.lt is not his fault that the EducationCom- paittee boggled over the rate of his remuneration in the first place, and as he has since proved him- -aelf a most capable official it is only fair that his salary should be raised to a sum commensurate With the pay for similar services in other towns.

Several other matters of interest and import- ance which were debated upon also merit passing; re. ference here. One was the unanimous resolu- tion in favour of a bridge over the river at Howley. Councillor iNlaginn made out a very strong case for thus connecting up two portions of the Borough which, in regard to one another, are most awkwardly isolated. We can see nothing but ad- Ystitage to be gained from filch an enterprise, and isyery'probable that considerabl3 profit will ulti- rnately accrue to the town by thus opening out an extensive,and hitherto unapproachable area.So far the Corporation is committed to plans and esti- mates only, but a distinct step forward has been made. The slack contracts of the Water Committee again, occupied attention. Coun- cillor Pierpoint manfully retracted a reflection he had made on the truthfulness of the officials as a whole, in the course of last months debate, and the fact was also disclosed that there is a report to come from the engineer at Win wick Which will throw light upon the peculiar adminis- tration of the Water Department in the past' Thanks to Councillor Stott, the unemployed prob- lem is being tackled in a practical manner, and the Committees have instructions to push on public works which will find labour for the deserving un- employed in the town. It is conceivable that a good deal may be done in this direction towards alleviating the distress which is so prevalent.

Tuesday was one of those rare occasions on which party politics cropped up in the Council chamber. It was all due to the suggested naming of an open space off Liverpool-road " Crosfield Park" by the Open Spaces Sub-committee. Alderman Bennett, with an absence of that tact and courtesy for which, as a rule his conduct is noticeable,raised an objection to this recommenda ton and the fat was in the fire, so to speak, in a .inoment. We acquit Alderman Bennett of party feeling in the matter, but we are surprised that he should, publicly, have taken a course so obviously discourteous to the family whose 'name it is pro- posed to perpetuate in the centrei of a district for which they have done so I.nuch. Shbsequent speakers were far from innocent of party spirit, and the discussion threatened very quickly to become heated. The majority of the, Conservatives would clearly have liked to call the park afteaord Lilford, and their attitude is very plainly indicated by a correspon- dent who, in another column, says the Council is 'Committed to an act of the ,greatest discourtesy to a gentleman whose name is so familiar to them as that of Lord Lilford." Comparisons are always odious, but we feel bound to Say that there is no comparison in the familiarity to Warrington ears of the names of Lilford and C.rosfield, or in the amount of service the respec- tive families have rendered the town. In fact we 'Should be puzzled to recoller.t what Warrington does owe his Lordship, and, furthermore. how many Warringtonians would know Lord Lilford from Adam if they saw him? With an approach- i,ng political contest there is evidently some Jealousy in Tory circles of all that pertains to the Crosfields, and it is to be regretted that the cloven hoof of: party feeling should be shown so 'unmistakably in the Council Chamber.

The earnest and devoted workers in connection With the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, have reason to congratulate themselves. On S.inday ,they were able to use their new chapel for the first time and it must have been an additional source of satisfaction to them to know that it was paid for. The entire cost—over £l,ooo—was raised or promised before the building was opened,and steps 4lre now being taken to raise an additional £2OO to Provide an organ. True to the worthy motives Which animated the late Mr. John Crosfield when he founded the Mission, his greatly-respected wife and the members of his'family are seeking to extend the work which has had such beneficial results in the Bank Quay district. The late Mr. Crosfield took a personal interest in the welfare of his wor,c- People, and although this type of employer is rapidly disappearing in consequence of the forms- of limited liability companies,it is satisfactory to learn that the firm of Messrs. J. Crosfield and :S°lla, Limited, has taken a commendable and Practical interest in this latest development of the mission.

After all, the users of penny in-the-slot gas Meters are to receivA a concession. The Gas Com- mittee yesterday decided to iyieleacie the quancity 2,f gas supplied for a penny from 25 cubic feet to ''46 feet. This is a step in the right direction, but lt was hardly to be expected after the lugubrious

report which was presented to the Council a short time ago in which it was shown that the Corpora- tion was receiving a smaller margin of profit from users of slot meters than from ordinary consumers. The success of the recent agitation for this conces- sion must naturally encourage those Who are seek- ing to induce the Tramways Committee to grant halfp9nny fares to children, to persevere. The trams are patronized very freely all things con- sidered, and the public is entitled to more concessions than are so far available. Half-penny fares to children special terms or sea- son tickets for regular passengers and half-penny stages would immensely popularise the tramways. The undertaking might not be able to show much profit but it would at any rate have better justified its existence if it afforded a cheap and rapid means of travel for the ratepayers who have provided it

Mr. Warner and his much-criticised team have upheld the honour of England in international cricket nobly, and they bring back from Australia with them not only the long-sought "ashes," but also a proof of the unquestioned superiority of the English team over their Colonial rivals. Noble and his men made in every match a great fight, and except in tha third encounter it may be con- ceded that whatever ill-luck there was in the game fell to their share. But the conclusion at which critics are bound to arrive is that in one department at least—the bowling —the'Australians were hopelessly outclassed all through; while in batting the Englishmen were able to hold their own for pluck and cleverness. Not a little of the success has been due to Mr. Warner's own good judgment. He has shown himself a capable c ip- tain, ready to face emergency, and never losing heart in apparent disaster. The test matches this year, if they have done nothing else, have proved that English cricket does not depend en- tirely upon a few, much-advertised " cracks"; Foster and Bosanquet,whose selections were ored at and sneered at by the friends of other and perhaps more favoured amateurs, have established beyond doubt their claim to rank in the forefront of first-class cricketers. The M.C.C. has good reason to be proud of the performance of the first team it has sent to Australia; and England may rest contented that the reproach to her character as a sporting nation involved in repeated defeat has been effaced. One word of praise to Noble is due. From first to last the Colonial captain fought stubbornly and brilliantly to save his side from defeat. That he failed only enhances the merit of his efforts.
