div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. The centenary of the British and Foreign Bible Society, which carries on the work of circulating the Bible in all parts of the world, will be celebrated at Warrington to-morrow (Sunday). Special services will be held in many places of worship, and a list of the preachers is published in our advertising columns. On Monday, March 21st, a great Centenary meeting will be held in the Parr Hall, when addresses will be delivered by the Bishop of Liverpool and the Rev. John Watson, D.D. (lan Maclaren). The Rev. F. Vaughan will preach his first sermon as curate-in-charge of Emmanuel Church, to-morrow (Sunday). The Rev. H. Dunnico will preach in the Royal Court Theatre, to-morrow (Sunday evening). The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees will preachon" The Bible in its simplest aspect" at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday evening. A mass meeting arranged bithe Liberal Association will be held in the Parr Hall on Wednesday evening. Mr. William Long will preside and the speakers willbe Mr. Joseph Howes, of the National Reform Union, and Sir J. T. Brunner, M,P., who will reply to the recent speeches of Sir Howard Vincent and Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P. An open meeting to celebrate the eleventh anni- versary of Wycliffe P.S.A. Society will be held to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon. Mr. C. E. Parker will be the speaker. A sale of work done by the inmates of the Work- house under the direction of the Brahazon Employment Society will be held at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon. The members of the Musical Society will render Gounod's "The Redemption " in the Parr Hall, on Wednesday, March 23rd. The soloist will be Miss Winifred Wynne (soprano), Miss Maud Turner (contralto), Mr. James Davis (tenor), and Mr. Charles Knowles (bass.) ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERA. WATERS.—Advt.

H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC IS the KING or ToNrcs.-43. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Mr. Fred Podmore. It will be interesting to bandsmen to know that in this month's " Musical :Opinion " there is a lengthy article on" Brass Band Reform," contributed by a local musician, Mr. Fred Fodmore, who has lately been appointed conductor of the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Brass Band.

BaCE BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER THE CLOCK.—AdVt The Soap Libel Case. • It was announced by Mr. Pickford, K.C., at the Liverpool Assizes on Saturday that Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons had decided to drop the use of Dr. Stuart's name in the sale of one of their soaps. His Lordship said the firm were behaving most generously and handsomely in taking that course.

FrRE GRATES of every description.—.T. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street,Warringion.—Advt. . The Hatchery in Bank Park. The hatchery in Bank Park is now open to the public on application to the park keeper (Mr. Ashton). The ova on the grills is now hatching out and affords a most instructive object lesson to anyone' interested in natural history. It is computed that there are 30,000 eggs on the grills. We are glad to notice that labels have now been placed on the tanks of the aquarium, giving the names of the different kinds of fish on exhibition. This improvement has been wanted for some time.

ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. A Warrington Artist's Work. We understand that the Town Clerk is arranging for an exhibition in the art gallery of a considerable number of the works of Mr. James Charles. It is hoped to get together a collection of at least 30 pictures and these will afford the inhabitants of Warrington an opportunity of seeing the fine work which one of their own townsmen has executed. Two works ofMr. Charles havebeen bought for the permanent collection in the art gallery and we are glad to learn that several of Mr. Charles' works have also been purchased by local gentlemen.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 5, 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 5, 1904

Warrington War Funds. The Borough Treasurer has this week issued in pamphlet form a report and statement of accounts of the various local funds raised in connection with the South African war. The statistics show that the money raised under the different heads for the benefit of local soldiers and their dependents during the course of the war from October 1899 to March 31st 1903 totalled £:3081 9s. id. and particulars are fully given showing how the money was and is disbursed. BASSINETTES AND MA.IL CARTS in latest art shades.—J. S. GAII.LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Bust of the King. - - -

The bust of His Majesty the King which was presented to the town by Mr. J. Charlton Parr has now been mounted on a handsome pedestal and placed in the vestibule of the Town Hall. It will be opened to the inspection of the public on any day next week. Acting on the advice of the artist, the bust has been covered by a glass frame, which while not adding to the artistic appearance of the statue, does not very much detract from it and will help to preserve the freshness of the marble.

PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER the CLOCK for BE3 BOCT 3 in LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Alleged Embezzlement. On stepping ashore from the Granville boat, which arrived at Jersey early on Tuesday morning, Joseph George Harrison, a member of a well known and highly respected Warrington family, was arrested on a warrant charged with embezzling money at Maccles- field, from . Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., Limited, brewers, Warrington. The prisoner when arrested said he could neither eat nor sleep. A five- chambered revolver, fully loaded, some loose cart- ridges, and £l4 in money were found upon him. He will be brought before the Macclesfield Bench next week.

UNDER the CLOCK" for GOOD BOOTS.—Advt. Warrington Man in Trouble at Wrexham. At Wrexham, on Thursday, Owen Jones, a wire- worker,of Winwick-rd Warrington,was brought before county magistrates on a serious charge. Mr. Crosfield, of Little Acton, stated that shortly after midnight on Tuesday he heard a noise, and on going downstairs saw the prisoner crouching against the ivy on the wall of the house. He covered him with his revolver, and asked him who he was. Prisoner replied that his name was Owen Jones, and that he belonged to War- rington and then decamped. Subsequently Mr. Oros- field found that the windows of the pantry and dining- room had been broken.—Police-sergeant Rees arrested prisoner in Warrington on Wednesday, and the magistrates remanded him uatil Tuesday next.

The Actuary at the SavingOank By the death of Mr. Thomas Tunstall, the office of actuary at the Savings Bank, Buttermarket street, became vacant. The Board of Management met on Tuesday to make the new appointment, Mr. W. Long presiding. It was unanimously decided that Mr. William A. Proud, the cashier, should succeed Mr. Tuustall, at a salary of 000, rising by yearly incre- ments of £2O to £lOO. He is to devote the whole of his time to the duties of the office. By his long and efficient service at the bank, Mr. Proud has fully earned the promotion. Mr. Edmund Osborne will now take up the duties of cashier. Election, of Elective Auditors. _

Warrington selected its two elective auditors for the ensuing year on Tuesday. Four candidates went to the poll. There were the retiring auditors, Messrs. Edwin Bradshaw and Laurence 131.t0n, as well as Mr. Joseph Rigby Williams,and Mr. James Ball, the last- named gentleman being the nominee of the Indepen- dentLabour Party. The result was announced by the Mayor at a quarter past nine in tfie evening, as fol- lows :—Mr. James Ball, 668 ; Mr. Edwin Bradshaw, 330; Mr. Laurence Bolton, 206 ; Mr. Joseph Rigby Williams, 249. Consequently Mr. James Ball and Mr. Edwin Bradshaw are elected. The result has given great satisfaction to local members of the Labour party who had worked well on Mr. Ball's behalf.

The Clara Butt-Rumford Concert. The artistes engaged for this grand concert next Thursday form a powerful company, Mr. Johnson hav- ing adhered to the principle which has always actuated him of placing before his patrons the best talent ob- tainable. Of Madame Clara Butt and Mr. liennerley Rumford nothing to the purpose can be said beyond what is general knowledge in this as in other dis- tricts, and the names of those who accompany them afford an unquestionable guarantee that the concert will prove a distinct artistic success. Tile programme contains a number of exceptionally choice items, and the excellent arrangements should ensure a bumper house. Madame Clara Butt by special request will sing, Liddles famous setting off " Abide with me" with organ obligato, and the lullaby " My Treasure," Mr. R. H. Pearson strongly advises early securing of tickets.

" Man in his Completeness." The Rev. John Wakeford, Vicar of St. Margaret's, Anfield, Liverpool, delivered an address to men on this subject at the Parish Church last evening, taking for his text the words "Stand up. I myself also am a man," Acts x., 26. He said they had come, somehow, to doubt whether a Christian was really a man. They needed to reconsider what they meant by manliness. Manliness should mean fidelity to the type, and if God made man in His own likeness it was plain that the nearer to God, the truer the man. The physical man did not retain his self-respect unless he knew himself to be something more than a mortal being. He must take account of his soul and spirit in reckoning his duty, to himself. Man needed the incentive and the inspiration that came from the knowledge of God. It was not enough that he knew himself one of many brethren. He must recognize his Heavenly Father. Physically men were weak, short-lived and little, but the body was not the standard by which they were to be measured. Morally and spiritually, they. surpassed in precious- ness.eand importance the planets sthemselves. They would outlive the world, and their true life here upon earth was the preparation, through discipline and ad- versities, for the life of glory eternal before the Throne.—Next Friday evening the Rev. J. G. McCormick of Liverpool, will speak on "Practice." A Prosperous Building Society. The annual meeting of the Borough of Warrington Incorporated Permanent Building Society was held at the office of the manager, Alderman Sutton, Legh- street, on Wednesday evening. Mr. John Andrews (chairman of the board of directors) presided, and there were also present :—Alderman Sutton, Messrs. T. H. A. Pilkington, Henry Houghton, Samuel F. Welsby, E. A. Jones, T. A. Sutton (surveyor), J. G. Chappell and J. H. Clarke (auditors). and W. D. Jeans (solicitor to the society). In their twenty-ninth annual report the direc- tors stated that the profit shown in the accounts ' for the past year was £204 ss. 10d., to which had to be added the sum of £3l ss. 3d., brought forward from 1903, making a total of £235 us. id., now to he dealt with. Out of this sum the directors recommended that a dividend of £4 per cent., free of income tax, be paid to the shareholders, and after allowing £6B ss. for working expenses, to carry the balance of :£ll ss. 9d. forward to next year's account. The number of members on the books is 49, of whom 11 are borrowers.—Alderman Sutton remarked that con- sidering that trade had been so bad, and the financial position of workingmen so unsatis- factory, the Directors thought themselves for- tunate in being able to recommend a 4 per cent. dividend.—Tho retiring directors (Messrs. John Andrews, George Holford, T. H. A. Pilkington, William Roberts, 'Henry Houghton, and Samuel F Welsby) were re-elected, together with the auditors. (Messrs. J. G. Chappell and J. H. Clarke) and the Surveyor (Mr. T. A'. Sutton).—A vote of condolence with Mrs. Shaw Green on the death of her husband, who was an auditor Of the society, was passed.—Mr. J. H. Death of Dr. Lister. The death is announcad, at his residence, in Leamington, of Dr. E. Lister, late of Haydock Lodge, Newtian, and for many years Surgeon-Major in the Ist South Lancashire Volunteers. Dr. Lister's daughter is the wife of Lieutenant-Colonel George Yates Bolton. Spiritualism.

At the meetings Qf the Spiritualist Society on Sun- day, Mrs. Cropper, of Ashton-under-Lyne, was the speaker. In the evening, after an earnest call to work making special reference to the removal of Mr. Pemberton, she performed the rather unique cere- mony of " naming " twin brothers, and followed with clairvoyance. On Monday evening the same lady was exceedingly successful in both clairvoyance and psychometry.

Infirmary Ball. —The Proceeds. The final meeting of the Infirmary Ball Committee was held at the Infirmary on Wednesday, Mrs. J. R. ?ickmere presiding. Mr. W. Peter Rylands (hon. secretary) presented his statement bf accounts, which showed that the receipts amounted to £74, 4s sd.The donations amounted to £4O 155., and net proceeds of ball £33 9s, 5d., the institution thus receiving alto- gether £74 4s. sd. The accounts were passed, on the motion of Mr. Roger C. Parr, and a vote of thanks was accorded to Hr. Rylands for his services as Hon. Secretary. Mr. J. Charlton Parr moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. J. R. Pickmere,who as President of the committee had helped so much to make the function a success.
FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. British Women's Temperance Association.

A meeting of the aboversociety was held on Tues- day afternoon in the Church Parlour, Bold-street. There was a good attendance, over which Mrs. Norman presided. Miss Bessie Dutton read business communications, and new members were introduced The Rev. J. F. Matthews gave a short, pithy address urging them as temperance women to use their own influence with women voters to help to return none but temperance men to the Council, as it is from the councillors that our magistrates who sit on our licensing benches are drafted. To have a minister at one of the monthly meetings is a new feature but it is hoped with the co-operation of the clergy and minis- ters to be able to hold meetings in the halls connected with the various churches of tin town. Mrs. Simpson secretary) gave a short reading from the Geneva convention paper. A. donation of 103. from Mrs. Holmes, Rugemont, Penketh, was received. An Innovation at the Saapery. -

The first of a series of lecturea dealing with scientific subjects treated in a popular way was given to the employees of Messrs. J. Crosfieldr,and Sons, Ltd., in the works assembly room on Tuesday last. The object of these lectures is to explain in ' an inter- esting way the fundamental laws which underlie the most important chemical and physical changes occurring in everyday life and employment. The lecturer on this occasion was Dr. Ormandy, who dealt withthe composition of properties of air regarded from the chemical standpoint. A. number of instances with regard to combustion were illustrated by experi- ments.ln conclusklag,the lecturer pointed out how certain injurious actioilf such as the rusting of iron, were explained by the laws which they had been consider- ing. In the ensuing discussion a number of similar instances were brought forward by Dr. Markel, such as the spontaneous ignition of oily waste, coal and the like. The necessity for certain of the stringent rules observed in the works was seen to rest on the sound scientific principles dealt with that evening. The next lecture will be given on Thursday, the 10th inst., by Mr. Allan, and will deal with " Air from the physical standpoint.

The Rev. J. F. Matthews.and the Press. At the weekly meeting of the Latchford Baptist Literary and Debating Society, held on Monday even- ing, the Rev. J. F, Matthews gave an address on "The Relation of the Press to Public Opinion." In the course of the pubsequent debate the opinion was unanimously maintained that it was a function of the Press to create a healthly ptiblic opinion based on righteousness. The view was expressed that the newspapers of the future would probably cease to be the mere instruments of political parties, and would become vehicles of a politico-ethical philosophy that found its ultimate source in the teaching of Christ. It was suggested that divorce cases and breach of promise actions should be kept out of public journals Mr. Matthews pointed out that it would be a bad day for English social life if such a suggestion ever took practical form, He advocated the excision of the prurient element in divorce proceedings, but the names and social status of the guilty parties should be made as riblic as possible. The only way of cleaning the Augean stables of high social life was by flooding them with the fierce light of a clean public opinion. It was also the one kind of punishment this class of moral lepers feared. An interesting evening was closed with a vote of thanks to the speaker. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER. the CLOCK, BRID GE-STREET.—Ad7t, Liberal Club. The " Euchre" competition in connection with the above Club came to a final issue and the prizes were distributed by Mr. Councillor Wilkinson on Thursday evening. The secrefary (Mr. G. F. Freeman) in ask- ing Councillor Wilkinson to distribute the prizes re- viewed the movement of the competition and pointed out the pleasureable evenings which had been spent in consequence of the games, and hoped that the next competition would be as pleasant as the past one. Councillor Wilkinson who was supported by Messrs. W. Ford, J. W. Bouchier, E. A. Sanders, fl-eorge Strange, E. Pierpoint, G-. H. Shaw and others, then presented the prizes to the following :—Messrs. J. Halliwell, J. Smith, Councillor Tinnion' P. P. Hawtin, W. Warburton, G. F. Freeman, It. Woods and George Simpson. Mr. G. H. Shaw propok)d a vote of thanks to the donors: Coancillor Wilkinson and Messrs. Reading, J. Halli well and Frank Plumpton. Mr. J. Wood seconded and said that the games had created great interest and pleasant evenings were the result. Mr. G. F. Freeman responded en behalf of the winners. Councillor Wilkinson in thanking the members for their vote of thanks said he was pleased to be of some little assistance in furthering the com- petitionsand what he had done he would be pleased to do again. The games had brought fresh blood into the Club and the enthusiasm was a proof of the pleasurable evenjngs spent during the winter. (Applause). The second competition will commence next week and Councillor Wilkinson again heads the list with a donation of 103. 6d.
H. M. ASHTON'S LIF/1 TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63. SA.NICEY-STRENT, Warrington.—Advt. Funeral of Mr. William Taylor.

The grave closed over the remains of thel late Mr. William Taylor, builder, on Mon- I day morning. All that remained mortal was conveyed to Farnworth and interred in the family burial ground. The service was impressively conducted by the Rev. Wright Williams, vicar of Farnworth. In additioneto the relatives, a large num- ber of sympathising friends attended to show a last mark of respect. The chief mourners were Mr. Joseph Taylor, and Mr. James Taylor, (brothers) and Mr. James Taylor (nephew), In local Free Masonry the late Mr. Taylor was a prominent figure, ftnd his loss will be greatly deplored by the brethren. He was a P.M. of the Gilbert G-reenall Lodge, had acted as D.C. for many years, and was the hon. treasurer and Charity Representative. His signal services to the lodge were only recognized a short time ago by the presentation to him of a silver tea and coffee ser- vice. He was a P.A.G.P. of the West Lancashire Province, and a P.G. Std. B. of the Provincial Chapter,and a P.Z of the Gilbert Greenall Chapter. In his masonic work he set a high example to the brethren generally. A. large number of brethren from the district attended the funeral. The Gilbert Greenall Lodge (1250) of Freemasons was represented by Brothers W. Hodgkirtson, S.W., Stanley Wilson, S., E. The Volunteers. The Warrington Volunteers will encamp on Salis- bury Plain from July 23rd to August 6th or 7th. It has been arranged to hold regimental races on Whit- Monday, probably near Wilderspool-causeway. Ladysmith Ball.

Tile warrant officers, staff sergeants and sergeants if the 8-40th Regimental District commemorated the anniversary of the relief of Ladysmith by holding a ball in the Gymnasium. About 150 couples were present, the room having been tastefully decorated for the occasion. Several sergeants from the Volunteer Battalion were present, chiefly from the Cyclist and Mounted Infantry Companies. .The music was sup plied by the regimental band.

Widnes Eisteddfod. Miss Gertrude Blair pupil of Mr. Charles Dawson, L.V.C.M., 28, Arthur-street, Warrington has won the prize, viz,, a silver medal (gold centre) at the above Eisteddfo. This is the fourth Ist class prize she has won at Eisteddfods for pianoforte playing. There were 15 competing candidates. The adjudicator, Mr. E. H. Harding, of Bangor, remarked on her expres- sion, touch and technique, and also on the excellence of the tuition she is receiving.
The Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society.

The annual meeting for passing the accounts and electing officers for this society will be held in Qairo- street school, on Wednesday evening. The directors in presenting the thirty-seventh annual report, state that as the funds of the society this year do not per- mit of a dividend being declared, they propose to pay off shareholders on notice of withdrawal to the extent of £450. The retiring directors are Messrs. John Critchle.y, T. Critchley, and P.C. Price. The two last named gentlemen offer themselves for re-election. Brick-street Mission Band of Hope.

In connection with the above, the sth entertainment of the season was held on Tuesday evening last. Mr. S. Fernley occupied the chair. Recitations were given by the following :—John H. Bibby, Harriett Howell, Nellie Allen, Minnie Marratt, Jane Riley, Ethel Bibby, Hannah Allen, Alice Starkey, and Elizabeth Hannah 'Bibby. Solos were rendered by Miss Eva Shaw, Miss M. Gallop, and Master William Barton. Selections on the gramophone were given by Mr. Langhorn. The entertainment was brought to a close by a humorous dialogue entitled "Apartments to let," the characters being taken by Messrs. J. Thorniley, J. Shaw, S. Gallop and James Shaw. Chamber of Commerce. A meeting of the Council was held at Market-gate Chambers, on Monday, the Vice-President (Mr. Fulton Smith) presiding.—A communication was read from the London Chamber asking the Council to support , the re-introduction of the Bill for the prevention of secret commissions, and the Secretary was instructed 'to communicate with Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P., g askin him to use his influence in that direction.— ' • Considerable discussion took place with reference to ' the desirability of introducing the metric system, and as a step in the desired direction Mr. Fulton Smith, who represents the Chamber on the Education Coin- ' mittee, was requested to bring the matter before that body with a view to promoting a thorough knowledge of the system in the local schools.—Allusion was made to the proposal to erect a new bridge across the river between Latchford and Howley, but, though consider- able approval was expressed with reference to the idea, it was not thought desirable to pass any formal resolution on the subject. The Training College. • - -

The authorities of the Warrington Training Cl loge have devised a scheme to give their best students the opportunity of obtaining aUniversity degree. Owing to the distance of Warrington from Manchester and Liverpool the necessary attendance at lectures at the University has hitherto been impossible. The diffi- culty has now been removed by the very generous offer by a friend of the College of a large commodious house capable of accommodating at least 12 students near Owens College, to serve as a hostel. This hostel will be opened in September to such students as wish to take a three years' course and study for a degree The advantages are obvious, for they embrace all those of the residential as well as the day college system. In addition to the advantages of attending lectures at the University and receiving their pro- fessional training at the day training college, the students will be afforded the furthet one of help and guidance in their private study. The authorities of the Victoria University have expressed their cordial sympathy with the college in their attempt to meet a growing need. A Farmer Sued. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour, Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., Messrs. Burton and Son, Manure Merchants, Liver- pool, sued Paul McGregor, Crowton Hall, near North- wich,for £ls,the price of a cargo of map.ure.—Mr.H.J. L-mgton appeared for the plaintiffs and Mr. A.lBrowne defended.—Plaintiffs' case was that at the Walton Show defendant gave them an order for three cargoes of manure at £l5 per cargo. One cargo was supplied but when another was sent defendant refused to accept it.—The dispute was as to whether the manure was sold by cargo or by weight. Plaintiff's said it was their custom not to sell the manure by weight, but in flat-loadsj—Mr. Burton gave evidence and denied that defendant stipulated a minimum weight of 80 tons per cargo'. The cargoes varied in weight—Mr. Browne : So that the farmers are at your mercy?— His Honour said it was difficult for him to see what protection the customers had—Defendant said a mini- mum weight of 85 tons per cargo was specified when the order was given. The weight of the 'first cargo was only 421 tons. Defendant had paid £7 55. into court—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiffsfor the amount paid into court, with a ,sts far defendant What is " Thermophor " . -

With the object of -getting to know a little more about a new invention, bearing the mysterious name of" Thermophor," a fairly-large number of people assembled on Wednesday in the showrooms of Mr. J. S. Garland, of Bridge-street, who is the sole im- porter and agent for Warrington and district, to witness a demonstration. In front of the audience was an array of " Thermophor" articles, such as milk jugs, coffee pots, entree dishes, milk warmers foot warmers, and a number of compresses for m3di' cal use. The virtue of these articles is that of being able to retain a permanent and high temperature I for hours at a time without fire or flame. The heat is developed by the meeting and congealing of a chemical preparation, which is hermetically enclosed in an india rubber or metal covering. By means of these " Thermophor " vessels, food, fluids, &c., can be kept hot without losing taste and freshness. Tea, coffee, &c.. can be drawn off and allowed to stand for hours without stewing; food can be sent to a distance hot and in good condition, and milk for infants can not only be kept warm for hours, but can be sterilized, and all bacteria killed without effecting its quality. The demonstrations on Wednesday attested the simplicity of putting the invention into practical use. If for instance a mother desired to keep milk warm for 9 or 10 hours without fire or flame she conld do so 'by buyinv, of Mr. Garland a "Thermophor milk warmer." This article consists of a cylindrical vessel termed the heater, which is intended for the milk bottle, and of an iscplator, which prevents the radia- tion of the heat outwards and the rush of cold air inwards. After being put into boiling water for the number of minutes indicated on the article, the vessel should be well dried by a cloth, and it is then fit for use. By turning a screw for a few seconds to let fresh air enter, the vessel will become self heating and will retain a high temperature for several hours without changing. The advantages- of this self-heat- ing apparatus have been fully realised for medical purposes and sick nursing and the" Thermophor " i already in great request in hospitals and sick rooms Thermophors compare favourably in price with non heat-retaining vessels and are of the greatest possibl use to all classes of the community.

div.head: FATALITY LAST NIGHT.
div.p: FATALITY LAST NIGHT.
An Engineman's Da3g3P3113 Prat ice

A. fatal accident occurred at the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Company, Ltd., shortly before six o'clock last evening. Thomas Childs, a single man, living in Hood-lane, Great Sankey, was engaged with two other men' in starting an engine in one of the mills, when the iron rod with which they were endeavouring to turn a huge fly-wheel, was suddenly swung round and it caught Childs a heavy blow on the forehead He fell to the ground unconscious and expired almost 'immediately, P.C. Woods of the Liverpool-road police out-station was telephoned for and rendered prompt assistance. The body was conveyed to the Mortuary, where it lies awaiting the inquest.

div.head: LIBERAL BAZAAR.
div.p: THE LIBERAL BAZAAR.

SOZIAL GATHERING OF WORKERS. At the invitation of Mr. Arthur Crosfield and Miss Crosfield, the workers and friends in connection with the forthcoming Liberal Bazaar, to be held in the Parr Hall in October next, spent a pleasant social evening in the Liberal Club on Wednesday evening' Unfortunately, Mr. Arthur Crosfield was detained in London on important business connected with the party, and was unable to attend. Miss Crosfield was present, and Captain Crosfield stayed a few minutes, but had to leave for a meeting in connection with the National Service League. Nearly a hundred persons responded to the invitation. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes presided, and amongst the gentlemen present were: —Alderman Pierpoint, Councillors Tinnion and James Evans, Messrs. J. Longland, W. Furness, W. Winstanley, J. Hill, E. A. Sanders, A. H. Sanders, G. Shaw, T. Vose, W. Clegg°, A. Downes, G. Colley, J. Turner, J. Hassall, and Edmund Osborne and E. V. Walker (hon. secs.l The CHAIRMAN reld a letter from Mr. Crosfield, in which the writer stated that he was extremely sorrry to be detained in London. Letters of apology were also read from Miss Bessie Dutton, and Mr. and Mrs. Zi4pa, Armitage, who are staying in Cornwall. In regrring to the impending bazaar, the Chairman observed that if it were successful—as he had no doubt it would be—it would be a good thing f3r the party in the near future. (Hear, hear.) At a later stage of the meeting the Chairman read a telegram from Mr. Crosfield, in which he expressed his delight at having obtained a promise from Sir John T Brunner, M.P. to address a mass meeting of Liberals at Warrington on the 9th inst. (Applause.) Although they had not the pleasure that evening, the Chairman continued, of seeing Mr. Crosfield, there was no doubt that Hr. Crosfield had been doing the party great service whilst in London. (Hear, 'hear). A brief progr3,mtne of vocal and instrumental items was submitted. Miss Edith Birchall played two violin solos with mazked ability and Miss Crosffeld greatly pleased the audience by a solo on the pianoforte. The vocal items were contributed by Miss Lucy Davies (Hollinfare) and Miss'Nellie Anderton. Both artistes were in good voice and sang with such accept- ance as to secure encores. The accompaniments were played with taste by Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes. During an interval an adjournment was made to the committee rooms upstairs, where refreshments were partaken of and a pleasant time spent in con- versation. Mr. Crosfield had very thoughtfully sent a basket of flowers, and after serving their purpose as table decorations, the flowers were distributed amongst the company. The catering was in the _safe hands of Councillor James Evans.

The proceedings were resumed in the reading room, where a brief statement was made by Mr. Edmund Osborne respecting the progress of arrangements for the bazaar. Mr. Osborne added that if there were any ladies who would like to be associated with any par- ticular stall he would be glad to hear from them. Whilst a great deal of work had already been done much more remained to be done, if the bazaar was to be made a great success. He believed they would shortly hear from the Countess of Crewe of her will- ingness to perform the opening ceremony on the first day. It was probable that the bazaar would open on Wednesday, the sth October and cantinue open until the end of the week.

Circulars were distributed explaining the object of the bazaar. "The grand old cause of Liberalism in Warrington,"it was stated, "has languished during recent years, and among several contributory reasons that of lack of funds has been severely felt. A grand service to local Liberalism was performed by the bazaar of 1891, and a sum of well over £l,OOO realised. There is even greater need for financial help now, and it is believed that another well- organised bazaar extending over three or four days, will do much towards relieving the straitened cir- Pumstanccs under which the Liberal party in War- rington labours. Every Liberal can, and it is hflped will, do something to make the bazaar of 1901 a success in every way." The musical programme was continued, further songs being sweetly sung by Miss Lucy Davies and Miss Nellie Anderton. Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes played a pianoforte solo and Mr. Ashton gave a humor- ous reading. A vote of thanks was tendered to the artistes,on the proposition of Mr. Furness,seconded by Mr. Alderman Pierpoint. The hope was expressed that social gath- erings of a like kind would be held more frequently than hitherto. On the proposition of Mr. Councillor Evans, seconded by Mr. Osborne, the Chairman's ser- vices were acknowledged, and a pleasant gathering terminated.

div.head: FIREMAN SUES HIS E:APLOYERS, Wrongful Dismissal.
div.p: A FIREMAN SUES HIS E:APLOYERS, Wrongful Dismissal.

At the Warrington Police Court yesterday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, Thomas Foy, brought a claim against the Warrington Borate Co., Ltd., to recover 7s. 61—a week's wages. There was a counterclaim against Foy for £lO damages alleged to have been sustained by the firm in consequence of his negligence.—Ar. C. H. Unsworth appeared for the plain- tiff and Mr. Browne defended. _

Mr. Unsworth applied for permission to amend the claim to one of £5 for wrongful dismissal. Mr. Browne said the defendants were fighting the case on principle. If the claim was amended, he was entitled to an adjournment. It was decided to proceed with the original claim, Mr. Unsworth said the plaintiff was a fireman in the employ of the company. About noon on Saturday February 13th, the managing director, Mr. Fleming gave instructions that the boilers were to be kept going all the week-end. Plaintiff was under the direction of the foremen named Naylor and Dean, and there was another fireman named Foley. Foy left work at one o'clock, on Naylor's instructions, and Foley had to take his place. Plaintiff again went to the works, as usual, at six o'clock on Sunday morning, but found that the fires had been allowed to go out. There was no one about, and he went home. He returned to the works on Sunday night and assisted in getting the boilers going again. On Monday he was told by the time-keeper that Mr. Fleming had said that he was not to be paid for his,work on Sunday night and he was dismissed. He went to ask Mr. Fleming for an explanation, but that gentleman waved his hand and told him he had to go, so plaintiff left the works. He (Mr. Unsworth) thought the magistrates would come to the conclusion that plaintiff had been made the scape- goat for someone else's wrong-doing. In cross-examination plaineiff said he knew the fires had to be kept going all the week-end, but he was not to blame if they went out, because Naylor gave him per- mission to go home. Mr. Browne said the pan of boiling salt was allowed to chrystalize and it took two men a day to clean it out.
Plaintiff denied that he was suspended until the pan had been cleaned, and not dismissed. In his opinion it ought to take only two hours bo clean the pan, and the loss to the firm would not be £lO.

The other fireman, named Foley, was called, and stated that he received his wages at one o'clock on the date in question. Naylor allowed him to go home to change his clothing, and Foy also left, Naylor stating that he would attend to the fires. At six O'clock in the evening Naylor allowed the fires to go out. Edward Beswick,timekeeper, said Foy was entitled to leave at one o'clock on Saturday. On Monday Mr. Fleming told witness to tell Foy to go home, as he was discharged, and would not be paid for Sunday night's work.

Mr. Browne said the case had assumed an entirely different aspect from what his instructions led him to believe. The directors were under the impression that Foy had caused the damage, and Mr. Fleming said he suspended him until the pan had been cleaned out. In face of the evidence it was impossible to answer the claim. _
The Mayor: That is our opinion. Judgment was then entered for Ithe plaintiff with costs.

div.head: GOOD NEWS FOR GAS CONSUMERS. A Welcome Reduction.
div.p: GOOD NEWS FOR GAS CONSUMERS. A Welcome Reduction.

"At a meeting of the Gas Committee yesterday it was reported that over 400 applications had been received for gas cookers from consumers who use penny-in-the-slot meters. In order to encourage the use of these cookers, and to meet the demand recently made for a ieduction in the price of gas to users of the penny-in-the-slot meters, it has been decided to increase the quantity of gas supplied for a penny from 25 feet to 28 feet. This will apply to all con- sumers using penny-in-the-slot meters. The decision of the commiti ee to increase the quantity of gas sup- plied will necessitate an alteration of the meters, and some time must necessarily elapse before all con- sumers will receive the benefit of the committee's welcome decision.

It may also be mentioned that consumers of gag outside the Borough are to receive a welcome conces- sion. Previously, consumers of gas outside the Borough have been called upon to pay sixpence per thousand cubic feet per mile in excess of the amount charged to consumers in the Borough. It has been decided to reduce this excess charge to threepence L per thousand feet per mile. The reduction will be discount allowed.

!WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT. A Batch of Failures. FRIDAY.---Before Mr. Registrar Ridgway. Re WILLIAM EDWARD BOYLEST.—This bankrupt, who had carried on business in Warrington as a wholesale and retail fruit, rabbit and poultry salesman,was further examined. His liabilities were expected to rank at £251 17s. sd. and the assets were estimated to produce £67 75. Bd., leaving a deficiency of £1.84 9s. 9d.—Mr. Steel represented the debtor.—Mr. Potter (assistant official receiver), said the case was adjourned in order that the bankrupt might file certain accounts. It was found impossible for him to do so as he had not kept proper books of account.—The examination was closed. Re THOMAS FORSTER, of 7, Duke-street, Run- corn, Bricklayer.—Mr. Hodge (Messrs. Browne and Company) represented the debtor. In his statement of affairs, the debtor showed liabilities, expected to rank at £llB 2s. 5d., and assets estimated to produce £l4 10s. leaving a deficiency of £lO3 12s. 4d. The causes of failure as alleged by bankrupt were "Loss of employment, sickness and deaths of nine children, and a liability incurred about four years ago as surety for my wife in respect of the drain- ing of a property which devolved on her about twelve months ago under her late mother's will." In his state- ment to the official receiver, the bankrupt stated that he had not since 1896 carried on business on his own account, and attributed his deficiency to liabilities in- curred as surety for his wife and mother-in-law in con- nection with property in Wellington-street/ and Duke- street, Runcorn, amounting to £87175. His wife was the owner of the equity of redemption in 5 dwelling houses situate in Wellington-street and Duke-street,the mortgagees of which had entered into possession.—The examination was closed.

Re WALTER CLARK, gentlemen's outfitter, 34 Queen- street, Earlestown. The debtor's liabilities were .C2lO 18s. Ild, and the assets £2B Bs. Id., leaving a deficiency of £lB4 us. 101 He alleged as the causes of failure "Bad trade, heavy expanses of a large fatally." The examination was closed.

Re JAMES POTTER, Deakin 's Farm, Croft, farmer. This bankrupt showed liabilities £126 7s. Bd.. and assets £l2 17s. (id., leaving a deficiency of £ll3 10s. 2d. The causes of failure as alleged by bankrupt were "Losses of horses; a wet season last year; heavy interest on loans; and household and personal expenditure in ex- cess of profits." This examination was also closed. A WARRINGTON PAINTER'S FAILURE.—George Plenry Hoult, plumber and painter, of Kir g-street, Warrington, appeared for his first public examination in bank- ruptcy. His statement of affairs showed liabilities £357 15s, 3d., assets £79 16s. 7d., leaving a deficiency of £277 18s. Bd. The causes of failure were attributed to "bad debts; bad trade ; household and personal ex penditure in excess of income or profits,and losses o contracts." In his statement to the Official Receiver the bankrupt stated that he commenced business in November 1896 with £5O borrowed capital. He carried the business on with a partner until July 1898 and sub- sequently alone.. Not having kept sufficient books of account, in particular neither cash book nor creditor's ledger, nor while in business, ascertained his financial position, he could not file a deficiency account. His wife claimed the whole of the household furniture, and a horse and trap as purchases partly out of moneys given to her by her father before her marriage.—The examination was closed.

_ FAILURE OF AN EARLESTOkVN GROCER.—Joseph Littler, residing at 3, Lawrence street, Earlestown, and carrying on business as a grocer and provision dealer and wine and spirit merchant at 13, Market street, Earlestown was examined by Mr. Johnson (assistant official receiver). The bankrupt's statement of affairs, showed liabilities £203 13s 10d, assets £lB4 5s 10d leaving a deficiency of £l9 8s Od. He alleged as the causes of failure : "insufficient trade; law costs, bad debts and sickness of himself." In his statement to the official receiver, bankrupt stated that he purchased the business for £175 in March, 1903. At the date of purchase he had £2BO free capital. Owing to illness he had been unable to superintend his busi- ness for the past six months. He first became aware of his insolvency about the beginning of December, and had contrracted debts since to the extent of £3O. He was hoping to recoup himself. He was previously manager of the shop.—The examination was closed sub- ject to the signing of the notes.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

FORTHCOMING LIBERAL SOCIAL.—On March 17th it is intended to hold a Liberal tea party and social in the Providence Schoolroom' Chapel-lane, Stockton Heath. —A Ladies' Committee has been appointed to assist the General Committee in carrying out the programme of the evening, which will probably prove to be of an interesting nature. Mr. King, the prospective Liberal candidate will be present, together with Mrs. King, and Alderman Pierpoint of Latchford has promised also to be present. It is hoped too that Mr. W. Long of Grappenhall will grace the proceedings with his pres- ence.—Other well known local gentlemen and ladies are expected to be present and in order to add to the enjoy- ment of the evening some music will be provided. FIRST WEDDING AT PROvIDE'NCE CHAPEL.—On Thursday last there was celebrated the first wedding that has taken place in the Providence new chapel, Stockton Heath. The happy parties were Mr. Drewitt well known insurance agent of Latchford and Miss Millington of the samerelace,,,ThE. Rev. J. F. Matthews officiated at the ceremony. Much interest was evinced in the event both the parties being well known, and quite a large number of visitors turned up to witness the affair,lthe ladies as usual who appear especially to interest themselves in these events, being considerably in the majority.

HILL CLIFFE AND STOCKTON HEA.TIt UNITED BAND OF , HOPE.—A well-attended entertainment was held in the Wesleyan Chapel on Monday evening. Tne occasion was "children's night" the meeting being entirely conducted by the younger members of the Socioty. The first part of the proceedings was in the hands of the fair sex, and was pleasingly directed by Miss Evelyn Beck. The young lady selected as a speaker was Miss F. Lowe, whose" maiden speech" was well delivered. The second part of the proceedings was supplied by the members of the "sterner sex," the chair being taken by Master Albert Bailey, Master Herbert Nicholls de- livering an address on the advantage of belonging to the Band of Hope. A capital programme was given. Miss May Isherwood saw-, Little pattering footsteps," and Master Thomas: Richmond received an encore for his song "The Flight of Ages." The action songs "The Farmer's Wife" and The Postman's Knock" were well rendered, and reflected great credit upon their trainer, Miss Woods. Masters Stanley Jones and Arthur Whitfield sang a duet very sweetly. The dialogue "Staunch Abstainers "by Elsie Whitfield, Ernest Whit field, Arthur Wheeler, Jane Harmer Bessie Pearse and Arnold Strange, five-year-dlds, was • a feature of the entertainment. Other dialogues were" The Band of Hope Fiscal Policy," by Stanley Jones and Arthur Whitfield; "A Slippery Track," by G Andrews, J. Whitfield, and W. Russage ; "Band of Hope Attrac- tions," by seven girls, and "Shoulder Arms,' by seven boys, each of whom displayed a Union Jack. Recita- tions were also given by Alice Cliffe, Dolly West, Gerty Cliffe, May Vernon, Mary Earle, and Lilly Hall, and Masters George Hughes, Sam Lloyd and Harold Jones. An organ solo was well played by.the youthful organist, Master G. A. Whitfield, who presided at that instrument throughout the even*.

div.head: MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS.
div.p: MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS.
Workingmen's Committee Formed.

On Thursday evening a well-attended meeting, con- vened by the Mayor, was held at the Town Hall with the object of appointing an auxiliary or Workingmen's Committee to raise funds for the proposed memorial to the officers and men of the South Lancashire Regi- ment (line, volunteersand militia) who fell lathe South African campaign. Mr. D. Davies we elected to the chair, and in opening the meeting said there was an impression that the movement had been somewhat de- layed and that tliere might have been a better response if earlier action had been taken. The services rendered by the regiment were, however, quite as greatly valued to-day as at the time when they were performed. They would always remembe: the sacrifices made by the soldiers with gratitude. A committee had been formed to further the project but it was considered necessary that all classes should have an opportunity of subscrib- ing to the memorial.

Mr. CATTERALL considered that the present time was inopportune for the effort, owing to the depressed state of trade. It would have been much better to have "struck while the iron was hot," but he now suggested that the meeting be adjourned for twelve months. Mr. W. L. WILLIAMS pointed out that the general committee had already commenced work and their efforts appeared to have been satisfactory as over .2400 had been raised. He was of opinion that a Working- men's Committee could do a great deal to supplement that work. The works managers could be approached with the object of ailing a meeting of tie employees to discuss the matter.
Mr. WINSTANLEY-was in favour of adjourning the meeting for six months as trade was usually better in summer. .

The CHAIRMAN thought it would be a misfortune to adjourn the meeting as the movement was now well under way. The effect would be to confine the memorial to those who had plenty of funds. Mr. T. RIGBY said that if they put their shoulders to the wheel he thought the movement would be suc- cessful.

It was ultimately decided on the proposition of Mr. Hope seconded by Mr. Rigby, that the work of raising funds should be at once proceeded with. The CI-LAMM:IN said the proposed statue to Colonel O'Leary would cost £1,500 but the form of the memorial would actually depend upon the sum raised. It was pointed out that 20 works were represented; 100 invitations to the meeting having been issued. It was decided that the representatives present should constitute a general committee, Mr. S. Davies being elected chairman; Mr. C. A. Newton, hon. secre- tary; and Mr. Hope, hon. treasurer. Meetings will be held fortnightly at the Town Hall.
The CHAYRIA-AN urged the desirability of strengthen- ing the committee, and invited new members.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough P3ilC3 Court.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough P3ilC3 Court.
Minor Cases.
Mosoar.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, Messrs. Birchall

and Wright. THEFT oF BOOTS.—A stranger giving the name of John Smith was charged with stealing a pair of boots, of the value of ss. from the shop of Mr. Lewis Fleming; Buttermarket-street.—Prisoner was seen by Mr. Dum- bell, hairdresser, to take the boots from the shop door- way and walk away. Mr. Dumbell followed him and handed him over to Superintendent Monagban.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month and the Bench specially thanked Mr. Dumbell for his prompt action. NAVAL DESERTER.—Frederick Broomfield, a youth, was charged with being a deserter from H.M.S. Pem- broke, stationed at Chatham, since September 19th.— The Chief Constable said Broomfield was arrested by Sergeant Cunliffe and P.C. Hodgkiss on information very properly supplied to the Admiralty by his father. He appeared to have deserted, through some fit or caprice, from Chatham Barracks where he was a member of the signalling corps.—Prisoner was handed over to the naval authorities.

TiluusDAY.—Before Messrs. John Fairclough (in the chair), F. W. Monks, and J. R. Young. SUSPICIOUS CONDUCT.—Patrick M`Donald, 2, Berry's- yard, was charged with being a person of suspicious character. He was found by a railway policeman in the Dallarn-lane siding of the London and North- Western Railway on Wednesday night. The prisoner, who had been previously convicted twenty-seven times, was sent to goal for a month with hard labour. A VICIOUS WOMAN.—Sarah Wilson, Scott-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brown- street at 6.40 p.m. on Wednesday. She pleaded not guilty. Police Constable Gilchrist proved the ease. The Chief Constable described the prisoner as a drunken, idle, and vicious woman. She was committed to goal for fourteen days with hard labour. SENT TO AN 'INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.—Harry Ratcliffe, Watkin-street, s‘ho was continually being found by the police sleeping out in the Market-place was sent to Ardwick Green Industrial School.
FRlDA.Y—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Roberts and Thornton, Dr. Fox, _Messrs. Birchall, H. Roberts, Hepherd, and

Wright. ROY IN TaoußLE.—Peter Ratcliffe, a small boy, was sent to an industrial school for wandering abroad with- out being under proper control. AN OLD OFFENCE.—Rebecca Riley was charged on a warrant with making use of obscene language in Plump- ton-street on May 27th, 1901.—P.C. Woods said the prisoner was drunk and made use of very filthy language to a constable who had since left the force. Prisoner absconded from the town—This was her 10th appear- ance and she was lined ss. with 10s. cost. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Peter Baguley, Sixsmith Farm, Sankey, was summoned for ill-treating a horse by causing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state.— Inspector Gibson proved the case, and defendant was lined in the costs (Ss. 6d.)—Thomas Rustage, of St. Helens, was summoned for cruelly beating a horse on February 24th.—Fred Nicholls, a storekeeper in the employ of Messrs E. Forsham and Company, said defendant, whilst under the influence of drink, severely thrashed the horse about the head and body with the butt end of a whip.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.

div.head: " Ethics of Socialism."
div.p: " Ethics of Socialism."

Under the auspices of the I L.P., a lecture on "The Ethics of Socialism " was delivered in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Sankey-street, an Sunday evening by Mr. Fred Bramley. The Rev. Herbert Dunnico presided. and, in introducing Mr. Bramley, expressed his sympathy with the endeavours of Socialism to raise the condition of the working classes. On the pro- position of Councillor Stott, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the rev, gentleman for presiding.

div.head: i THE EDUCATION POLICY OF THE 1 i FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: i THE EDUCATION POLICY OF THE 1 i FREE CHURCHES.

Forthcoming Newcastle Annual Council. Rev. Thomas Law, General Secretary of the Free Church Council informs us that at a very largely attended meeting of the Executive of the National Council just held, the terms of the Education Resolu- tions to be submitted to the Annual Council at New- castle next week were finally decided upon:— The first resolution expressing condemnation of the Acts is as follows :—That this Council once more ex- presses its unanimous emphatic condemnation of the. Education Acts of 1902 and 1903 as violating the estab- lished principles of the Constitution, as involving grave wrong to many consciences, and as inconsistent with educational progress. This will be moved by Mr. R. , W. Perks, M.P., and seconded by the Right Hon. James Bryce, M.P. I The second resolution expressing irinpathy with con- scientious objectors to payment of ucation rate will be moved by Rev. Dr. Robertson Nichol, and seconded by Mr. J. Bamford Slack, M.P., aufl is in the following ' terms :—The Council expresses its deep sympathy with ' den and women who, on conscientious grounds, have deemed it their duty to refuse voluntarily to pay the , denominational portion of the education rate. The Council urges the importance of such an immediate reform of the law as will obviate any further necessity for this form of protest. After these resolutions have been dealt with the assembly will proceed to consider the future educational policy suggested by the Executive. , In presenting these proposals, the Executive have in I view the establishment of a truly national and efficient system of education, which shall secure justice to every citizen and to conform to what the Executive believe to be the mind of the British people Subject to the essential principles involved in the fol- lowing proposals being secured, the Executive expresses the hope that the claim of other members of the com- munity may be duly considered and that a solution may be reached which will wound no conscience and will bring about a lasting educational peace. 1. That the system of education shall recognise only one type of public elementary schools, viz., schools provided and controlled by a public education authority. 2. That denominational school buildings, if required and suit- able for use as provided sohools, may be rented or pur- chased on equitable terms for the purpose of elemen - tary education, due regard being had to the existing rights of the public in such buildings. 3. That all schools maintained by public funds, whether by rates or taxes, shall be under the sole management and control of representatives appointed by the method of popular election 4. That there shall be adequate provision for the train- ing of all teachers of public elementary schools free from theological and ecclesiastical tests, and under the sole management and control of popularly-eleoted education authorities. 5. That no ecclesiastical or theological tests shall be applied in the appointment of teachers of publicly-supported schools or training colleges. 6. That no distinctively denominational teaching or formulary be given or used in public schools inschool hours, but simple Biblical instruction maybe given according to a syllabus, as is general at present in provided schools ; attendance at such instruction shall be subject to a conscience clause. 7. That the foregoing provisions shall also have reference to secondary education, as far as they may be applicable. 8. That women shall be eligible for election to any local education authority throughout England and Wales, and including London. These resolutions will be spoken to by Rev. Dr. John Clifford, Rev. J. Scott Lidgett M.A., Sir George Keke- wich, Rev. J. H. Shakespeare M.A., Rev. J. Hirst Hollowell, Mr. D. Lloyd George M.P., and others. The whole of Wednesday morning March 9th will be devoted to the discussion of these resolutions. Mr. Lavv states that there is likely to be a record attendance at Newcastle. Already considerably over a thousand representatives have been appointed. In addition to the hospitality provided by 6. Newcastle friends the hotels of the city and districts are being booked up. Those wishing to become personal mem- bers should apply to Mr. Law, Memorial Hall, London at once. The Committee has unanimously decided to, nominate Dr. R. E. Horton as President off Council for 1905.

div.head: WARRINGTON SEIETII.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON SEIETII.
Annual Meeting.

Mr. C. Madeley presided at the annual meeting of this Society which was held at the Old Academy on Monday evening.—ln their /annual report the hon. secretaries (Alderman Bennett and Mr. E. J. Hall) alluded to the celebrations of the Priestley Centenary in Warrington, Birmingham and Leeds. "Warrington" they continued "is sadly short of statues—it has only one, indeed, at present, the statue of Oliver Cromwell which we owe to the generosity of one of our own members (Mr. Frederick Monks)—but we are glad to know that a movement is on foot to commemorate the 'valour of our local regiment in the receat South African war by erecting in Queen's Gardens a portrait statue of the late Lieutenant-Colonel MacCarthy O'Leary, who lost his life whilst leadinc, his men in the final charge on Pieter's Hill, which 'cleared the way for the relief of Ladysmith, ami to place tablets on the base of the memorial recording the names of all the soldiers in the regiment (whether regulars, reservists, militia, or volunteers), who died on service during the war. In this connection, we may say that a street has already been called after Colonel O'Leary, and a beauti- ful oak screen and brass tablet erected in the Parish Church as a memorial of the services of the South Lancashire Militia. We trust the members of the War- rington Society will liberally support this later and more general memorial. We trust that in due course, the illustrious memory of Priestley and of Howard, at least may be commemorated not less worthily. A statue of Howard would be specially appropriate on the broad flagged area in Howard-place. In the meantime, we must be content with tablets; and, as soon as the necessary funds are forthcoming, the execu- tive desire to dignify a number of other interesting local houses by erecting on them suitable in- scriptions, probably in bronze. Any donations towards this object will be gratefully received." I Reference was made to the death of Mr. Robert Garnettand to the departure from Warrington iof the Rev. E. W. Lummis. The society was now ' numerically in a stronger position than ever before. Financially, its position was not yet so satisfactory as they would like. Many members had contributed most generously towards its various funds, and, in the early part of the year, a special effort was made to reduce the overdraft, which resulted in a fund of £27 5s 11d. This, however was contributed by 19 members only, and they felt that any futureeffort of thekind should receive the support of all who shared in the privileges offered by the society. The dozen guarantors, who undertook to make themselves responsible for the rent of the Academy for a term of five years from the Ist of Jan- uary, 1899, have not been called upon in that capacity, but they had shown their interest in the Academy and in the general work of the society by contributing not I less than £207 lOs towards its general funds. Hitherto I they had been legally responsible for the government of its affairs, although, in practice, they had left the man- agement entirely to the rank and file. Henceforth their obligation ceased but the secretaries were sure that every member of the society would warmly thank them for having rendered its existence possible, and they trusted that, as ordinary members, they might long continue to support its aims, and aid its efforts to promote the best traditions and the highest welfare of the town.

Alderman BEN-NErr said the general income had been £154 4s. 2d., and there waf: a deficiency of £l9 175., on the normal working of the society. There was a mem- bership of 136. He thought there was a reasonable ex- pectation of making ends meet next year. (Applause.) The report and financial statement were adopted. A discussion took place as to the best means of plac- ing the society in a sounder financial position. It was decided to impose an entrance fee of 10s. 6d. the question of the increased subscription to be referred to the General Purposes Committee for con- sideration, and report to a special meeting of the society. The report and statement of accounts were then agreed to.
