div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 5 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 5 1904
THE UNEMPLOYa.
THE CORPORATION TO PROVIDE WORK.

The attention of the Warrington Town Council was directed on Tuesday evening to the unemployed ques- tion. Councillor STorr moved "that in order to provide work for unemployed Warrington citizens during the present trade depression, the Corporation shall immediately proceed with some of the contemplated street improvements, ond any other work which can be commenced without unnecessary delay." If any man ought to have the sympathy of the Council, he said, it was the man who was out of work. It was one of the most difficult positions that a workingman was ever placed in—that of wanting work and being unable to get it. At the present time there was a great amount of unemployment. Apart from the men who were out of employment, they had to consider those who were working short time. He was told last week that there were men engaged in the iron trade who were only working one day per week on the average. These men seemed to be forgotten. He mentioned it to show that ,the men-who were supposed to be employed were able to assist those who were totally unem- ployed if any work could be found. The question had been considered by the General Purposes Com- mittee and various suggestions had been made. It was suggested that the Corporation should proceed with- out delay with some of the contemplated street im- provements. There was plenty of work which the committees knew perfectly well about that could be taken in hand immediately. Bradford, Leeds, Hali- fax and Glasgow had proceeded with work which it was not intended to have taken in hand for some time, in order to find work for the un- employed. Objection had been raised to this course being taken on the ground that it was national work. He agreed, but at the present time there seemed no passibility of this question being taken up nationally. The subject was thought to be of such little importance that there were only about a dozen members present in the House of Commons when the matter was brought forward. That ought to convince the members that something should be done locally. In Warrington there was plenty of work contemplated, including street improvements, the pulling down of buildings for street widening, the laying of a bowling green at Latchford,and the altera- tions to the open space at Orford-lane. He believed a large amount of .unskilled labour could be employed. He did not ask for work to be found for skilled artisans. Trades Unionists had many difficulties to contend with. When a man was out of work he had a tend- ency to accept employment at any price and thereby injure those who had had the common sense to organise by pulling down their wages. He looked upon the question he had introduced from a pnrelk sympathetic point of view, because when there were men willing to work,ithey ought to try,if possible, to provide them with some employment. COURCHIOTPETBR. PRICOCK, in seconding the motion said the question of the unemployed unfortunately was one which was engaging the attention of the various local authorities in the country, and they in Warrington should certainly do something towards alleviating the distress which was existing to a great extent, and particularly In Bewsey Ward where the iron trade was having its full share of depression. He felt sure that the various committees could find labour for a large number of willing men, and he ventured to suggestithere was plenty of urgent work which was wait lug—if only the members and officials would look round. He would point out the desirability of having a good, share, if not all the street making done by the Corpora- tion, and instead of allowing quagmires as substitutes for streets, we should commence at once in preparing the foundations for paving, and this would, together with the recreation ground between Orford-lane and Win Wick-road which could be commenced, do some little towards keeping the wolf from the door. Let the members of the Council look at the disgraceful state of many of the streets and roads, and if they could not realize the condition of the same properly with the naked eye, cycle over them—(laughter)—and they would find plenty of work which unskilled labour could assist in putting right. There were other improve- ments which were most pressing and he felt sure the members of the Council should rise to the occasion and do their duty. On the other hand, if out of all the committees, no immediate employment could be given, he would respectfully ask the Mayor to call a meeting with a view of opening a public subscription to temporarily relieve pressing cases,which were numerous and save the necessity of building extra accommodation at the Workhouse, a building which was now too full to properly meet the present requirements. Several depu- tations had waited upon him, and he understood some other members of the Council had also been seen, with a view of approaching the Mayor to devise some scheme to get over this temporary difficulty. (Hear, hear.) Councillor ROGBR.S said he knew that in the Bewsey district some workingmen and their families were literally starving. A deputation waited upon him and asked him to support the resolution. E-13 was very pleased to hear one of the. members of the deputation say that they preferred the opening out of relief works to the establishing of soup kitchens. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in supporting the motion. Alderman PIERPOINT said he had also been waited upon by a deputation, and he supported the motion. An intimation was given to him that the men—and he was speaking more particularly of those engaged in the iron trade—were vary anxious that the Corporation should look at the question from a charitable point of view. These men wanted work, and he was given to understand that there were 180 puddlers and 20 by-turn men employed by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, who had only done 17 turns since Christmas. It was explained to him that a turn meant a day's work. The men assured him that, their children had gone to school that morn- ing without having breakfast before they turned out. If these facts given him were correct there must be at the lowest computation 1,200 men, women and children nearly on the verge of starvation. It was very difficult for a Corporation to take aimatter of this kind in hand. He hardly knew how to start it. Perhaps the appointment of a sub-committee to take the matter in hand would facilitate matters.

Commitfor Tinnion thought a good deal might be done by the respective committees. The Paving and Sewerage ;Committee had decided,without anyone asking them, to instruct the Borough Surveyor to proceed with any work that would not interfere with the present year's estimates. The committee did a good deal of private work and the committee could authorise sueh work to be taken in hand at once. He thought there were other Committees of the Corporation that might deal with work in this way. Wherever work could be done that did not interfere with the present year's esz timates it ought to be taken in handat once. Alderman SMETHURST said he would be very pleased indeed as Chairman of two committees to do what he could in the direction indicated. He hoped other Chairmen would do likewise. Councillor STorr hoped the resolution would not be considered a pious expression of opinion, but that some- thing would be done immediately. .

Councillor BURTON said he wa's in sympathy with the resolution. When there was no work at the manufactories they could not Jet the pantile starve. He thought the matter ought to The dealt with by the Council. Some years ago when there was great distress in !the town, the Corpora tion, found a good deal of work for the unemployed. He did not see why they could not do so now. There was no necessity to wait for a sub-com- mittee to consider the matter. If the Borough Sur- veyor were consulted, he could look round and see what work could be given out immediately.

Councillor tiODDs said he would lika to put Mr Alderman Piet-point right on one point. He referred to 180 puddlers and some other ironworkers having only done 17 days' work since Christmas. The three rate- payers who called upon Alderman Pierpoint also called upon him, and he told them he was prepared to help them privately and as a member of the Council. The statement in the book which was brought by the deputa- tion,referring to 17 turns since Christmas,only referred to the men who brought it. He knew that of his own knowledge. __

Councillor IVIAGINN thought steps could be taken to construct the new road across Victoria Park to give access to the proposed now bridge across the river at Howley. He was anxious to do what he could to find work for the unemployed. He was pleased to hear that the Unemployed would rather have work than soup kitchens. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried.

div.head: BLACKPOOL'S "GIPSY SARAH" DEAD.
div.p: BLACKPOOL'S "GIPSY SARAH" DEAD.

Gipsy Sarah, who has been one of Blackpool's stand in" attractions on the sands at South Shore for 77 years hasjust passed away at the age of 98. Sarah Boswell, to give her her full name, was a native of Kent, where she was born in 1805' and it was her proud boast that she was a descendent of the wise men from the East. The Biswells hove long been regarded as the only genuine descendents of the gipsy tribes,and Alma,Gipsy Sarah's eldest son is left behind at the head of affairs. She leaves four Children and 18 grandchildren. The name of Gipsy Sarah has been a familias one to thous- ands of visitors to Blackpool, and her quaint figure and pleasing manner will be greatly missed. She will be interred with the customary nomadic rites at the Black- pool Cemetery to-morrow.

The Oldhamia, a large steel screw steamer intended for the Manchester Ship Canal trade of Messrs. Sive- might, Bacon, and Co., has been launched from the yard of Messrs. Furness Withy and Co., West Hartlepool,and christened by Miss Andrew, of Oldham. The boat is 364 feet long.

div.head: YELLOW LABOUR QUESTION.
div.p: THE YELLOW LABOUR QUESTION.
REV. JOHN YONGE AND VIRTUAL SLAVERY.
STRONG CONDEMNATION FROM THE

Preaching in Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Yonge made a solemn protest against the proposal of the Government to import Chinese labourers into South Africa to work in the gold and diamond fields on conditions of virtual slavery. There was a large congregation. He based his remarks on the text "Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteausness and his chambers by wrong" Jeremiah 22c. part of 13v. When a man or a nation, he said, sought to "build houses by uarighteousness, or chambers by wrong," it was necessary for Christian people to prevent the attempt, if possible, or at any rate to utter unequivocal testimony as to its evil. Such an attempt was now being made by the rulers of the British Empire, and therefore it was the solemn duty of all who truly feared God and regarded man in his highest welfare to protest against it.

THE DUTY OF THE CHURCHES. An occasion had clearly arisen wherein the Christian churches were called upon to earnestly interfere in the politics of the empire. such intervention could not justifiably be deemed an intru- sion. The pulpit of the church had a duty to the State as well as to the individual. It ought not to display an unseemly partizanship and advooate or deprecate any especial line of policy which might be proposed by a political party—unless as was now the case—the policy of a party was manifestly unrighteous in principle and design. The occasions were rare in which the pulpit should speak upon distinctly political subjects, for its message was supremely spiritual and evangelical. But when theirights of humanity were imperilled; when the nation was counselled to a course that would put men in physical and social bondage. when Christian Britain wasproposing to bring in to what appeared practi cal slavery thousands of a heathen people—then the occasion had come for plain speech in every freedom- loving, Christ-obeying pulpit, and for earnest and ever indignant remonstrance by all the churches that were faithful to the World's Redeemer. Doubt- less by politicians who sought to promote the policy, any Christian minister who used his pulpit to protest against it (especially if he be himself a Liberal in politics) would be suspected of and charged with speaking from motives of partizanship. But in the present case, the attitude of remonstrance and pro- test was being shared by a considerable number of Con- servative politicians, and also by a considerable num- ber of Anglican ecclesiastics, Episcopal and clerical men who were sensible both of the political inexpedi- ency and the political unrighteousness of the policy that was now being rushed through .the legislature. This, therefore, was not a party question. It was a national question, an imperial question, even a humanitarian question, and it behoved every freedom-loving citizen of this great empire, and every follower of Him who sought to save men from all bondage, to speak and act against this revival and this licence of a measure of slavery within the dominions of Great Britain.

THE HOME OF FREEDOM. Christian England had been the home and the friend of freedom for long centuries. Sims, at any rate the abolition, nearly a century ago, of Nthvery in the West Indies, England had made it her boast that wherever her flag was unfurled and planted there freedom was established. Its citizens vociferously sang "Britons never shall be slaves." Sometimes its citizens might have sung it loudest when their own physical condition had most contradicted it. But whether sober or other- wise;they meant it; if need arose they would fight in the last ditch, to the last man, to prevent the destruc- tion of their liberty. If ever England needed a second Cromwell he would be found somewhere among her sons, and her sons would rally round him and carry the cause of British liberty to Ivictory—unless indeed which Goal forbid—the old British freedom should one day miserably die. For his own part he could not believe that the British people would permit the pro- posed policy in South Africat THE YELLOW LA.BOURER.

After recalling the action of England in 1875-6 when British feeling against the recognition of slavery in. any degree whatever, and the nation stood out for free- ing the fugitive slave at any and every risk, the preacher proceeded to explain the actual case that has arisen in South Africa, and quoted the Government ordinance, to arrange for the importation from China of large bodies of Chinese, who will work in the mines, it was stated for sevenpence a day. It was notorious, he continued that Chinese labourers could live on food upon which neither African native nor British work- man could exist. and they could dwell in physical con- ditions so insanitary as would be death to the people of the West. These Chinese were to be brought over by " importers," who would reap large profits by the trans- action. They were to be housed, not like human beings but herded like cattle—they were to be confined in com- pounds, from which they would be forbidden to go out, even in hours not devoted to work,. save by permit ob- tained from the employer. Any employer might transfer these labourers to other employerstaltoaether apart frost consent of the men themselves. Any labourer trans- gressing the regulations was to be imprisoned or fined in sums, one would think, absolutely impossible of pay- ment. Any person aiding a labourer to escape from his employer was to be fined or imprisoned. The men were to be bound for a term, and thou ,fit the expiry of it, shipped back to China; not allowed, however worthy, to find either place or lot in the land of their servitude. Virtual slave dealing was formally sanctioned and regularized by a clause which stipulated that "any im- porter may, with the sanction of the Lieutenant- Governor,and under the regulations made by him, transfer in writina, his (the importer's) rights under any con- tract witil any labourer to any other person who has a licence to import labourers under the ordinance, and thereupon such labourers, and such other persons, shall be bound &c.," in certain specified ways.

div.head: OTHER SIDE OF THE CASH.
div.p: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE CASH.

There were people who said that this,after all this was not 'what was popularly understood as" slavery." They said first of all, that according to the scheme no Chinaman was to be deported from. China to South Africa without distinctly under- standing the conditions he was accepting. They said, secondly, that the Chinaman was entering upon a con- tract to serve the mine-owner similar in kind and conditions to that of a man who enlisted in the British Army to servo the King. It might be questioned whether either of these allegations was correct. It would not be probable that the large numbers of Chinese labourers to be imported could be made to clearly comprehend the very elabwate details of this extra- ordinary scheme. Nor was it likely that the most ignorant lad from the country would be beguiled into enlisting in the King's Army, if he supposed that he was to be subjected to conditions that completely deprived him of all personal liberty. These allegations therefore could hardly pass.

div.head: SATIRE UPON OUR CHRISTIANITY.
div.p: SATIRE UPON OUR CHRISTIANITY.

But the thing to be noted was that the slavery aspect of the scheme had been reaognised by no less a person- age than the Chinese Ambassador in London, who had put his finger upon it. He saw the mischief that might go on under these "importers of labour," Who would ever have dreamed of England in the 20th century creating a new system of virtual slavery, which should need a protest, and oall for the interference of the ambassador of a heathen power, in the interests and for the safe-guarding of humanity! It was certain that the heathen Chinee did not trust the Christian employer of, labour. in South Africa! The echoes of American slavery had not yet died away. The crack of the slave- owners' whip still resounded in the memories of men. And so the heathen ambassador sought to put statutory fetters upon the freedom ,of Christian employers, lest they should be tempted to treat their human serfs as if they were but cattle! This was a most scathing satire upon the possibilities of British Christianity. The preacher quoted the opinion of Dr. Miller Maguire, a fam9u9 army coach and a fervent Unionist, who declared the scheme to be "outrageous wickedness and folly." The colonies in other parts of the world were declaring against the scheme. The Progressives in Cape Colony —which was the only colony in South Africa where there are at present representative institutions—spoke in terms of horror and repudiation of it. Experts stated that no need existed for this expedient, and thus abundant reasons, even of expediency, combined to counsel its rejection. It was not however, neces- sary to argue the matter from any other standpoint than that of human freedom and Christian principle. The scheme violated both the one and the other.

div.head: WHITE SLAVERY M ENGLAND.
div.p: WHITE SLAVERY M ENGLAND.

The principles of Christ were the contradiction of all slavery, in all its forms and degrees. They con- tradicted and condemned many forms of white slavery which still existed here in the very midst of a free empire. There were many slaves in many a workshop and labour den in this country, who worked for a merest pittance, and in horrible conditions. Laws were gradu- ally reforming these abuses and labour unions were watching over the welfare of the working classes. But
Fels-Naptha
Soap differences: no other labour-saving soap; no other clothes-saving soap; no other money-saving soap; no other moneyback soap.
Fels-Naptha 39 Wilson street London E C

this case of the importation of Chinese into South Africa was the most flagrant violation of personal liberty that this age had known in our empire. Of course it was true to say that the Chinese need not be imported unless they chose ; that they were not going to be carried off into slavery as the negroes used to be from Africa to America by main force. So far that, no doubt, was true. But if they came, they must in one way or another sign away their liberty. They must agree to be kept within bolts and bars ; they must sub- mit to rules as yet perhaps, unwritten, but which when once the owners got hold of them, they would enforce despite every protest. All this was inconsistent with human freedem,and an empire that claimed to be the friend and upholder of liberty could not be right in permitting it.

A PARLIAMENTARY SNEER. In Parliament, the other day a Cabinet minister sneered at what he called "The Episcopal and Nonconformist conscience," and spoke of it as now extending into a sphere that was not its own. It was an unworthy sneer, and probably the statesman who indulged in it had regretted it since. But the sneer revealed a covert scepticism which was common. Thera were many who did not believe in religion—or the • rights of humanity —as primefactors in affairs of State and Churches only did their Christian duty by insisting that the State should not contravene Christianity. Experts told them that the mine-owners could obtain abundant labour, if they would pay properly for it. The Kaflirs would work, if pay were right, and conditions of living were safe. Moreover, they knew only too well what multitudes of workless people there were in this country. They knew also how South Africa had crowds of them to-day ; wanting work willing to work, but they wanted a living wage,and they ought to have it. They could have it,yet leaving a wide profit for employers—so experts declared. That being the case, the need for importation of labourers was not so extreme as the promoters of the scheme asserted. The real need for the scheme was in the gold hunger of the mine owners. John Burns,speaking at Birming- ham' said the lobby of the 11-louse of Commons was being thronged with secretaries of mining companies interested in the introduction of this slavery. It was by the use of slaves that they could increase their divi- dends, and also work low grade mines and levels which could not otherwise be exploited.

div.head: PLUTOCRATS OF SOUTH AFRICA.
div.p: THE PLUTOCRATS OF SOUTH AFRICA.

rhus, continued the preacher, it • was-. the Plutocrats of South Africa—most of them living in London—who wanted cheap, enforced labour. This scheme promised it. His (Mr. Yonge's) earnest hope was that the pro- mise would long tarry of fulfilment, and be broken in the finish. Here then, appeared to be a critical matter which called for the prompt action of Christian people. If the churches could not now find voice in behalf of national righteousness, when would they? This was a wrong against humanity, to which the Church of the World's Divine Emancipator could never silently consent. He wished very earnestly that something more could be done there that night than the delivery of that address. Many people had great dislike for any transaction connected with a religious service which had a decided political character. Upon this particular question, it was represented to him that a division of opinion existed—even among religious people --which would make the submitting of any defin- ite resolution undesirable. He extremely regretted it, if that be really the case. Personally he had thought they might have asked the congregation to assent to a united declaration of an abhorrence of the scheme, and their earnest desire that Parliament should even yet rescind the sanction accorded. If, however, they were not prepared for a united expression of such an opinion, perhaps the review of the subject might help to promote a pablio opinion in its disfavour. He firmly believed that the nation was being led into most serious evil by this policy. The South African difficulty would be augmented by :it. The Empire would yet discover at how terrible a cost it had pur- chased its new possessions, and to what unrighteous uses and ends those possessions were being devoted. At least, they could unite in the patriotic prayer that God, the supreme Ruler of men, would save our Empire from every policy that dishonoured religion and degraded mankind.

div.head: OUR LEAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LEAL CHURCHES.
S3PIiC.IS for the Paopie.

The Royal Court Theatre was crowded on Sunday evening, when the Rev. H. Dunnico preached. He ex- pressed the great pleasure he felt in addressing himself to "the people," and by the people he meant the workers and toilers. The people, the preacher stated, had distinctive and peculiar needs. They needed three things, viz., a vision of God, saving from all evil and a larger and a fuller life, and he showed that Christ could meet all their needs.] The idea of God was an in- dispensable factor of life. Men's lives were governed by the conception they had of God, and it was seen how the national life of ancient Corinth and Athens was directly a reflection of the gods whom the people worshipped. Before Christ came to the world there was no perfect conception of God, but He gave to the people a fresh revelation of God as their Father, and with that there came the sublime conception of the brotherhood of man. Christ could help men to overome all that was evil and to live grand and noble lives. It was sometimes said that the Kingdom of God upon earth was long in coming, and while admitting that the Christian churches had hindered by their indifference and apathy, the preacher appealed to the workingmen, and asked what they had done to advance that Kingdom. In our midst at the present day was the drink trade, and workingmen, as the backbone of EnFland, were by their very numbers responsible for the existence of that traffic. He would not go so far as to say the drink trade should be banished, but that it should be kept in its proper place. Then with regard to elections, how many were prepared to sell their votes, and he urged men to cast their votes only on the side of sobriety, truth and righteousness. If men would take Christ for their Saviour, their example, and carry His spirit into their politics, busi- ness, and all the affairs of life, the Kingdom of God would come. upon earth. The preacher closed with an earnest appeal to the young people to enter into the larger and fuller life in dhrist Jesus.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

• The usual meeting was held on Sunday, when there was an average attendance. The Hon. Sec. (Mr. B. Farrar) presided, and said that was the last" Sunday of another year—the eleventh year of the society's exist- ance—and the meetings had been quite as full of inter- est as any of the previous years. He asked them to think of what could be done, if every member of the brotherhood made up, his mind that that P.S.A. should have even larger numbers, and a greater usefulness in this town. He next reviled 'to the remarks of the Bishop of Manchester and others, upon the P.S.A.work. If the society was not making as many members of churches as they would like, neither did any churches, for that matter, yet P.S.A. brethren were under the blessed influences of the Gospel.—Mr. A. King, of Man- chester,drew useful lessons from the life of the Apostle Luko.Though a Gentile,yet he became a worker for Christ and a helper of the Apostle Paul in his three journeys. The lesson of helpfulness was beautifully worked out, and the speaker urged all present to seek to be helpers in their daily life, their Christian life, and their P.S.A. life.—The Chairman feelingly expressed the feelings of sympathy of the brotherhood,with one of the members, Mr. J. Taylor, on the death of his brother Mr. William Taylor. He also hoped all the brethren would become missioners on behalf of the society during the week, so that they could have a good start on their eleventh anniversary day and open meeting.—Mr. J. Owen and S. Rowlands also took part in the meeting.

div.head: Emmanuel Church, Warrington.
div.p: Emmanuel Church, Warrington.

The vacancy in the pastorate of the above church caused by the death of the late Rev. A. G. D. Gee has been filled by the appointment of the Rev. F. Vaughan who is announced to preach his first sermons as curate- in-charge on Sunday next. Mr. Vaugham, who is a staunch Protestant and Evangelical churchman, has, for ths past six years, held the post of Evangelist of the Scripture Readers Society of Liverpool, which position he has filled with much success and as a mission preacher he has been in groat request. The subjects of the special sermons on Sunday are in commemoration of the Centenary of the Bible Society and are entitled "The living Word of God" and "The Victories of God's Book.

div.head: NEW BRIDSE AT HOWLEY.
div.p: A NEW BRIDSE AT HOWLEY.
COUNCILLOR MAGIAN'S MOTION CARRIED.
The Victoria Park of the Future.

At the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening Councillor Magiaa introduced the following motion of which he had given notice :- 1. That it is desirable that a suitable bridge be constructed across the Mersey at Howley. r. 2. That plans, specification and estimate of a single span iron girder bridge be prepared. 1 In the course of his speech he said he could not claim the honour of being the originator 'of the scheme, as it was discussed about ; seven years ago, and by the best brains of the Council was considered a fit and proper means of developing that part of the town. Unfortunately then, as at the present time, the feeling of procrastination ruled, so the Council decided that it was a good scheme, and left it over for the future. He hoped they: would not adopt the same course that , night. Land in Howley district, to the extent of 25 acres, was being wasted because there was not a new road into Cheshire. Nine years ago the Corporation purchased the Old Warps estate with the avowed intention of making it into a park. They even went so far as to name it "Victoria Park," locked the gate, and let ic to a farmer. (Laughter.) He believed that estate was a good investment to the itown, and the purpose for which it was bought was the right one. But what, in the name of goodness, I was the use of a park without any road leading to it? People living in the neighbourhood of the Cetnetery had, in order to visit the Park by way of Warrington Bridge, to travel a quarter of a mile farther than people coming from Lymm. Was that sensible or reasonable? A new bridge at Howley was necessary I for ale development of the Park. What was the position in the Howley district itself? He contended that on the land now vacant there should be ereeted 1400 houses, with a population of 2,000, and a rateable value of £lO,BOO. It was estimated that the cost of a new bridge to replace Warrington Bridge would ba £15,000. He would put down the cost of a bridge Id Howley at £lB,OOO, which was equivalent to a rate of a, in the pound. Two hundred and fifty new houses a" Howley would bring in the extra penny, but he con- sidered that in one year the number of houses would be increased by considerably more than 250. He estimated , that in five years the new bridge would have reduced the rates by at least sd. in the 2 and cost only ld.in the £. Thera were 52 acres of land at Victoria Park and it I was let to a farmer at a rental of .265 per annum. The cost of the park each year, in interest, &c., was £4OO, so that. the Corporation was losing £335. A now bridge at Howley would open out the district, and relieve the traffic over Warrington bridge by at least one fourth or one fifth. It would also enable the Corporation to pro- vide the best possible circular tram route. The park would be one of the finest recreation grounds in Lancashire and Cheshire if properly de- veloped. He suggested that the Corporation might follow the example of Sheffield and other towns and let some of the land to townspeople to cultivate as flower, fruit and vegetable gardens. Prizes could be offered to encourage the hobby and a rental of about £2O a year charged for each plot. He had nothing against the proposed bowling green, but would it not be more beneficial to bring the people a little more closely into touch with nature, and teach them to grow something useful as well as beautiful. He also advocated the construction of the new bridge as a means of pro- vidincr work for the unemployed. Alderman BBNNETT seconded, pointing out that he had been favourable to the scheme all along. They could only hope to develop the park and make full use of it, by erecting the bridge. The members must be struck with the force of what Councillor Maginn said with reference to the way in which the opening out of anew road would improve the value of land in Howley, tend to the erection of property and the inoreasing of tho rateable value. A further advantage would be that the residents in Howley and Fairfield Wards would be brought into touch with .the park and, if the Corpora- tion did not spend money on the park, the people would at any rate have the opportunity of running in green fields und indulging in sports. The bridge would also very materially reliere the overcrowding of War- rington bridge. Councillor ROGERS said it had been suggested times without number that the Corporation should acquire more open spaces but if the bridge were erected, they would not require any more recreation grounds in the Howley and Fairfield districts.

Alderman PIERPOINT remarked that they already had a plan of a single iron girder bridge. It was eminently desirable that there should be a bridge at Howley, and he would be very pleased if the Council would enter into the project as soon as they could do so with any- thing like financial ease.

Arderman SMETHURST said that if the Council saw lit to go into an expenditure of £lB,OOO he had nothing to say against it. A new bridge was very desirable,but he must warn the Council that the rates were going up. ,4The DEPUTY-MAYOR: The rates have not gone up. They are the same that they have been for years. Alderman SMETHURST, continuing, said that in less than two years they would have to build schools at a cost of .E 20,000 or £30,0.0. The DEPUTY-IVIAYOR: That means a penny on the rates.

Alderman SMETHURST: The bridge at Howley will be a penny and a new Warrington Bridge would be another penny. We don't know where the rates will finish. I hope the Council will not sanction the expense on a bridge at Howley. If you want to spend that amount, spend it at Bridge Foot. We' want to spend something like £lOO,OOO in widening streets. We are asked to find work for the unemployed. Would it not be better to pull some buildings down? Councillor MAGINN : And reduce your rateable value Alderman Smuraußs'e : And erect shops that will bring in a higher rateable value. Councillor DODDS said be apprehended that the Coun- cil, if it passed the resolution, would not be committed to taking up the scheme at once. The MAYOR: You are not committed to anything except the preparation of plants. Councillor STOTT thought that if the Council took up the matter in earnest and built the bridge, the rate- payers would "gleefully" pay the small amount which it would cost. He would like to ask whether all the land required was in the hands of the Corporat:on ? The TOWN CLERK: Yes. Councillor STOTT : In that ease, the argument I was going to use would not apply. The TOWN CLERK: Do you mean the land required for improving the approaches to the proposed bridge on this side? _

Councillor SToTT: Yes I mean the approaches. The TOWN CLERK: That land has not been bought. Councillor STOTT : Well my argument is this: the longer we delay the scheme, the more we will have to pay. Continuing Councillor Stott said that from the point of view.of providing a healthy recreation ground for the people at the Howley end of the town, the ques- tion of paying an additional penny in the £ on the rates ought not to hinder the scheme. If this money were spent he thought they would hear less about it from the ratepayers than some members supposed. The Corpor- ation had spent money which the ratepayers had objected to but he did not think the ratepayers would object to this scheme. (Hear' hear.) Councillor TINNION said the Council was only ex- pressing a pious opinion on the scheme that evening. They did not commit themselves to anything definite regarding the bridge, except that it should be 60 , feet wide. He was rather inclined to the opinion that they ought to make it even wider than that. He would like the resolution better if the width of the bridge were left out.
Councillor MAGINN : I will not stiok to the bridge being 60 feet. ___

Coimoillor-ThrmoN : If this resolution is passed,you will have to stick to it. (Laughter). When you get a double line of tramway across the bridge you will re- quire a greater width. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH (who presided in the tempor- ary absence of the Mayor whilst declaring the result of the auditors' election): He did not propose anything about a double line of tramways. Councillor MAGINN : I am willing to withdraw the words "60 feet wide." Councillor TINNION said he would protest against anything being withdrawn. He (Councillor Tinnion) had been the unfortunate mover of resolutions and he had not been allowed to alebr anything. If they de- layed the construction of the bridge for ten years.— Councillor MA G INN : Procrastination again,— Councillor TINNION (continuing) said if they delayed the work for ten years they would only postpone a small repayment of the cost for that number of years. He understood that the Corporation would be allowed 50 years in which to repay the money expended on the bridge, so that they would only delay the payment of a proportion of the cost for ten years by delaying the work for that number of years. Alderman PIERPOINT : If you delay it ten years I shall notfsee it. (Laughter). • Alderman FAIRCLOUGH stated that in 1896 the Cor- poration was granted an extension of the Borough. A differential rating clause was inserted for the benefit of the ratepayers who were brought into the Borough by the extension. It was stipulated that at the end of five years, these ratepayers should pay one-third of the

Borough rates, at-the close of ten years, two-thirds of the rates, and at the expiration of fifteen years, the full amount of the rates. in 1906, these ratepayers would commence to pay the two-thirds portion of Borough rates, and reckoning this increase on the present basis it would represent an amount equal to a penny in the R. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MAGI NINT contended that the spirit of pro- crastination had been the curse of Warrington. What would they think of a man, he said, who had a gold wateh and put it by in a drawer for the benefit of his grandchild, and himself went about the place looking for the Town Clock. (Laughter.) The town purchased the Victoria Park estate for £lO,OOO in 1897 and had made little use of it. It was costing the ratepayers £335 per annum. Instead of leaving this estate to the future, let the Council •get a little good out of it in their own time. (Hear, hear.) Even if they spent £lB,OOO, £20,000 or £25,000 on a bridge, roads and park, it would be money spent in the town and would increase the trade of the district. This craze for wide streets was one of the silliest things in bad times. They knocked down buildings and put up nothing in their place, thus reducing the rateable value. They could afford to wait for good times to spend money on fine buildings and fine streets. It was the same with regard to the construction of cantilevers on Warrington Bridge, which in a few years would have to be,knocked off again. Looking at Church-street, no one could deny that if it had a good outlet it would be one of the finest business streets in the town. There would be an inorease in rateable value which would pay back the yearly instalment for the bridge. He hoped the Council would support the scheme, but he did not wish them to vote for it with the idea that they would hear nothing more about it. He would see that it was kept to the front. The motion was carried.

div.head: FISH AS AN ARTICLE OF DIET. Its Great Importance.
div.p: FISH AS AN ARTICLE OF DIET. Its Great Importance.

All doctors agree as to the great importance of fish as an article of diet, but, unfortunately, there is a same- ness in the ways of sensing fish that prevents its wider use. We must have our palates tickled, or we do not relish what we take. What is wanted is a greater variety in serving the commoner sorts of fish. To obtain this, fish should be served with a variety of simple yet tasty sauces. Such sauces are now within the reach of all, and in Brown & Poison's booklet, "Simple Fish Sauces," written for otdinary households, by a leading expert, a number of exallent recipes for such sauces are given. These are quickly and easily made, and give snap, flavour and richness to the commonest fish. The thickening for such sauces is Brown & Poison's " Patent " Corn flour. Application for this booklet should be made at once, to Brown & Poison, Paisley, enclosing Id. stamp.

div.head: HELPING THE INFIRMARY. -- What the Warrington Workingmen
div.p: HELPING THE INFIRMARY. -- What the Warrington Workingmen
Have Done.

That valuable institution the Infirmary, derives a great deal of its financial qupport from the working- men, and the task of organizing the collection of thw subscriptions devolves upon the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee which is composed of representatives of the works in the town and district. Interesting details of the past year's operations were forthcoming at the annual meeting of the committee which was hold at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Bolton). There was a large attendance.

The MAYOR said he was gratified to see the success of the Infirmary—an institution which, he thought, would recommend itself to all. They knew the splen- did work it accomplished, and the great benefit it was to the workers of the town and neighbourhood. The need of an infirmary was most essential, and the admir- able way in which it was supported by the working nten was very pleasing. As would be seen from the great number of cases treated, it was doing a very use- ful work. Considering the state of trade during the year the collections had been very satisfactory, add were a credit to them as delegates. THE YEAR'S SUBSCRIPTIONS. Mr. HIMPSON. treasurer, submitted the statement of accounts, which showed that during the year £727 4s. had been received from works, as against £703 us. id. They would agree that that was satisfactory, consider- ing the circumstances. They had a decrease of £27 from Messrs. Armitage and Rigby owing to the cotton corner,the employees being out of work for some time. Messrs. Platt and Wilkinson's contribution had also gone down from the same cause. There were differ- ences in other cases, owing to bad trade, and in some instances the amount had increased, notably Messrs. Greeningland Sons and the Whitecross Co.,Ltd. In 1601 the amount received from works was £607; in 1902, £703; and in 1903, £74. At the rate of increase between 1901 and 1903, they really ought to have had .£l,OOO in 1903, and doubtless that would have been receivedjhad it not been for the cause stated. Apart from that theyhad obtained new sources of income, and some of theflrms had adopted the plan of weekly sub- scriptions, which was really the best. (Hear, hear.) Cdtmcillor JOHN ROBERTS, in moving the adoption of the balance sheet, paid a tribute to the excellent work of Mr. Hampson. Alluding to the progress of the com- mittee, he said that in 1880, when the Working Men's Committee was organised, the subscriptions amounted to £162 19s. 4d.. and the statement that afternoon showed how well they had progressed. If trade had been prosperous they might have got their subscriptions up to £l,OOO, but they would endeavour to reach that sum for 1904. If they managed that the Working Men's Committee would have done their duty well. (Applause). The balance sheet was unanimonsly passed. Mr. GEORGE WALKER, the representative of the com mittee on the Education Committee of the borough reported at length upon the work of that authority.

div.head: COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE COMMITTEE.

The RECTOR proposed that the delegates present form the General Committee, with power to add to their number. He thought that next year they ought to have no difficulty in raising £l,OOO. It was a great credit to the working men that they had raised such a large sum as .C 727 by actual subscriptions. Mr. SPENCE seconded,and the motion was approved. t OFFICER S ELECTED.
Councillor JOHN ROBERTS was unanimously re-elected chairman—a position he has held ever since the forma- tion of the committee.
Owing to a bereavement, Mr. Joseph Taylor resigned the position of secretary and seyeral speakers eulogised his services to the committee duridg the past twelve!. ye_ars._
Mr. Reuben Higham was elected to the position. Councillor Roberts and Burton and Messrs. Watkin and Wilkinson were elected representatives on the Board of Management of the Infirmary.

div.head: INFIRMARY EXTENSION NE-CESSAR f.
div.p: INFIRMARY EXTENSION NE-CESSAR f.

Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOTIGH said the Committee of Man- agement were beginning to feel that *their Infirmary was getting overcrowded. The beds were pretty well taken up every week, and they were very much pushed for accommodation, and the time had now arrived when the Infirmary would have to be enlarged. To do that they would not only require money to enlarge the present premises, but larger finances to carry on the institution afterwards. If they proceeded with the ex- tension he hoped the working men would behave aS nobly as they had done hitherto if not better. Councillor BURTON said that at their works they had had the extension question under consideration, and at the annual meeting the Forge department voted £25 for that special pirpose. (Hear, hear.) He thought that fact might induce others to subscribe. The £25 was available any time they desired. (Applause.) Hearty votes of thanks were accorded to the Chair- man, deputy-chairman, secretary, treasurer, hon. auditor (Mr. C. Jackson Holmes), and representative to the Education Committee for their services during the past year. A similar compliment was paid to the Chief Constable and police, Warrington Rugby Football Club, the committee of the May Day procession of horses, and Mr. T. J. Down and the members of his band. Colonel BUCKTON proposed a vote of thanks to the hon. medical officers, senior and junior house surgeons, and matron and nurses, which was carried. Dr. RICHMOND returned thanks, and said that with reference to the Infirmary itself, they were greatly behind the times. They had made representations to the committee, and had been told that they could not get the money to do what was necessary. He did not believe that; it only needed asking for and they would get the money. The MAYOR was thanked forpresiding and allowing the use of the Council Chamber.

St. Mary's Dramatic Society. The committee after careful consideration of the very large number of lists of plays submitted for competition have awarded the prize of a guinea to Miss Lily Phair, 66 Battersby-lane who is to be con- gratulated on her success. The winner's list of plays is on view at Messrs. Dolan Bros. Very many excel- lent suggestions were made by the competitors and these will no doubt be of service to the St. Mary's Society in the future.

div.head: KNUTSFORD DIVISION.
div.p: THE KNUTSFORD DIVISION.
VISIT OF LORD HUGH CECIL. Free Trade Upheld A Political House on Firc."

A demonstration organised by the Knutsford Divi- -I°4 Branch of the Free Trade League, was held on aY night at the Drill Hall, Wilmslow, the prinni- vaL sPoaker being Lord Hugh Cecil, M.P. The meeting, which was largely attended, was presided over by Lord Sta_nley of Alderley. 1-11 e Chairman regretted the necessity for going back uPon the past; but the economic system under which this country had striven for the past fifty years was now allenged, and they must examine the principles and prepared to give a reason for the faith that was in tousnl• The question was, had the policy of Free Trade sell a failure, or had it been a success? Some people told them that they had no rig,htto describe their policy as a policy of Free Trade, that they ought to call them- selves free importers, and that the could be no Free Trade unless that principle was universally accepted. Re did not admit that for one moment. He believed the policy of Free Trade to be a sound one, and that it woU ld be good for all countries. Proceeding to analyse .!.he proposals of the Protectionists, he said if they pro- ined one trade they would have to leave others out the cold, and once they began tinkering with the subject there was no telling where it would end. In his °Pinion

PROTECTION WOULD BE DISASTROUS to the country,and freedom ,of international trade was essential to secure that margin which made the differ- ence between brisk and slack trade. Lord Hugh Cecil 'moved a resolution affirming 'unshaken belief in the principles of Free Trade, and el`Prossing the conviction that Free Trade was now 1443 re than ever necessary for the well-being of the ted. Kingdom. Addressing those Unionist members of the audience wit° were Free Traders, he said thait wa.s the time to speak out. That implied no dis- •2Yalty to the Government, who had not yet committed themselves to Protection. Recent signs showed that Government were hesitating how far they would go. a, nd that they were more inclined than over they were :lefore to adhere, in substance, to the Free Trade policy. 'We are really," said Lord Hugh, "in the position of vsons livkniin a house in which a fire has broken out. is our business to put out the fire by pouring water 11,i)00 it. That is a policy which may injure some of "0 furniture, but it would be substantially, not only in our interest, but in the interest of the home which is rne, if we could stop that ancient building from the weciger that thmatens it. We must not lay down our tram until Nye have relegated Protection altogether eyond the region of practical politics." THE BEST PROTECTION FOR THE COTTON TRADE. When examined he did not think it could be main- lained that in character our exports were in anything 'jut a very healthy condition. We sent out of the country what foreign countries wanted, and by no 4_laa,nipulations of tariff would they induce foreigners to 'dke what they did not want. They would by this means Only restrict the whole foreign trade, both imports and "Ports, and would be so much worse off. There was n 0 greater security against monopoly in trade than a Wide open door,andhe believed that after the difficulties "Perienced in the cotton trade during the past year there would be a considerable stimulus to the produc- tion of cotton in other parts of the world—in Egypt and West Africa—and the upshot would be that the area of supply would grow larger and larger, and in that "buld be fnund thebest protectionagainst such dangers PI the future. Dealing with the question of dumping, ne said that upon the whole the more it was studied the !tore it was seen that the Protectionist policy proposed /0 itself a false object. It conceived the dumping of goods to be an evil when, in fact, it was a benefit. In the first place it grossly exaggerated the extent of the eVii, and the remedy proposed was wholly ineffectual.

DANGERS OF PREFERENCE. As to the question of preference with the colonies, it Was a scheme for adjusting conflicting interests, and the whole idea had seif-interest as its basis. He could 1?.ot conceive anything more likely to lead to a loosen- ing of the tie which at present existed between the In_other country and the colonies. Then they must r ware of any lowering of public life in this count ry f.:t3 long as the mother country maintained her weal th TA her character the empire would have a great centre '9 which it could look up and feel a pride in. If they I.l.llowad a system of Protectionist lobbying to come Into tel existence, with its "boss" trusts, and all the hate- nomenclature of corruption, there would be at once a great lowerin,, in the ability with which public affairs Were conducted'. _.&ondly there would be great distrust as to the racter of politicians. Everybody would be thought he thinking of his own personal profit and gain, and di'tre would be such an atmosphere of suspicion and afster"t that separation and division would result. And, tariL ail!, they must face the fact that a protective U as ItA, 'ITINERY FOR TRANSFERRING WEALTH FROM THE to Irk POCKETS OF THE PEOPLE hootoni it naturally belonged, into the pockets of sat "ller set of people. If that sort of thing was once sadllP they would find corrupting influences spread far "ide, because everyone would naturally desire to tr„"inold of the handles of the machine and turn a the golden stream their way. In vonclusion he said: "Let us keep our old repute- ; let us guard our old greatness and our character; be:us maintain the fiscal system which has been so good th for ourselves and our colonies." The resolution was seconded and adopted with en- thusiasm.

WORKINGMEN'S MISSION BANK QUAY.' .
MRS. CROSFIELD OPENS TilE NEW CHAPEL.
SPEECH BY MR. A. H. CROSFIELD.

A. new era in the history of the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, was entered upon on Saturday when MI s. Crosfield formally opened the commodious chapel erected in Thewlis street to replace the old building in Liverpool road which has been acquired Iby Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd, for the purposes of works extensions. The chapel adjoins he handsome new schools, and will seat about 320 persons. Whilst there has been no attempt at elabor- ate ornamentation, the building is eminently suitable and:is very tastefully furuished.An effort is now being made to raise £2OO to provide a new organ. The total sost of the chapel and organ will be about £1240 but thanks to the generous help of Mrs. Crosfield and other friends, and to the untiring exertions of the members of the mission themselves, only £2OO now remains to be raised. There was a large attendance at the opening ceremony. which was made the occasion of interesting and encouraging addresses. Amongst those present were Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Trude Crosfield, Miss Bessie Dutton, the Revs. John Yonge and J. S. Hughes, Coun- cillor James Evans, Mr. T. Ashley, Mr. T. Dale Mr. A. Tilling, and Mr. G. Wallington (the builder of the chapel). Mr. Ashley handed a silver key to Mrs. Crosfield, who opened the door of the chapel. The congregation then entered, and Mrs. Crosfield said "It gives me muoh pleasure to declare this chapel open for the worship of God." The Rev. John Yonge conducted the opening service and in the course of his address, said they were all glad anal thankful to lee present to take their several parts in the opening for worship of that new building. Personally he felt very much in- debted to the friends for asking him to come into their midst and to express, as an old fellow-townsman and a friend, his good wishes for the success of the mission. He trusted they would have a continuance of wkat they understood as good times" in the years to which they were looking for- ward. Since they had to remove to the new school, they had gone on flourishing, and now that they had %chapel once again in which they could carry on worship, per- haps with greater comfort and convenience, they could hope that the blessing of God might rest more mani- festly still upon them, and thatithe chapel might become the birth-place of many souls. It must be remembered that worship was not the mere bodily presence at a ser- vice. It was the bowing of the heart, the humbling of the spirit, and the communion of faith. The nearer they got to the conscious realization of God the nearer they came to the better and brighter estate in which they trusted they would all hive in the future. He hoped they would enjoy much Chria- tian fellowship and have true sympathy with one another. Let everyone know that the building was a home as well as a church, into which they might come and set aside all feelings of distance and diffidence, and he was perfectly certain that they were coming into the midst of a friendly circle where they would be welcomed. He was sure' they would continue to carry on the work with earnestness, cordiality, and perseverance. Churches and chapels were not worth their existence unless they were centres of uhefulness, They must not be mere preaching places, but working places. He hoped that mission would be a line of in- dustry, all the members seeking to contribute their share, and striving together in the hope of the gospel. If that were their aim and spirit, the days to come would witness increased usefulness peace and joy, The Rev. J. S. HUGHES congratulated the congrega- tion upon the completion of their enterprize, upon the realisation of their hopes, and the larger sphere of use- fulness which was opening out before them. He had heard of their labour of love, and had witnessed their zeal and devotion in the work of God, and he prayed Oat with their enlarged opportunities they might have larger blessings, richer benedictions, and greater imbu- meat of divine power,that the glory of that latter house might surpass exceedingly the glory of the former. Mr Hughes alluded to the unity which was evidenced by the fact that the representatives of four or ive different denominations were taking part in the service. It would demonstrate, he Lipped, to the world, that they were all one in essentials • that they were all loyal to the great heed of the church, and that they were all exceedingly anxious for the advancement of their common Christianity, by whomsoever advanced. Ho prayed that that catholic spirit might over prevail amongst them. The speaker then called attention to the simplicity of the service. There was, he said, no ornate programme; no elaborate ornamentation in any shape or form ; no costly ceremonial ; but simply a meeting together and the pouring out of their hearts in praise to God, and the joining together at the throne of grace to ask God to bless and pros- per the work which they had in hand. That service, he thought, was in perfect harmony with the simplicity that was to be found in Christ. that chapel, continued Mr. Hughes, was no doubt a monument of blessings they had received in the past, and a memorial of good men and devoted women who spent of their best amongst them. He asked all present to take the opportunity of consecrating themselves afresh to the service of God. • Miss Bessie Dutton also delivered a short but extremely interesting address, alluding to the feel- ings of thankfulness , which must be uppermost in their minds on seeing the - completion of a labour of love. She did not know whether the work w:s ended in the sense that all the money had been paid, but she had no doubt that they had been very successful in that direction, because the members of the mission had worked well themselves. There was so much indifference and selfishness at the present day, that they were glad when they saw earnest hearts, out of their fulness. and yet ott of their penury, making an offering to God. Appropriate hymns were sung, Mr. Prod Atkinson presiding at the organ. TEA AND ENTERTAINMENT. MR. A. H. CROSFIELD AND RELIGIOUS TOLERATION

After the service a company of about 300 assembled in the schoolroom for the *annual congregational tea meetings, and the function was a decided success. Trays had been contributed by the following :-10s. trays, An old scholar and Mrs.R.Tanner,Mr. and Mrs. Barratt, Mr. and Mrs. D. Hill, Mr. and Mrs. J. Hassan, Mr. and Mrs. S. Hill, Mr. Joseph and Mrs. A. Tilling, Mr. John E. Tilling, Mr. J. Wooley, Mr-and Mrs. N. Hough, Mr. and Mrs. T. Taylor,Mr. and Mrs. S. Dale, Mr. and Mrs. F. Atkinson, Mr. and Mrs. A. Tilling, jun., Mr. and Mrs. T. Dale, Mr. and Mrs. Rose, Mr. W. Dobbins, Mrs. E. Wallington,Mr. and Mrs. F. Gray,Mr.S. Haasall,Mr. and Mrs. J. R. Taylor members of mission society class (2) ; ss. trays, Mr. and Mrs. S. Millington' Mr. J. Birch, Mr. and Mrs. Atherton, Mr. and Mrs. A. Lowe, Mrs. Haddle Mr. H. Gray and Mr. B. Kendrick,' Miss Walliniton,'Mr. T. Lowe, Mr. and Mrs. Blunt. Mr. and Mrs. Schofield, Mr. and Mrs. Strange, Mr. and Mrs. Oakley, Mr. and Mrs. Massey, Mr. A. Pemberton, Miss E. Dobbins.

The room was filled to its utmost capacity for the enjoyable entertainment which followed. Mr. A. H. Crostield presided, and was accompanied on the plat- form by Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Crosfleld, and Mr. N. Hough. After a well executed pianoforte duet, "La Reven," by Messrs: F. Atkinson and E. Rickers • Mr. A. TILLING presented the annual report. He said that on looking back through their Church records, he fousd that the first annual report entered in the minute books sounded the keynote of thanksgiving to their Heavenly Father for His goodness and mercy to His people in that corner of His vineyard. The report for 1903—the last year in their dear old chapel—must follow in the same strain; for they had much to be thankful for. The last year's work in the old chapel could not be regarded, by any means, as the least in importance. In every respect it had been a very busy year. Although special efforts had had to be put forth to provide the new chapel, and trade had been depressed,they were thankful to say that on the old chapel account, of which Mr. Edwards was secretary, there was a credit balance. The amount brought forward from 1902 was £2 is Od. During 1903 the income had totalled £45 17s 100, and the expendi- ture £42 Ms 11d, leaving £5 is 110 in hand. On the poor fund, which was ably,administered by Mr. Thomas Dale, there was a credit balance of s)3 Cs 9d. Mr. Tilling proceeded to emphasise thetincreased importance of church membership, pointing out that as the new chapel was their own trust property, it was necessary that the members should have a voice in the government of the church and the appoiatmeat of the committee. During the year two members of the mission—Brother Wall and Sister Simms—had passed away. In regard to the new chapel, the committee believed the building was a suitable one. No doubt various items alight have been improved upon, but the question of cost had to be con- sidered. When the first set of plans was drawn up by Mr. R. M. Roberts, the cost was estimated at £1,500 but as that was more than it was considered advisable to give, the plans were amendea and the coal reduced to about £l,OOO. Their congratulations were due to Mr. R. M. Roberts, the architect, to Mr. John Hassall, who had superintended the building free of charge, and to Mr. G. Wallington, the builder. The actual cost of the chapel was esti- mated by the architeet at £l.OlO 15s. Adding £2OO for a new organ, and £3O to cover sundry expenses, the total expenditure would be £1240 15s. The amount received up to date was £837 15s. 11d. which included :—Messrs. Joseph Orosfield and Sons, Ltd., £300; Mrs. Crosfield, £200; monthly collections, £2l Os. 9d. ; Monks, Hall and Co., £0; bazaar profits, £232 13s. 3d. ; Men's Class, £3O 7s. 6id. Mr. Henry Roberts had promised a donation of £lo,leaving an amount still to be raised of £392 19s. id. He was however, thankful to say that Mrs. Crosfleld had very generously promised to clear off the balance of £192 due on the chapel building account—(applause)—and they had therefore only to raise £2OO for the organ. It was impossible for him to adequately express their feel- ings of thankfulness to Mrs. Crosfleld, but he hoped they would prove worthy of the confidence she had placed in them. The committee for the ensuing year had

been:elected as follows :—President,Mr. .Nathan Hough; vice-president, Mr. Thomas Dale; Committee Messrs. Thomas Ashley, J. Edwards, T. Taylor Wooley, P. Hill, George Dale, F. Atkinson, W. Worrell, H. Gray and A. Tilling. He trusted the opening of the new chapel would stimulate them all to greater efforts, so that further good might be accomplished. (Applause.)

The Ciiaartat LT said he was sure eveiy' sone of 'them felt sincere gratitude to Mr. Tilling for the unremitting efforts and the constant work by which he had furthered the success and the well-being of tbe mission, more particularly during the past twelvemonths. (Applause.) In his report, Mr. Tilling referred to the commence- ment of the mission thirty•three years ago, and he (the speaker) was afraid it made him begin to think he was quite middle-aged—(laughter)—becanse he had a lively and vivid recollection of the earliest beginnings of the missibn, and he had a still more vivid recollection of the many occasions on which he had heard his father express himself in that emphatic way some of them might remember, and say that he never in his life spent any money which gave him such unqualified satis- faction as the money which he spent when the old chapel was built. (Applause.) One thing that impressed itself particularly upon his (Mr. Crosfield's) mind was the fact that he had to make his first appear- ance upon a platform two or three years after the mission was commenced, when his father insisted upon his reciting—he was afraid, a little unwillingly—a poem called "The Comedian." The piece ought to haw, been very funny, but he did not think his recitation at all did justice to it. (Laugh- ter.) Continuing, Mr. Crosfield said he had not been in close touch with all the zealous and earnest work which had been done to further their cause during the past year or two, and therefore it was not possible for him to refer adequately to the meritorious work of individual members. It was because the people hiLd had their hearts in the religious and social success of the mission which his father started, that it had been such a continuous success He would like to add a word in reference to the benefi- cent influence which their pastor, Mr. Dale, always exercised in that part of the town—and he (Mr Crosfield) knew he had specially exerted himself during the past year. He was quite sure that the money which Mrs. Crosfield had spent on the mission would, as Mr. Tilling had expressed the hope, be a source of satisfac- tion to her all her life. He knew from many conversa- tions he had had with Mrs. Crosfield that she really had at heart the well-being of the community, which in that part of the town was associated with their work- people and with the workpeople of other firms. She had, in fact, the well-being of the mission at heart as sincerely as ever his fatherhad. (Applause.) - It afforded him (the speaker) great satisfaction to feel that their firm had had some share in that latest develop- ment of the mission. They had heard it said many a time that a company had no conscience. He was glad that their company had shown that their might be exceptions to rule—(hear, hear)—and if further proof were wanted, he could give them a little history of what had been done by the firm in the last few years to civilise the employment of labour, which, he believed, would give them very great satisfaction. He was quite certain that if his father were alive to-day, great as the progress of their business and their commercial developments had been in recent years, the marked pro- I gress which they had made as employers of labour would in his (the speaker's) firm conviction have given him more satisfaction than anything else. He had ven- tured respectfully to mention that, to show them that the firm which was so closely connected with the Bank Quay Mission was not, as some firms were supposed to be, entirely indifferent to the responsibilities which fall upon it as a large employer of labour. (Applause.) For the remarkable development to which he had referred, all of them owed a great deal to the energy, the initiative, and the thoroughness with whioh his co-director, Dr. Markel hadhelped them to carry through that work. While mentioning that, it was a matter of great satisfaction to him to tell them that there had been absolute unanimity amongst the whole board of directors in supporting Dr. Markel and encouraging him to carry that great piece of work through He (the Chairman) expressed his deep satisfaction at the progress the mission was making, at the enlarging of their circle, and its increasing influence in that part of the town. There was nothing that would have given his father greater satisfaction than that. When he started the mission he did.so upon very simple lines. His father never was a sectarian, and he had often heard him say with very great satisfaction that there was only one sect represented in that mission, and that was the broad sect of Christians. Nonconformists, members of the Church of England, Unitarians, even Roman Catholics, he had heard him say, would take part in the religious work of the mission, and his object in , encouraging it, he knew well, was that they should have preached he gospel of peace and goodwill toward men. (Applause.) All who kept their eyes open knew very well that that gospel, unfortunately, in these days, was not always all-suMcing. They had only to look round the world and see how man, "the fighting animal," as Professor Huxley called him would persist in showing his teeth and claws, and that only showed how necessary—how much more necessary, if possible, in these days, it was to have the qualifying 'influence of that sovereign gospel of pity which was preached Sunday after Sunday in that chapel, and he, for one, recognizing the bitterness and strife there had been in the world's history—bitterness which had been intensified more in religious quarrels than in any other strife on record—felt that it was a grand thing to have had in that town a religious assembly' of the kind he , had mentioned, where the leading note, the guiding tone, in all their religious observances, was toleration. (Applause.) For that reason, for the good it did to the workpeople of their own firm, and all other firms in that neighbourhood, and not least because it was furthering a work in which his father took so great an interest, he hoped and sincerely trusted that the Mission would flourish, prosper, and increase in numbers more and more as the years went on. (Applause). A most enjoyable programme was submitted, songs being rendered in good style by Miss Lena Dobson, Miss Lucy Davies, Mr. G. Gough, and Mr. S. Hassell. The voices of the Lyric Quartette party (Missss Wood- land and Fairhurst, and Messrs. P. George and N. Cook) blended beautifully in "God is a spirit," and a hearty encore was accorded. The instrumental selections by the ladies' orchestra were much appreciated, the members being :—Pianoforte, Miss V. K. Finney; violins, Misses M. Leigh, J. M. Finney, M. Chesworth, and E. Greenough. mandoline Miss P. Chesworth ; 'cello, Miss L. M. H. Burchall ; effects. Miss H. Leigh. Mr. Frank Hickman was an efficient accompanist. On the proposition of Mr. GEORGE DALE, seconded by Mr. NATHAN HOUGH, and supported by Councillor JAMES EvANs, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chair- man, Mrs. Crosfield, the artistes, and all the ladies who had assisted.

div.head: SUNDAY'S SERVICES.
div.p: SUNDAY'S SERVICES.

There were large congregations at the special open- ing services on Sunday. Mr. G. Hunter (president of the Independent Methodist Connexion) was the preacher both morning and evening. In the afternoon ascholars' service was held in the chapel, when an address was delivered by Mr. Hunter. Solos were rendered by Mr. S. Hassall aad Mr. G. Gough, the same gentlemen also giving a duet. A quartet was sung by Messrs. Milling- ton, Taylor, Hassall and Birch, and an anthem by the choir. At the evening service Mr. Pearce was the soloist, his rendering of "Arm, arm ye breve," being very effective. The choir (under the cond,ictorship of Mr. P. Atkinson) again contributed two anthems. Mr. Owen presided at the organ.
