div.head: LETTERS TO THE __EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE __EDITOR.

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday.

Soup Kitchens for the Poor. Sir,—With your permission, we beg to inform the public that excellent arrangements exist at the Warrington Ragged School Mission for making and distributing soup during the/ present distress in the town. But soup cannot be made without ingredients and labour; we are willing to lend our kitchen and -utensils, and to give a helping hand, if the necessary materials are forthcoming. If those who are well-fed and well-clothed would but shake off their apathy, and try and realize that a very larre number of people in Warrington are at the present time suffering terribly from hunger, they would surely respond to the appeals that are continually being made, without avail, for help. Amongst the poor children, especially, the privation and suffering is extreme. We beg to acknowledge the receipt of a number of children's hats, kindly sent by iVIr. Mounfteld, Horse- market-street.—On behalf of the Committee, J. W. HOWARTH.

Labour Representation. Sir,—The remarkable success of Mr. Ball, the Labour candidate, at the recent election of Borough Auditors, should greatly encourage all who desire to see a change in the Parliamentary representation of Warrington. A general election may be opening upon the country, much sooner than is expected, and it behoves the work- ing men of Warrington to be up and striving if they, desire to have a member of their own choosing. In no real sense can it be said that Messrs. Pierpoint and Crosfield are fit and proper persons to serve them in Parliament. Both are rabid party politicians,and being aristocrats they can have no real practical knowledge of the needs and aspirations of the working classes, and both gentlemen spend a good deal of their time in amusing themselves abroad. Besides, their present shibboleths have not much interest for workers : one extols Protection,aml the other preaches what is erroneously called-Tree Trade. Well, a good deal is known of the misery and distress which followed in the wake of Protection; and to-day when Free Trade, so called, is in full swing, it is said that nearly a third of the workers in England are in poverty and want, and many thousands of parsons willing and able to work can find no work to do. Protectionand Free Trade are only political cries to divert the attention of the people from the real evils which oppress and impoverish them. The subjects which] above all others, are of vital interest to the working classes are the reform of our unjust land laws; the abolition of the liquor traffic, and a very sub- stantial reduction of the enormous charges for war. Until these reforms are accomplished no tinkering legislation will ever avail to relieve the majority of the workino, classes from the depressing circumstances under which they live.—Yours truly, lONA.
March 4th, 1901. " Crosfield " Park.

Sir,—lt was with very great regret, not untinged with amazement, that I read the report of the proceedings of the last Council meeting so far as they related to the proposed "Crosfield " Park. It will, I feel sure, be anything but gratifying to the public of Warrington to find that by the action of a majority of their represen- tatives in the Council they are committed to an act of the greatest discourtesy to a gentleman whose name is so familiar to theta as is that of Lord Lilford. What are shortly the facts? A recreation ground is to be opened off Liverpool-road, about half of the necessary land having been acquired by the Corporation, the re- maining half being the gift of Lord Lilford. The questioth of the name to be given to the recreation ground was discussed at a meeting of the Open Spaces Sub-Committee, who sent a recommendation to the General Purposes Committee that the Park should be called " Crosfield" Park. This was passed by the General Purposes Com mittee,whose minutes came before the Council for confirmation on Tuesday. Now, Sir, one would naturally have thought that as half the land was obtained as a gift to the town,the reasonable and courteous course would have been to have associated the name of the donor with that of the Recreation Ground. If for some reason it was not thought desir- able to perpetuate the name of the donor it surely would have been easy in accepting the gift to call the Recreation Ground by some local name (such as " Whitecross "as suggested by Alderman Bennett) which would not have offered any discourtesy to the donor of the land. Unfortunately,the Council,for some reason,did not adopt this course,but decided to ignore the donor and to associate with the Recreation Ground a name which, however respected, had no connection in any shape or form with it. The sole argument in favour of the course adopted seemed to be that the Crosfield family has proved benefactors to the town. No one wishes for a moment to belittle anything which the Crosfteld family may have done. Their name, however, is already handed down in the cases of Crosfield-street and the Crosfteld Conservatory in Bank Park. If this was not considered sufficient, surely the name could have been further honoured by association with some public building provided by their generosity or with some public building or space acquired by the Corporation otherwise than through the gift of a third party.— Yours &c., CITIZEN.

div.head: CRIPPLED GIRLS FLORAL PRODUCTIONS.
div.p: CRIPPLED GIRLS FLORAL PRODUCTIONS.

What May ba Seen at the Parr Hall. The beginning of March, with its keen winds and frosty air, is hardly the time when one expects to see the choicest of flowers. Yet,the visitor to the,Parr Hall this week finds himself surrounded by every kind of bloom—from the rich, spreading chrysanthemum and full-blown rose, to the modest violet and delicate pansy. How came they here? a reader may ask. True, they are not the perfect work of Nature, but they do realize, save in the sweetness of scent, the charms of English garden flowers. On the production of these flowers hangs an interesting story—a story of true philanthropy which appeals to one with peculiar force. It is not many years since the problem "what to do with our poor crippled girls" seemed insurmount- able: IThe sad lot of many afflicted children in London, who were being brought up amid scenes of squalor and misery,—forced to eke out a bare livelihood by selling flowers in the streets—so touched the heart of the late Earl of Shaftesbury that the Watercress and Flower Girls' Ghristian Mission, with well-appointed homes for destitute and crippled children, was founded. So rapidly has the work grown, that crippled girls from all parts of the country now find a place in the homes. Theyj are-Strained to become self-supporting, by making the beautiful flowers that we now see in such rich profusion at the Parr Hall. The floral artists are well paid, and only a small charge is made against them for board, the rest of their earnings being placed at their disposal. Thus the spirit of independence, of which we in England are so proud, is cultivated in those to whom life at one time seemed almost a burden. "If you treat a beggar well, he always comes again" said the Rev. Wigton" A. Groom, who is superintending the exhibition, at the opening on Monday afternoon. Warrington people have previously given whole-hearted and generous support to this beneficent work. So encouraging WAS the success of the exhibition held twe years ago, that it is not surprising that a second visit was: undertaken. The venture will, it is expected, be fully justified, for Parr Hall has been the resort of large numbers of townspeople throughout the week. The exhibition is made doubly interesting by the fact that one can witness the actual process of floriculture. With deft fingers a contingent of crippled girls pursue their calling, and right happy they are at their work. On see- ing them one immediately realizes what a fine workthe Mission is doing in giving these girls a true aim in life and an opportunity to cultivate their talents. Another inducement to visit the hall is that each evening there is an excellent musical programmce. Mr. Tom Booth- royd's well-trained orchestra plays selections, while Mr. Tom Boothroyd himself displays his skill as a violinist, There are also enjoyable songs by Miss Polly Houghton (soprano) and Mr. Edward Pownall (bass). Mr. Albert Trow is an efficient accompanist. The Mayor and Mayoress attended to open the exhi- bition on Monday afternoon, and wish it every success. His Worship said he was very pleased to find that the institution from a charitable point of view had suc- ceeded in bringing together a class of people who had needed help, but who were now earning their own living. This was one of the most beautiful pursuits they could possibly have; in fact, any institution that made better members of society was a very laudable one and deserved support. A little crippled girl otepped forward and handed a lovely bouquet of artificial roses to the Mayoress. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor and Mayoress on the proposition of the Rev. G. H. Carnson, seconded by Alderman Smethurst. Business then commenced and has proceeded briskly each day, the takings being :—Monday, ; Tuesday, £3O; Wednesday, £4l; Thursday, £4B. The stalls have been in charge of the following :—Parish Church stall Mrs. and Miss Willis; St. Paul's stall, Mrs. Bracecamp ; Wesleyan stall, Mrs. Carnson ' • Cairo-street Chapel stall, Mrs. C. Harvey Cook; and Wycliffe Church stall, Mrs. Yonge and Mrs. H. Roberts. The exhibition closed to-night. GRAPPENHALL.

THE CRICKET CLUB CoNCERT.—The result of the concert held before Christmas to help to defray the expenses in connection With the new pavilion, showed a balance of three pounds. A further effort will shortly be made taking the form of a rummage sale. YOUNG MEN'S CLUB.—At a committee meeting held on Tuesday last, it was decided to give an assault-at- arms and gymnastic display on 24th March, by the members of the gymnasium in connection with the above club assisted by members of the gymnastic staff At Orford Barracks.

div.head: FISCAL QUESTION. PUBLIC DEBATE AT STOCKTON
div.p: THE FISCAL QUESTION. PUBLIC DEBATE AT STOCKTON
HEATH.

Spenhes by Messrs. McDermott, E. L. Jones, H. J. Westbrook, E. England, and W. L. Williams. The subject of "whether Nlr. Chamberlain's propose' would benefit the working classes, or otherwise," wag discussed at a public debate held in the Providenoe Schoolroom, Stockton Heath, on Monday evening. The discussion wits conducted entirely free from party bias and the Chairman (Ar. J. Clarke) maintained a neutral attitude. He had no difficulty in meiutaining order and the subject was very fairly discussed. In commencing the proceedings, the Chairmen referred to the importance of the subject, and said it was engaging the attention of all intelligent citizens in this country and the Colonies. As it was likely to be the chief topic before the electors it was necessary that they should hear both sides of the question and forman opinion upten it. As Chairman of that meeting it was not his intention to impress his views upon them, but to see that the discussion was carried on in an orderly and fair manner. THE CASE FOR MR. CHAMBERLAIN. 1 Mr. McDermott. in opening the de'eate, took the affirmative side and held that Mr. Chamberlain's pro- posals would benefit the working-classes. After refer- ring to the debate as being the outcome of a Liberal meeting held in that schoolroorna short time ago, when 'the subject under discussion was Free Trade v. Protec- tion, he said he was induced to take part in that dis- cussion. As one who was not accustomed to speak, he °asked for their consideration and indulgence. His accent might be a little broad, and perhaps his sen- tences might not be strictly accurate but he trusted they would bear in mind that he came from the foundry and not from the Academy. (Hear hear.) The-large attendance that evening showed the interest that was being taken in the question. It was fashionable nowadays fot some people to say that they did not belong to a party, but he was not one of them. So long as party government was the recognised form of government no one need apologise for having politi-- caeopinions one way or the other. It was.the d sty of everyone to form political oeinione and associate him- self with a political party. (Hear, hear.) He did not feel himself called upon to defend or advocate protec- tion in the conventional sense. Free Trade had been definedas the free exchange of products or commodities between countries or nations. He asked them to reflect whether that accurately described the con- dition of affairs at the present time. He contended that what we called free trade was nothing more than free imports. We had no free- dom to freely exchange goods with other countries in the sense of the word described byCobden. What were Mr. Chamberlain's proposals? It was only reasonable that they-should go to Mr. Chamberlain for them. He had been a good deal amused at some Libeeal meetings, where the speakers had set up for themselves something which they called Mr. Chamberlain's proposals and then proceeded to demolish them to their own satisfaction. They would then square their shoulders and say" See how easily I have done it !" Instead of fighting the question they were really fighting shy of it. (Hear, hear.) This to his alin.d was borne out by the resolu- tion passed at the last Liberal meeting in that room. The Chairman: I hope Mr. McDermott will not introduce political controversy. Mr. Westbrook: Don't you mean party politics ? It is impossible to make it unpolitical. Mr. McDermotteaid he would endeavour to raise the question without causing any political animus. It was quite apposite in discussing the questions At the meet- ing a resolution was proposed and carried, condemning the taxation of food and raw materials. (Hear, hear.) He wished to point out an important fact which was completely ignored, namely that taxation of food in this country existed at the present time. A revenue of £103,000,000 was raised by the taxation of food. (Hear, hear.) Then he would ask any fair-minded man whether in Mr. Chamberlain's proposals there was any sugges- tion of the taxation of raw materials. Mr. Chamber- lain had said distinctly that he did not suggest the taxation of raw materials. Mr. Chamberlain contended that the changes which had taken place since the adoption of the present fiscal. system in the conditions of international exchange, the comparative posi- tion of foreign nations, and our relations with our Colonies pointed to the necessity of the consideration of our fiscal question. Mr. Chamber- lain pointed out that the original object of Cobden and his colleagues was to secure free exchange of products at their natural price with all nations in the world. The open door had not been followed and that bad interfered with the natural interchange of com- modities. Foreign producers had been able to maintain their own markets by effective subsidies and tariffs, and also able to undersell British manufacturers in neutral markets, and even seriously attack our own home trade. Mr. Chamberlain proposed that by re-arming ourselves with the weapon of moderate tariffs we might defend our home market against unfair competition, and at the same time secure a modification of foreign tariffs, which would open the way to a fairer exchange of products than we had been able to obtain. By a system of pre- ferential tariffs to our colonies, Mr. Chamberlain hoped to effect a nearer approach to a commercial union within the empire. Mr. Chamberlain contended that these changes could be brought about without loss to any class or individual by a slight transfer of , existing taxation. This transfer of taxation would not increase existing burdens but would benefit our trade. The questions were more vitally important to working men, since they depended upon their daily employment for their daily subsistence. At the time that our fiscal system was adopted there was no such thing as competi- tion in manufactures. This country had a monopoly in exporting manufactured goods and was in a sense the workshop of the world. No doubt for a time the system of free imports suited us. He did not contend that we had not prospered under it. But still in later days, and in more recent years, by the development of hostile tariffs in other countries, foreign producers had developed commerce and industries of their own and were now manufacturing, not only sufficient for themselves, but a large surplus, which they were able through our fiscal system, to send into our market and undersell us. That was the one point which effected British labour very much. It had caused a considerable decreasevin the exports of British made goods, and en- couraged thelmportation of goods made by foreign. labour, which meant the restriction o? the labour re- quired in this country. We were thus being hit both ways. Alongside more unemployment and part employ- ment we had the fact that there was a considerable increase in the products of foreign labour sold in this country, the labour of which legitimately belonged to large numbers of unemployed men. All that the workers of this country asked for were fair and equitable con- ditions of exchange. The working classes did not ask a favour. They had never asked the Executive Govern- ment to supply them with bread and butter, but what they had a right to expect was that the Government should meet the action of outside Governments so as to secure a fair field and no favour for the products of this country. (Applause). Proceeding to refer to the desirabitity of a commercial union with our colonies, Mr. McDermott said our colonies were likely to prove in the future our best markets. These markets were : legitimately ours and they were offered to us. We ' should be foolish if we did not accept the means . offered to secure them. Discussing the proposed transfer of taxation from tea, sugar, coffee, cocoa. &c. to foreign corn and meat Mr. McDermott contended that this would be the means of giving us better colonial markets for the pro- ducts of British labour, an increase in the wages of the working-classes and greater prosperity throughout the country. (Applause.) •THE NEGATIVE. Mr. E. Lloyd Jones replied in the negative. Referring to the financial bearing of Mr. Chamberlain's scheme, he said they must assume that prices of all kinds of food would be increased in exact proportion to the duties on imports. (Hear, hear.) On this assumption the national exchequer would receive on the basis of present supplies, about £6,000,000, in the first year. namely £3,300,000 on corn, £1,350,000 on meat and £1,350,000 on dairy produce. The consumers in this country, however, would have to face an increased price of £8,171,000 on corn, whether imported or produced in this country, of £3,975,000 on meat and of £4.130,000 on dairy nroduce, a total of £16,300,000, of which only £.950,000 would be paid into the exchequer. £8,170,000 would go into the pockets of farmers or tlandowners in this country—(hear, hear,)—and £1,300,000 into the pockets of Colonial producers. The I teta per cent. on manufactured goods would increase the I price of all home manufactured goods, not Possibly in Ithe same proportion, because the demand would be reduced, but still the increase of prices all round would I be considerable, and as the home consumption of manu- factures was enormously greater than the imported or ' exported manufactures, it followed that the increased price paid by consumers in this country of manufac- tured articles, whether imported or produced at home, i would assume immense proportions. It had been esti- mated at from 30 to 60 million pounds. This would be equivalent to a new tax ~n consumers. (Hear, hear.) Dealing with the effect. of these taxes on the farmer, Mr. Jones stated that whilst £8,000,000 a year would go to those engaged in i agriculture, everything the farmers required would be 1 dearer by 10 per cent at least. Farm implements, machinery, clothing would be dearer by more than 10 ' per cent and the food of farmers and their families and feeding stuffs other than maize for cattle would also be . , increased. The agricultural labourer stood to lose all ' round. Those engaged in milk production, who did not suffer from foreign competition, would certainly suffer from the proposed duties as would also market garden- ers. The food and clothing, boots and shoes of the labouring people would be dearer, whilst a decrease in their wages would he more likely than an advance. (Hear,hear.) Discussing the effect upon the manufactur- ing industries, Mr. Jones showed that a general scheme of protection all round would tell aeainst the great cotton industry in a hundred ways. Flour, for instance, was a very important item in the manufacture. whilst dyeing and bleaching requisites, leather, iron and steel, oil, tallow and other accessories would be raised in price. The aggregate would be serious and would raise the cost of manufacture and reduce the narrow i

margin of profit. It would be little short of madness to risk a vast trade like cotton, one so highly exotic in the sense that it depends for the whole of its raw material on foreign countries, by increasing the cost of manufacture under a general scheme of Protection. Above all, the rise in the price of food—the raw material of labour—would lower the efficiency of the workman. If they raised wages in some import- ant manufactures, how was this to benefit those engaged in domestic service, in sLipping, in building, in education ;and so on? The probable result would be to lower wages in employments that wore not protected. Besides the increased cost of manufacture in particular industries there would be greatly increased taxation due to the enhanced charges on Government departments and on local governing bodies. There must be a great addition to the cost of the Army and Navy for food and clothing for war material of all kinds, from cartridges to ironcla.ds. The poor in the Workhouse, the prisoners in goal, the lunatics in asylums would all cost more for food and clothing. Taxes and rates would consequently be greatly raised. We were told that Protection was needed against what was called "damping." It was worth recalling that not long ago one of the favourite arguments in support of Protection in America was that the English manufacturer sold goods below cost. This dumping argument, was a dangerous and double-edgqd weapon. It implied that the home producers sold toitheir own countrymen at a dear price and to the customer outside the gates at a low price. Were we in England prepared to pay a dear price at home so that the export trade might be en- couraged? Then we were asked to adopt a policy of rotaliation. Retaliation involved a sacrifice, espei- ally on the pact of the working-classes. What benefit would we derive by a duty of 10 per cent., if the Unitedl States and Germany put a 30 or even 50 per cent duty on our goods? Retaliation would do us a greater injury than we could possibly inflict on the foreigner. If the foreigner smote us on one cheek were we to smite ourselves on the other? We had not gained our present position in the commercial world by barricading our ports, but by superior technical skill, by manufacturing utility, by knowledge and busi- ness habits. We must rely on these weapons in the future, if we were to retain our high commercial position. Technical education, improved methods of production, and the study of foreign requirements, and the adaptation of goods were the weapons with which we must fight our commercial battles. MR. WESTBROOK A "FREE TRADER."

foreigner.) Nothing of the kind. The foreigner suffered from dumping. Over-protection in protected countries was caused by trusts and great combinations to make dividends, and caused the workingmen to pay higher prices for their food. We got the benefit of dumping. He would like Mr. Westbrook to accept a challenge to discuss the question of dumping of labour. Mr. Chamberlain's proposals, he affirmed with all the emphasis possible, would increase poverty and de- crease the amount of labour. Alluding to the McKinley tariff Mr. Jones said the immediate effect was that the steel trade of South Wales, which depended upon the United States, went down. Like staunch true Britons the manufacturers looked out for new markets and to-day the steel trade of South Wales was in a far better position than it was before the imposition of the tariff. Mr. Jones contended that in protected countries workingmen received less wages and worked longer under bad conditions. Free Trade was not responsible for the poverty and destitution in England. Last year was the best financial year we ever had. Eighty per cent of our import trade and 60 per cent of our export trade was transacted with foreign countries. Were we going to be the biggest fools in the world to fall out with these splendid customers? Only about one-seventh of our total sea- port trade was done with our self-governing colonies. A colonial preference was impossible unless •we were prepared to sacrifice the well-being of our industries and population in return for the dubious advantage of a small rebate in colonial duties on our manufacturers. We could not do this, and we would not do it. During Mr. _Lloyd Jones's speech, Mr. Williams rose excitedly several times to reply, but he was greeted with cries of "Sit down" and was not allowed to sub- mit any further arguments. The Chairman was cordially thanked for presiding on the proposition of Mr. H. J. Westbrook, seconded by Mr. McDermott.

Mr. H. J. Westbrook complimented both speakers on setting before them Mr. Chamberlain's proposals. He quite agreed that Mr. Jones would have preferred to talk on the broad subject of Free Trade and Protection. There was far greater scone for wandering away from the point. (Laughter.) He (Kr. Westbrook) was a Free Trader—as strong a Free Trader as any man in that room, (Laughter.) He saw Mr. England nodding his head—(laughter)—but he crave his word as an English- man that he was as strong a''Free Trader as any man in that room, and it was because he believed Mr. Chamber- lain's scheme was one of the methods of getting it that he supported the proposals. (A Voice: Never.) It was an appeal to workingmen, and he contended that the , working man was on the side of Mr. Chamberlain. The workingman adopted protection in his trades ußion, and he also protected himself by Factory Acts, Truck Acts, Fair Wages Clauses, and he was now only asked to go step further and complete the logic of his position. The workingman protected himself against sweating at home but left the door open for the products of sweat- ing abroad. He was now asked to complete the system and protect himself against the products of foreign sweating. (Applause.) He could not agree that dump- ing was not a very serious thing. He admitted that we us3d to dump our goods into foreign countries. But these countries had protected themselves against it and we ought to do the same. (Hear, hear.) Now that we had been stopped we must stop others from doing it. If foreigners handicapped our workmen, we must handicap their workmen, and if they gave us freedom of trade in their country we would do the same here. This question of dumping was a question of dumping labour. The opponents of Mr. Chamberlain's scheme put the cart before the horse. They only considered the consumer, whereas the producer ought to be considered first. (Hear, hear.) The workingman was both a producer and a consumer, and he must earn if he was to eat. They must first pro- tect that which enabled them to buy food. Mr. West- brook proceeded to quote figures showing that during the past decade there had been an increase of over 20 per cent in the number of persons employed in pro- tected countries.

ifiCENGLAND AND THE TARIFF PROPOSALS. Mr. E. England referred to Mr. Westbrook's asser- tion that he (Mr. Westbrook) was a Free Trader, and contended that no man could support the tariff pro- posals without being a protectionist. It was an im- possible and illogical conclusion to support preferential tariffs and at the same time hold Free Trade opinions. (Hear, hear.) Personally he (Mr. England) was an absolute Free Trader. He hoped they would be greater Free Traders 50 years hence than they were to-day. Their local Mr. Chamberlain—(laughter)—had just said that if the foreigner handicapped our workmen we ought to handicap the foreigner,, The foreigner did not handicap our workman, the foreigner handicapped him- self by his system of tariffs. (Hear, hear.) Mr. England proceeded tol quote from a speech of Mr. Chamberlain in which he referred to the screw trade. Although other countries put a duty on imported screws, English manufactured screws were sent into every country in the world and protected foreigners were unable to com- pete with them successfully. Mr. Chamberlain then went on to say that any proposal to tax corn was a proposal to put money into the pockets of landlords and any proposal to tax manufactures was a proposal to put profits into the pockets of parti- cular favoured manufacturers_ (Hear, hear). Mr. Chaplain was admittedly a friend of agriculture, but what did he say about the proposed duty of 2s a quarter on4wheat ? He said the thing was absurd, and it would require a duty of 20s before agriculture could receive any benefit. There was no doubt that the duty of 2s Tould very soon be increased if Mr. Chamberlain's scheme were adopted, but he thought the working men of the country would have more sense than agree to a tax on food. (Hear, hear). Advocates of protection were very fond of talking of the unemployed. Those who opposed the scheme said that better land laws were the true remedy. (Hear, hear). But what was the state of the unemployed in protected countries ? In Ger- many,four per centof the workers were out of employment whilst in America the per centage was six. In England the per centage was only two. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Westbrook went into the question of wages but the we ges in England had gone up in a greater pro- portion than in foreign countries. In the United Kingdom wares had increased 23 per cent, United States 10 per cents Germany 22 per centand France 14 per cent. In Germany, the workingman was crying out for Free Trade. One of the main objects of the German Socialist party was to secure Free Trade. If our system of Free Trade had been the wrong one for this country, we should have been getting poorer and poorer, but instead of that we had been getting richer and richer. We ex ported more goods to foreign countries than did Germany, and the United States put together. Mr. England proceeded to refer to the importance of our shipping trade which would certainly he injured by adopting any system of tariffs.
The Examiner, Saturday, March 5, 1904

div.head: MR. WILLIAMS AS A TRADES UNIONIST.
div.p: MR. WILLIAMS AS A TRADES UNIONIST.

Mr. W. L. WILLIAMS was the next speaker. He stood before them, he said, as a trade unionist. The union to which he belonged had rules protecting the members against the introduction into Warrington of goods made at places where the standard rate of wages was not paid Inithis country there were, according to Sir H. Camp- bell Bannerman, twelve millions of people on the verge of starvation. (A VOICE : How many in Germany?)—That, he contended,was due to the dumping which resulted from Free Trade and which - had the effect of throwing English workmen out of work or decreasing the amount of their employment It was quite correct that members of the shipping trade objected to protection, but they did so from personal motives because they knew that Protection woul d affect their trade. They ought not to consider simply one trade, but the whole system, and he was firmly convinced that Mr. Chamberlain's policy would greatly benefit the working classes. THE CONCLUDING SPEECHES.

Mr. McDermott, in a second speech, dealt with Mr. Lloyd Jones's argument that rates and taxes would be increased. Even if that were so, the money would remain in the country, and would be used by the Government for the benefit of the people. Mr. Lloyd Jones said our present position was gained by superior skill and commercial application. Many who °noosed Mr. Chamberlain's policy contended that Free Trade was responsible for that position, whilst others said we had been beaten by the superior skill of German and American workmen and the commercial methods-adopted in those countries. Mr. Chamber- lain's proposals were not put forward in any sense as a remedy for lack of skill on the part of the workmen, or lack of commercial enterprise by the manufacturers. These matters must be dealt with by the manufacturers and workmen themselves. Mr. Chamberlain had told them that a tariff of 2s. on corn would be sufficient to obtain the object he had in view, and he thought they might give him credit for knowing something about what he was speaking of. The nature of the imports and exports to and from this country had greatly changed in recent years. The greater volume of exports used to consist of manufactured goods, but now it was very largely raw materials. The imports, which before ere almost exclnsively raw materials, were now very largely manufactured goods. If Mr. Chamberlain's proposals were adopted, they !would inevitably result in a greater volume of trade in the country and an increase in employment and wages. He contended that as only the nature and the direction of the imports—which would be obtained from the colonies instead of from foreign countries —would be changed, the volume of our shipping trade would not be curtailed to any great extent. Where Mr. Chamberlain and his proposals were best known they were the best appreciated, as was evidenced by the South Birmingham result. Mr. E. Lloyd-Jones, contended that trade unionists were not protected in the sense of the Protection that Mr. Chamberlain put forward. (Cries 9f "Quite" and "No.") Trade unionists were protected from unjust and unfair conditions of labour. (Hear, hear.) They existed for workmen's rights and to protect them agai nit wrong doing,—(hear, hear)—but that was not the Pro- tection they were there to discuss. (Cries of "Yes.") Dealing with the dumping, Mr. Jones said it was caused by over-protection in the country from whioh the goods came. Who benefitted by dumping? (A voice: The

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

ingbi Football. By " Ovalist." There was nothing very daZzling about Warring- ton's play on Saturday, though they did beat Hull Kingston Rovers by 11 points to nil. In many res- pects the form of the homesters was such as to drive their supporters to despair. Behind the scrummage for instance, the homesters were very poorly repre- sented, the four centre men being far too slow in their movements to render very great service. The absence of Dickenson gave the Warrington Committee an opportunity of trying one of the experiments which has been so widely advocated of late, but instead of putting Fish in the centre position and giving Kenyon a chance at Warrington, they introduced Davies with the result that the attacking line was slower than ever. In his proper place Davies is a good man, but he does not possess the speed for three-quarter play. The Warrington wings are, of course, fast enough for anything, but their powers are of little avail when the slowness of the other backs results in the ball coming to them only on the touch-line.: It is the want of opportunity Fish and Harris get that has caused so many members to advocate a change in the positions and personnel of the backs.

Warrington were by no means 11 points better than the Rovers. The latter were a man short for half the game, and still they gave the home side plenty to do. A, fairer indication of the play by the score would hive been ten points to five, but fortune was not for the visitors! They had their share when operating at Craven-street on October 31st, for Warrington con- sidered themselves very unfortunate to lose by a penalty goal to nil. That defeat has now been avenged according to expectations. Since they came to Warrington as a second division team and won in hollow fashion by over 20 points, the Rovers have never done anything at Wilderspool.

Opinions differ as to whether the game was a good one or not. Certainly it was well-contested, but War- rington from my point of view were so ragged and unscientific in their methods as to quite spoil the dis- play. Up to half-time there was no score, though at least a couple of tries should have been put to Warrington's credit had the combination been even respectable. Afterwards, Fortune provided War-. rington with the opportunities they had failed to make—and they took them. Isherwood got posses- sion rather luckily at centre and with a fine dash he got through the defence and save Harris e, chance which was turned to profit in resolute style. Though tackled, the determined right-winger burst through. Not long after, Davies got away in similar style and some really good passing by the forwards resulted in Thomas scoring his first try for Warrington. One feature of this movement rather amused the crowd. When Davies got away, Fish ran alongside and made frantic efforts to attract the Welshman's attention, but to no purpose, he was looking in the other direction. A pass to Fish would have resulted in a try under the posts for he was splendidly placed, but he was fated not to score a try on Saturday. Near the close Hockenhall went off and Fish came centre but never got a pass. Meanwhile Isherwood picked up in the loose and ran behind the posts with an ease which proved that the Hull defence was caught napping. Fish kicked a goal.

Two efforts by the Rovers deserve mention. A fly.. kick by Davies failed and West sprinted away with the ball in front of him. After a fine run he just missed a try at the corner by inches. This was before Warrington had opened their account and if the speedy little wing man•had succeeded I fancy the Rovers would have taken a lo.of beating. Later on when only a try behind:Reed.made one of the best runs in the centre that has been seen on the Warring- ton ground this season and eventually got over though tackled a yard from the line. I was rather surprised that the try was disallowed. The effort certainly deserved the five points which would have accrued.

The forward argument was pretty well balanced, though, curiously enough tho Rovers got possession with far greater frequency when they were a man short. Starks was very conspicuous and played a good game, while the same may be said of Fairhurst and Thomas for Warrington. "Silver" seems to have renewed his youth. His cleverness in the loose was most marked. I was pleased to see Isherwood showing better form, especially as, during the first quarter he could do nothing right. Behind the scrum Bate and Hockenhall shaped Tar worse than they did in the rain and mud at Swinton. In fact if they had handled the ball anything like so well, the horns score must have been nearly doubled. Some- how or other Warrington cannot get the half-back positions filled in a satisfactory manner. Whichever pair are selected they are never reliable for more than a match or two.

The top positions in the League underwent a further change on Saturday, for the great performances of Bradford and Broughton over Leeds and Hunslet opened out the possibilities still more. Salford and Bradford now tie for the top position, but any one of the first five clubs may ultimately secure the champion- ship and he would be a clever prophet who could forecast the winner. In my view, however, Bradford and Broughton are the best teams in the competition and the one point lead of the former club might just possibly carry them through. The League table up-to-date, is as follows . : For. Against. _ _ _ _

Warrington will be afforded an opportunity to-day of avenging defeat by Oldham on November 7th. That day the homesters had much the better of the play but Oldham got the points,chiefly because the absence of Fish made so much difference to the team. Perhaps he will make amends by winning the match for War- rington at Watersheddings. In recent seasons War- rington have given some good displays at Oldbam,and it would be a grand performance if they could best the" rough-yeds " to-day.. The latter are nothinr, like so formidable a combination as they used to be, and Warrington should remember that they have not lost a match in the Manchester district this season. After defeating T3roughton and Salford, and drawing at Swinton,surely they can do as well at Oldham.

A full team has been selected as follows: Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harris, threequarters ; Bate and Davies, half backs ; Board- man, Thomas, Cook, Edmondson, Naylor, Jolley,Lunt, and Harmer, forwards. lam sorry to see that Fair- hurst has been dropped. On last Saturday's form he should have been one of the first men selected. Fearful and wonderful are the ways of the Warrington Committee at times!
Compensation Against Pearson and Knowles

At Wigan on Tuesday, Mary Alice Sinclair, of James-street, Lower Ince, was awarded £221 4s. compensation against the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, for the loss of her husband, a drawer, who was killed by a fall of roof last Decem- , be r.

inferences from that fact. However, he would acquit them of the charge of introducing party politics. He (Alderman Pierpoint) wished to bring the Council back to a sense of what he called fair justice in the matter. He quite understood the position which had been taken up by Councillor Stott. It was a fairly logical one, and judging from his political creed he was perfectly justified- _

Councillor STOTT : I didn't object to it from a. political standpoint. Alderman PIERPOINT continuing, said that if he had made a mistake he begged to withdraw it Alderman Bennett was a great namer of streets, no doubt with the- best intentions, but some of the names had been ex- tremely absurd, and would have been better left alone. One street for instance, was named Barbauld street. The name to his mind was not very euphonious, and so far asile was concerned as an old inhabitant he might say that Mrs. Barbauld never went down that street,because there was no street there when she lived. If the street had been named after an old family like Leyland, he could have understood it. As to the point of gratitude he contended that the name of Crosfield would have been given to the park behind the Town Hall, but for party purposes. (Hear, hear).They were always willing to accept, he would not call it the charity,but the dona- tions of the Croslield family. Only a few months ago Mrs.tCrosfleld in honour of her deceased husband erected one of the finest additions to the park in the shape of a new conservatory. Alderman SMETHURST: And it is called the "Cros- field_Conservatory."
_ Alderman PIERPOINT: I hope the Council will put aside 2.11 party politics. Councillor MA.GINN rose to .peak, but was ruled out of order.

Councillor DODDS said he thought if anyone present could claim to be outside political parties he could. He thought that in a matter of this kind they should try and avoid political discussion. He was certain Alderman Bennett in what he said had no idea of mak- ing this a political matter and he hoped they would vote entirely without any idea of party. They should give honour to whom honour was due' and if it was due to the Crosfields, they should give it to Crosflelds, and if it was due to Lord Lilford they should give it to him.

Councillor LORD said the cost of the land was £425 per acre—about a penny per yard. Councillor TINNION said he was sorry the discussion had taken the spirit it had,and Alderman Bennett ought to have been man enough to acknowledge that he had been fairly defeated at the committee meeting. He was sorry that he had thought it desirable to bring the matter forward that night. He hoped the Council would decide the matter upon a proper basis, and that the Crosfield family would he recognized. There were conditions other than the actual price attaching to the bargain. The Council would have some streets to make adjoining the land. On a vote being taken there voted : FOR THE AMENDMENT. AGAINST.
